JOIN applications a ON a.id = c.application_id
WHERE cs.resolved_at IS NULL;
  2. Operators on both sides should NOT initiate switchovers. Switchover is the wrong operation here — it migrates an application, but here the application is fine; only the control link is broken.

docs.title: Manual reconcile after partition heals
docs.text:
1. Agents in site B reconnect; the offline buffer replays.
  2. Obtain fresh checks and compare them with the last recorded state; distinguish buffered observations from new evidence.
  3. Inspect affected operation/command histories and the external provider's current job/resource state. Record the reconciliation before retrying an action with an unknown effect. Do not infer an automatic reconciliation workflow or task resume from event replay.

RTO/RPO: measure reconnection, new checks, reconciled operations and missing events. A bounded offline buffer cannot guarantee zero loss for an arbitrary partition. Database records and external effects have separate recovery boundaries.

docs.title: 6. Database corruption
docs.text: PostgreSQL reports invalid page header, tuple concurrently updated, or refuses to start. Append-only tables show inconsistencies.

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
# Verify corruption with a PostgreSQL self-check
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SELECT count(*) FROM action_log;"
# If this errors with relation-block corruption, escalate.

# Recommended: pg_amcheck (PostgreSQL 14+)
pg_amcheck --all $DATABASE_URL > amcheck.log 2>&1
grep -i error amcheck.log

docs.title: Read-only fallback
docs.text:
Until corruption is resolved, switch the backend into a read-only failsafe by setting READ_ONLY=true. In that mode the backend keeps serving authentication, all GET requests, health probes and the break-glass endpoint, but rejects every state-mutating request (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable and Retry-After: 60. Authentication endpoints under /api/v1/auth/, /api/v1/oidc/, /api/v1/saml/ and /api/v1/break-glass/ are exempted so an operator can still log in. Otherwise:

  1. Scale backend to 0 to prevent writes. 
    kubectl scale -n appcontrol deployment/appcontrol-backend --replicas=0
  2. Take a fresh pg_dump even of the corrupted DB, to preserve the maximum possible data: 
    pg_dump -Fc -f preserve_before_pitr.dump $DATABASE_URL

docs.title: Point-in-time recovery (PITR)
docs.text:
If WAL archiving is enabled:

# Restore base backup
pg_basebackup -h archive-host -D /var/lib/postgresql/data -X stream

# Configure recovery target time
cat > /var/lib/postgresql/data/recovery.signal <<EOF
EOF
echo "recovery_target_time = '2026-05-13 10:30:00 UTC'" >> /var/lib/postgresql/data/postgresql.auto.conf
echo "restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://wal/%f %p'" >> /var/lib/postgresql/data/postgresql.auto.conf

# Start PostgreSQL — it replays WAL up to the target
systemctl start postgresql

docs.title: Validation queries
docs.text:
-- Count rows in append-only tables — must match the last known-good values
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM action_log)        AS action_log,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM state_transitions) AS state_transitions,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM switchover_log)    AS switchover_log,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM check_events)      AS check_events;

-- Last action_log entry should be ≤ recovery_target_time
SELECT max(created_at) FROM action_log;

-- Verify FK integrity
SELECT al.id FROM action_log al
LEFT JOIN users u ON u.id = al.user_id
WHERE u.id IS NULL LIMIT 5;

docs.title: Bring the system back up
docs.text:
kubectl scale -n appcontrol deployment/appcontrol-backend --replicas=1
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- curl -s localhost:3000/ready

RTO: 1–4 h depending on backup size and WAL volume. RPO: WAL archiving interval (typically 1–5 min) or backup cadence.

docs.title: 7. Mass agent disconnection (>50% offline)
docs.text: A large fraction of agents goes offline at once — usually after a network event, a DNS outage, or a corporate firewall rule change.

docs.title: Triage
docs.text:
-- Count agents by connection state
SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE last_heartbeat_at > now() - interval '5 minutes') AS connected,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE last_heartbeat_at <= now() - interval '5 minutes') AS disconnected
FROM agents WHERE is_active = true;

-- Identify common pattern (subnet, label)
SELECT labels->>'datacenter' AS datacenter, count(*) AS offline_agents
FROM agents
WHERE last_heartbeat_at <= now() - interval '5 minutes'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY offline_agents DESC;

docs.title: Prioritize critical apps
docs.text:
-- Which applications have ≥ 1 component on a disconnected agent?
SELECT DISTINCT a.id, a.name, a.tags->>'criticality' AS criticality
FROM applications a
JOIN components c ON c.application_id = a.id
JOIN agents ag ON ag.id = c.agent_id
WHERE ag.last_heartbeat_at <= now() - interval '5 minutes'
ORDER BY criticality DESC NULLS LAST;

docs.title: Batch reconnection
docs.text:
Most agents recover on their own once the network event clears. For agents that do not:

# Distribute a re-enrollment script via your config-management tool
# (Ansible, Puppet, SaltStack)

# Each host runs:
sudo appcontrol-agent --enroll https://gateway.example.com:4443 --token <token>
sudo systemctl restart appcontrol-agent

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
After a mass disconnection, file an incident report and inspect:

-- What did the heartbeat monitor do?
SELECT count(*), trigger FROM state_transitions
WHERE next_state = 'UNREACHABLE' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 hour'
GROUP BY trigger;

RTO: typically self-healing within 5–30 min. RPO: 0 thanks to the agent offline buffer.

docs.title: 8. Site loss requiring full DR switchover
docs.text:
The primary site is completely unavailable for one or more applications. The DR site is healthy.

The engine can sequence configured source/target procedures and collect their results. A real site-loss procedure also needs recoverable data, target capacity, a safe source-stop/neutralization contract and an explicit traffic step. If the required evidence cannot be obtained, do not proceed merely because the source agent is unreachable. The local simulation does not qualify those infrastructure/data guarantees. See User Guide — DR Switchover.

docs.title: The 6 phases and rollback semantics
docs.text:
Phase Current behavior Cancellation / return 1 PREPARE — record the selected source/target and intent Cancellation before operational changes 2 VALIDATE — check target mapping, agents and required recovery contract Cancellation before operational changes 3 STOP_SOURCE — execute source stop and positive stop checks Automatic rollback is refused from this phase onward 4 SYNC — currently returns skipped; no data replication or restore is performed Verify the external data-recovery procedure before advancing 5 START_TARGET — execute verified target restart, then activate its component/site contract Reconcile partial changes; a source return needs an explicit verified procedure 6 COMMIT — recheck target infrastructure, integrity, network, health and post-start evidence No automatic traffic switch or reverse recovery

The site/component contract becomes active after verified START_TARGET; COMMIT supplies another set of fresh checks. Neither step changes the client's load balancer/DNS. A completed AppControl switchover is therefore distinct from confirmed client traffic on the target.

Cancellation is supported only while the recorded phase is PREPARE or VALIDATE. It journals ROLLBACK/completed for the same UUID with operational_changes=false and source_restored=false: the source was left unchanged, not restored. After operational changes, verify/reconstruct the source and use an explicit reverse switchover and traffic procedure. Automatic data synchronization, external fencing and post-change rollback remain integration/implementation work.

docs.title: Step-by-step from a site-loss event
docs.text:
1. Confirm the site is lost. Distinguish from a transient network partition (§5). If unsure, wait — never switch over on a flapping primary.
  2. Verify DR agents are healthy. 
    SELECT count(*) FROM agents WHERE is_active = true AND labels->>'site' = 'dr';
  3. Review the target recovery contract. Verify the profile/site mappings and preview the target recovery plan before starting the switchover. Confirm all required checks, source-stop evidence, the external data procedure and traffic/return procedures with their owners. SYNC does not enforce a data-recovery gate today; do not treat an unimplemented check as passed.
  4. Launch the switchover with explicit mode.
  5. FULL for total migration.
  6. SELECTIVE if only a subset of components is recoverable on DR. The current API accepts FULL or a nonempty SELECTIVE scope. PROGRESSIVE is not supported by this path. Nested applications, fan_out and manual-task components are blocked by the recovery contract.
  7. Monitor each phase in the UI or via API. 
    curl -s https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/<id>/switchover/status \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq
  8. Commit when validated. Once START_TARGET succeeds, COMMIT collects fresh target checks. Verify the terminal COMMIT/completed history and the associated recovery operation outcomes.
  9. Route and verify traffic explicitly. Execute the client's authorized network step, observe the target from the actual client entry point, and validate the business transaction and recovered data. Record its result separately; a failed route change is not successful service recovery.

docs.title: Roll back at each step
docs.text:
Recorded phase Available action PREPARE / VALIDATE POST /api/v1/apps/<id>/switchover/rollback cancels before operational changes; source/traffic stay unchanged STOP_SOURCE / SYNC / START_TARGET Automatic rollback is refused; reconcile changes and follow the verified source recovery/return procedure COMMIT / completed Verify the source and perform an explicit reverse switchover plus the separate traffic/data procedure

RTO/RPO: measure from the incident through accepted client traffic and recovered data. The phase count or completion record does not establish a production RTO/RPO; application-data loss depends on the actual backup/replication procedure and its measured recovery point.

docs.title: 9. Doomsday — primary + DR simultaneously lost
docs.text: Both sites are gone. The backend, both gateways, and both replicas of every application are unavailable.

docs.title: Recovery sequence
docs.text:
1. Provision new infrastructure. Order: PostgreSQL → backend → at least one gateway → frontend.
  2. Restore PostgreSQL from off-site backup. See Backup & Restore. Verify cross-region or cold-storage backups; if your only backups were on the lost sites, AppControl audit history is lost.
  3. Restore the CA private key. The CA is stored in pki_authorities (encrypted). If the CA is lost, all agents must be re-enrolled from scratch.
  4. Bring up the backend. Migrations run automatically.
  5. Provision a fresh gateway. Issue a new gateway cert (CLI: appctl pki issue-gateway).
  6. Distribute agent binaries and re-enrollment tokens via your config-management tool.
  7. Reconnect agents and verify each application.

docs.title: What you cannot recover without backups
docs.text:
• action_log, state_transitions, check_events, switchover_log — these are append-only audit; if your last backup was T-24 h, everything after T-24 h is gone.
  • config_versions — same.
  • Component state caches will be rebuilt by the next health check, so this is recoverable.

docs.title: Cross-region backup is mandatory
docs.text:
To make this scenario survivable, your PostgreSQL backups must be replicated off-site (different region/provider). A backup co-located with the primary site does not help.

RTO: days. RPO: last off-site backup (typically 24 h for cold-storage daily, 1 h for cross-region streaming).

docs.title: DR drill checklist (run quarterly)
docs.text: Practicing recovery is the only way to verify your RTO/RPO claims. Run this drill on a non-production AppControl instance every 3 months.

docs.title: Quarter N — drill agenda
docs.text:
• §3 — Single-gateway loss. Kill the only gateway pod; verify all agents reconnect within 1 min.
  • §4 — HA gateway failover. Kill one of two gateways; measure agent reconnect time.
  • §7 — Mass disconnection. Block egress from a subnet for 10 min; verify agents recover from offline buffer.
  • §8 — Full switchover. Run a FULL switchover on a non-prod app; measure RTO end-to-end.
  • §8 — Cancellation before changes. Cancel in PREPARE and VALIDATE; verify the same UUID has terminal cancellation evidence, source/route remain unchanged and advancing is refused.
  • §8 — Return after changes. Verify automatic rollback is refused after STOP_SOURCE; rehearse the explicit source recovery, reverse switchover and traffic procedure.
  • §1 — Backend interruption. Stop the backend during an isolated recovery exercise; reconcile the external job and recorded operation before any retry. Do not expect automatic task resume.
  • §2 — Backend + DB recovery. Restore a backup into a staging cluster; verify row counts, FK integrity, and agent reconnection.
  • §6 — PITR drill. Restore PostgreSQL to T-1h on a sandbox; run the validation queries.
  • Document RTO/RPO achieved. Compare to last quarter; investigate regressions.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
After each drill, export the audit trail and file it for regulatory evidence:

curl https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/reports/dora-drill \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -o "dr-drill-$(date +%Y-Q%q).pdf"

The drill record is itself evidence under DORA Article 11 (continuity testing). See Compliance — DORA / NIS2.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Backup & Restore — how to take, verify, and restore backups
  • High Availability — preventing some of these scenarios
  • Runbooks — incident-scoped step-by-step procedures
  • Troubleshooting — symptom-to-fix mapping for non-DR issues
  • Compliance — DORA / NIS2 — what regulators expect from DR documentation

docs.title: Plan: Dynamic Config Push & Application Suspension
Objectif
docs.text:
1. Push dynamique : L'agent reçoit automatiquement les configs quand une map est importée/modifiée
  2. Suspension de map : Possibilité de "mettre en pause" une application (l'agent arrête les checks)

docs.title: 1. Migration SQL
docs.text:
-- V031__application_suspension.sql
ALTER TABLE applications ADD COLUMN is_suspended BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false;
ALTER TABLE applications ADD COLUMN suspended_at TIMESTAMPTZ;
ALTER TABLE applications ADD COLUMN suspended_by UUID REFERENCES users(id);

-- Index pour filtrer les apps actives
CREATE INDEX idx_applications_suspended ON applications (organization_id, is_suspended);

docs.title: 2. Modifier send_config_to_agent
docs.text:
Exclure les composants des applications suspendues :

SELECT c.id, c.name, c.check_cmd, ...
FROM components c
JOIN applications a ON c.application_id = a.id
WHERE c.agent_id = $1
  AND a.is_suspended = false  -- NOUVEAU: exclure les apps suspendues

docs.title: 3. Fonction utilitaire push_config_to_affected_agents
docs.text:
Créer une fonction réutilisable qui : 1. Trouve tous les agents affectés par une liste de component_ids ou application_id 2. Envoie un UpdateConfig à chaque agent

// Dans backend/src/websocket/mod.rs ou un nouveau module
pub async fn push_config_to_affected_agents(
    state: &Arc<AppState>,
    application_id: Option<Uuid>,
    component_ids: Option<Vec<Uuid>>,
) {
    // 1. Trouver les agent_ids distincts
    let agent_ids: Vec<Uuid> = if let Some(app_id) = application_id {
        sqlx::query_scalar(
            "SELECT DISTINCT agent_id FROM components
             WHERE application_id = $1 AND agent_id IS NOT NULL"
        )
        .bind(app_id)
        .fetch_all(&state.db)
        .await
        .unwrap_or_default()
    } else if let Some(comp_ids) = component_ids {
        sqlx::query_scalar(
            "SELECT DISTINCT agent_id FROM components
             WHERE id = ANY($1) AND agent_id IS NOT NULL"
        )
        .bind(&comp_ids)
        .fetch_all(&state.db)
        .await
        .unwrap_or_default()
    } else {
        return;
    };

    // 2. Envoyer UpdateConfig à chaque agent
    for agent_id in agent_ids {
        if state.ws_hub.is_agent_connected(agent_id) {
            send_config_to_agent(state, agent_id).await;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 4. Points d'appel du push dynamique
docs.text: Événement Action Import wizard termine push_config_to_affected_agents(app_id) POST /components push_config_to_affected_agents(component_ids) PUT /components/:id push_config_to_affected_agents(component_ids) DELETE /components/:id push_config_to_affected_agents(component_ids) PUT /components/:id (agent_id change) Push aux 2 agents (ancien + nouveau) POST /applications/:id/suspend push_config_to_affected_agents(app_id) POST /applications/:id/resume push_config_to_affected_agents(app_id)

docs.title: 5. API Suspend/Resume
docs.text:
// PUT /api/v1/applications/:id/suspend
pub async fn suspend_application(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    Path(app_id): Path<Uuid>,
    Extension(user): Extension<AuthUser>,
) -> Result<Json<Application>, AppError> {
    // Vérifier permission >= manage

    sqlx::query(
        "UPDATE applications
         SET is_suspended = true, suspended_at = now(), suspended_by = $2, updated_at = now()
         WHERE id = $1"
    )
    .bind(app_id)
    .bind(user.id)
    .execute(&state.db)
    .await?;

    // Notifier les agents
    push_config_to_affected_agents(&state, Some(app_id), None).await;

    // Log action
    log_action(&state.db, user.id, "suspend_application", "application", app_id, json!({})).await;

    // Retourner l'app mise à jour
    get_application(&state.db, app_id).await
}

// PUT /api/v1/applications/:id/resume
pub async fn resume_application(...) {
    // Inverse de suspend
}

docs.title: 6. Comportement côté Agent
docs.text:
Quand l'agent reçoit un UpdateConfig : - Il compare avec sa config actuelle - Les composants absents de la nouvelle config sont retirés du scheduler - Les nouveaux composants sont ajoutés au scheduler - Les composants existants sont mis à jour si les paramètres changent

C'est déjà implémenté dans scheduler.update_components() : 

pub async fn update_components(&self, configs: Vec<ComponentConfig>) {
    // ...
    // Remove stale check state for components no longer in the config
    check_state.retain(|id, _| new_ids.contains(id));
    // Replace component configs
    components.clear();
    for config in configs {
        components.insert(config.component_id, config);
    }
}

docs.title: 7. Frontend
docs.text:
• Ajouter bouton "Suspend" / "Resume" dans la toolbar de la map
  • Afficher un badge "SUSPENDED" sur les maps suspendues
  • Les composants d'une map suspendue affichent un état visuel distinct

docs.title: Fichiers à modifier
docs.text: Fichier Modification migrations/V031__application_suspension.sql Nouveau crates/backend/src/websocket/mod.rs Modifier send_config_to_agent, ajouter push_config_to_affected_agents crates/backend/src/api/apps.rs Ajouter suspend_application, resume_application crates/backend/src/api/import_wizard.rs Appeler push_config_to_affected_agents après import crates/backend/src/api/components.rs Appeler push_config_to_affected_agents dans CRUD frontend/src/api/apps.ts Ajouter hooks useSuspendApp, useResumeApp frontend/src/components/maps/MapToolbar.tsx Ajouter bouton Suspend/Resume frontend/src/pages/DashboardPage.tsx Afficher badge SUSPENDED

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
1. Importer une map → agent reçoit immédiatement la config
  2. Suspendre une map → agent retire les composants du scheduler
  3. Reprendre une map → agent reçoit à nouveau les composants
  4. Modifier un composant → agent reçoit la config mise à jour
  5. Changer l'agent_id d'un composant → les 2 agents sont notifiés

docs.title: Fan-out clusters
docs.text:
Use fan-out mode when every instance of a clustered component must be checked and operated independently. Each member has its own agent, commands and state; AppControl derives the parent component state from those member states.

Use aggregate mode instead when one command already checks or operates the whole cluster, such as a vendor cluster-management command.

docs.title: Health policies
docs.text:
Set cluster_mode to fan_out, then choose cluster_health_policy:

Policy Parent is running when all_healthy every active member is running any_healthy at least one active member is running quorum a strict majority of active members is running threshold_pct the configured cluster_min_healthy_pct is reached

Members intentionally stopped by an operator are excluded from the active health denominator. When every member is stopped, the parent is stopped.

docs.title: Commands and state
docs.text:
The parent component can define the default check, start and stop commands. A member can override each command. Both shell and native commands are supported; a member override takes precedence over the parent command. Inherited native commands are templated with the member hostname and optional installation path.

The backend marks a member STARTING or STOPPING when its command is dispatched. The next member health check confirms RUNNING or STOPPED. A failed ordinary health check first produces DEGRADED, then FAILED; a failed check after Stop confirms STOPPED.

docs.title: Operating members
docs.text:
From a component's Members tab:

  • Start or Stop one member to operate and wait for that member independently.
  • Select members and use the bulk buttons to dispatch them in parallel.
  • Start or Stop the parent component to use the application's normal dependency sequencing across all eligible members.

A parent can already be RUNNING under any_healthy, quorum, or threshold_pct while some members are stopped. Starting the parent still starts those stopped members.

docs.title: Limiting concurrency
docs.text:
The default parallel mode dispatches all eligible members immediately. For large tiers, set:

{
  "cluster_mode": "fan_out",
  "cluster_concurrency_mode": "batched",
  "cluster_batch_size": 3
}

AppControl dispatches one wave, waits for the members in that wave to reach their target state (or time out), and then dispatches the next wave. It does not wait for the parent aggregate between waves, because later members have not received their commands yet.

Importable examples are listed in the repository's examples/README.md.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
This page defines every term used across the AppControl documentation. Use it as a quick reference when reading the User Guide, Architecture, or Security Architecture.

Entries are listed alphabetically. Each entry includes a cross-reference to the page where the concept is detailed.

docs.title: Index
docs.text: A · B · C · D · E · F · G · H · I · M · N · O · P · Q · R · S · T · U · V · W

docs.title: Action log
docs.text: The append-only PostgreSQL table (action_log) that records every user-initiated action before it is executed. Each row contains user_id, action_type, target_id, details (JSONB), and the timestamp. No UPDATE or DELETE is allowed — the table is the regulatory evidence required by DORA Article 16. See Compliance — DORA / NIS2.

docs.title: Advisory mode
docs.text: Operational mode in which AppControl observes components but never executes start/stop/restart. The agent reports check results normally, but the backend rejects any execute command. Used during onboarding to build confidence in the dependency map before granting operational autonomy. See README — Garde-fous par conception.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text: The lightweight Rust binary (~8 MB static) installed on every monitored host. It executes health checks, integrity checks, and start/stop/rebuild commands; it sends deltas to its gateway over mTLS WebSocket. Survives crashes thanks to double-fork + setsid process detachment. See Agent Installation.

docs.title: Aggregate cluster
docs.text: Cluster mode in which the cluster is represented by a single component whose state is computed by the check_cmd itself (e.g. an Oracle RAC srvctl status script). The cluster's members are cosmetic — there is one FSM, one set of commands. Contrast with fan-out cluster. Defined in migration V035 and V049.

docs.title: API key
docs.text: Non-interactive credential for schedulers, CI/CD pipelines, and CLI usage. Format: ac_<random>. The plaintext is shown once at creation; the backend stores only its SHA-256 hash in the api_keys table. API keys inherit the permissions of their owning user. See Configuration — API Keys.

docs.title: Application
docs.text: The top-level operational entity in AppControl. An application is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of components plus metadata: name, primary site, optional DR site, tags, and per-application settings. Stored in the applications table. See User Guide — Application Management.

docs.title: Approval workflow
docs.text: The 4-eyes mechanism that requires a second approver before executing a high-risk operation (switchover, rebuild, break-glass). Configured per operation risk level. See Security Architecture §9.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: The collection of append-only event tables — action_log, state_transitions, check_events, switchover_log, config_versions — that together provide the DORA-compliant record of what happened, who did it, when, and why. See Backup & Restore for retention guidance.

docs.title: Auto-discovery
docs.text: The feature that lets an agent scan its host for running processes, listening ports, and service definitions, then propose a draft topology. The operator reviews and promotes the draft to a real application. See User Guide — Auto-Discovery.

docs.title: Auto-PKI
docs.text: Deployment mode in which the backend generates a per-organization CA on first startup. Agents enroll via POST /api/v1/enroll to obtain mTLS certificates. Eliminates manual cert handling. See Configuration — TLS Modes.

docs.title: Bastion
docs.text: A privileged control-plane agent used to execute both infra_check_cmd and rebuild_infra_cmd against another host. Configured via components.rebuild_agent_id. It is intentionally separate from the runtime agent: the bastion remains available when the target VM has failed and is typically the only host with the credentials and network reach to query the cloud inventory or invoke the approved XL Release/Ansible workflow. If none is configured, AppControl falls back to the runtime agent for backward compatibility. See Backend CLAUDE.md — Rebuild Engine.

docs.title: Binding profile
docs.text: A named mapping of component → agent for an application, used during import and DR switchover. Examples: prod, dr, bench. Exactly one binding profile is active per application at any time. Stored in binding_profiles and binding_profile_mappings (migration V030).

docs.title: Break-glass
docs.text: Emergency access procedure using pre-provisioned accounts whose credentials are stored in an external vault. Activation triggers immediate alerts to all admins, time-limits the session (default 60 min), tags every action with break_glass: true, and rotates the password after use. See Security Architecture §10.

docs.title: CA (Certificate Authority)
docs.text: The root authority that signs all gateway and agent certificates. AppControl supports three setups: per-organization auto-generated CA, enterprise PKI, or cert-manager (Kubernetes). The CA private key must be backed up and protected — losing it forces re-enrollment of every component. See Hardening.

docs.title: Check event
docs.text: A single row in the check_events table representing one execution of a check command on one component. Includes check_type (health | integrity | post_start | infrastructure), exit_code, truncated stdout, and duration_ms. The table is partitioned by month and append-only. See migrations/V005.

docs.title: Check type
docs.text:
One of the four kinds of probes AppControl runs against a component:

Type Frequency Drives FSM? Purpose health every check_interval_seconds (default 30) Yes "Is the process alive?" integrity every 5 min or on-demand No "Is the data consistent?" post_start once after start No Initial smoke test after start infrastructure on-demand only No "Is the OS / FS / prereqs OK?"

See also Diagnostic levels.

docs.title: Cluster
docs.text:
A multi-host deployment of a single logical component. AppControl supports two modes:

  • Aggregate — one FSM, one set of commands, the check_cmd rolls up cluster state.
  • Fan-out — each member is a first-class monitored entity with its own agent, commands, and state.

The chosen mode is stored in components.cluster_mode. See migration V049.

docs.title: Cluster health policy
docs.text:
For fan-out clusters, the rule that derives the parent component's FSM state from its members' states. Stored in components.cluster_health_policy (V049).

Policy Component is RUNNING if … all_healthy every member is RUNNING any_healthy at least one member is RUNNING quorum strictly more than half the members are RUNNING threshold_pct at least cluster_min_healthy_pct % of members are RUNNING

docs.title: Component
docs.text: A single managed process or service inside an application. Stored in the components table. A component has a type, an owning agent, optional commands (check_cmd, start_cmd, stop_cmd, integrity_check_cmd, infra_check_cmd, rebuild_cmd, rebuild_infra_cmd), timeouts, and visual position. See Component types.

docs.title: Component types
docs.text: Built-in catalog values for components.component_type: database, middleware, appserver, webfront, service, batch, custom, application (the last lets a component reference another application — see Referenced app). Migration V031 removed the SQL CHECK constraint, so any string is now accepted; the component catalog defines display attributes for each type.

docs.title: Config version
docs.text: A snapshot of an application's configuration captured in the config_versions table on every change. Stores both before and after as JSONB, plus the user, timestamp, and change type. Append-only; provides DORA Article 8(2) traceability for the dependency map.

docs.title: Cross-site probe
docs.text: The backend probe (every 5 min) that asks the passive site's agent to run a component's check_cmd. If it returns 0, the component is flagged as "running on the wrong site" — a split-brain warning. See User Guide — Cross-Site Probe.

docs.title: Custom command
docs.text: An operator-defined per-component command (log rotation, cache flush, etc.) stored in component_commands. Each custom command declares a min_permission_level (default operate) and an optional confirmation requirement.

docs.title: DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)
docs.text: The structure of an application's components and their dependencies. AppControl enforces acyclicity: import or edit operations that would introduce a cycle are rejected. The sequencer uses Kahn's algorithm to compute start/stop levels. See Architecture — DAG Sequencing.

docs.title: Delta sync
docs.text: The agent's policy of sending a CheckResult only when the result changes (different exit_code than the last one). Reduces gateway and backend load by ~95 % on stable systems. See Architecture — Health Check Cycle.

docs.title: Dependency
docs.text: A directed edge from one component to another, stored in the dependencies table. AppControl currently treats every dependency as a strong dependency: a parent must be RUNNING before its dependents start. See also Strong / Weak dependency.

docs.title: Diagnostic levels
docs.text:
The three independent probes that together describe a component's health:

Level Name Command field Drives FSM? 1 Health check_cmd Yes 2 Integrity integrity_check_cmd No 3 Infrastructure infra_check_cmd No

The diagnostic engine combines the three exit codes into a recommendation (Healthy, Restart, AppRebuild, InfraRebuild). See Architecture — 3-Level Diagnostic + Rebuild.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: See Auto-discovery.

docs.title: DORA
docs.text: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 — Digital Operational Resilience Act. Applies to financial entities and their critical ICT providers in the EU. Effective 17 January 2025. AppControl maps to Articles 8 (inventory + mapping), 11 (continuity testing), 12 (reconstruction), 16 (incident records), 25 (cyber scenarios). See Compliance — DORA / NIS2.

docs.title: DR (Disaster Recovery)
docs.text: The capability to migrate an application from its primary site to a secondary site. In AppControl, DR is a first-class operation with a 6-phase switchover engine. Not to be confused with DRaaS (cloud-hosted DR services). See Disaster Recovery.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: Simulation mode for any operation: validates the DAG, checks permissions and agent reachability, reports the expected execution sequence, and exits. No state change. Recommended before every switchover. See User Guide — Dry Run.

docs.title: Enrollment token
docs.text: A single-use (or limited-use) credential, prefixed ac_enroll_, presented by an agent or gateway to obtain its mTLS certificate from the backend. The backend stores only the SHA-256 hash; tokens declare a scope (agent or gateway), an optional max_uses, and a valid_hours window (default 24 h). See Agent Installation §3.

docs.title: Error branch
docs.text: The failed component plus all its downstream dependents. Rendered pink in the map view. The "Restart error branch" operation stops the branch (top-down), restarts the root cause, and brings up dependents (bottom-up). See User Guide — Error Branch Restart.

docs.title: Effective permission
docs.text: The maximum of the user's direct permission on an app and the permissions granted via every team they belong to. Computed by core::permissions::effective_permission() and refreshed on every API call. See Permissions.

docs.title: Fan-out cluster
docs.text: Cluster mode in which each member (host, instance) is a first-class entity with its own agent assignment, its own override commands, and its own FSM state. The parent component's state is derived from members' states by the cluster health policy. Defined in cluster_members and cluster_member_state (migration V049).

docs.title: FSM (Finite State Machine)
docs.text: The state model that drives every component. States: UNKNOWN, RUNNING, STOPPED, FAILED, DEGRADED, STARTING, STOPPING, UNREACHABLE. Transitions are validated by common::fsm::is_valid_transition() (crates/common/src/fsm.rs). Every transition is logged to state_transitions. See Architecture — FSM State Machine.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text: A stateless WebSocket relay that sits between agents and the backend. Each network zone (PRD, DR, DMZ) typically has its own gateway. The gateway terminates mTLS from agents, forwards traffic to the backend, holds no database connection, and exposes POST /enroll for token-based agent enrollment. See Configuration — Gateway.

docs.title: Heartbeat
docs.text: The 60-second-interval message an agent sends to the gateway containing CPU, memory, and system info. Missing 3 consecutive heartbeats (default 180 s — organizations.heartbeat_timeout_seconds) marks the agent stale; the heartbeat monitor task transitions its managed components to UNREACHABLE. See Backend CLAUDE.md — Heartbeat Monitor.

docs.title: High availability (HA)
docs.text: Deployment mode where the backend runs as multiple replicas behind a load balancer with HA_MODE=true (rate limiting moves to PostgreSQL). Gateways are stateless; agents implement client-side failover across multiple gateways. See High Availability.

docs.title: Hosting
docs.text: A logical grouping of sites by physical datacenter or cloud region. Example: hosting "DC Paris" contains sites prod-paris and staging-paris. During switchover, the UI distinguishes intra-hosting from cross-hosting failovers. Stored in the hostings table (migration V046). See User Guide — Hostings.

docs.title: Infrastructure check
docs.text: Level-3 diagnostic probe (infra_check_cmd). On-demand only; informational. Verifies from the configured bastion that the target VM, OS, filesystem and infrastructure prerequisites exist. Runtime connectivity and required network flows remain separate evidence: a reachable VM does not prove that an application port is open. See Diagnostic levels.

docs.title: Integrity check
docs.text: Level-2 diagnostic probe (integrity_check_cmd). Runs every 5 minutes or on-demand. Verifies data consistency (e.g. transaction log alignment, replica lag). Does not drive the FSM. See Diagnostic levels.

docs.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
docs.text: A standardized protocol for connecting AI agents (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, …) to external tools. AppControl exposes a native MCP server with 7 tools (status, diagnose, start/stop/restart, switchover, rebuild). The MCP server runs as a sub-module of the backend, available over stdio or HTTP. See crates/backend/src/mcp/.

docs.title: mTLS
docs.text: Mutual TLS — both endpoints present X.509 certificates. AppControl requires mTLS between agent and gateway. The CA, gateway, and agent certificates are managed by the PKI layer. The agent's certificate CN must match its agent_id UUID derivation (verified by the gateway). See Security Architecture §3.

docs.title: Native command
docs.text:
A typed JSON payload alternative to a shell check_cmd / start_cmd / stop_cmd. Useful on hosts where shell utilities (curl, wget) are not installed. Currently supported kinds:

  • http — HTTP probe with method, URL, expected status, headers, optional body.
  • tcp — TCP connect to host:port (planned, same column).
  • process — process-name match (planned, same column).

Stored in components.check_native / start_native / stop_native (JSONB). When non-null, the agent uses the native spec instead of the shell command. See migration V053.

docs.title: NIS2
docs.text: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 — Network and Information Security 2. Applies to essential and important entities across critical sectors. AppControl supports Article 21 (risk-mitigation measures) through RBAC, audit, BCM, mTLS, and the hardening checklist. See Compliance — DORA / NIS2.

docs.title: OIDC
docs.text: OpenID Connect — the SSO mechanism AppControl uses for browser logins. Tested with Keycloak, Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace. Configured via OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. See Configuration — OIDC.

docs.title: Organization
docs.text: The top-level tenant in the AppControl data model. Every user, application, agent, and gateway belongs to exactly one organization. Stored in the organizations table. Most installs run a single organization; multi-tenancy is supported by isolating data via organization_id.

docs.title: Org role
docs.text: A user's platform-wide role: admin, operator, editor, or viewer. Stored in users.role. The org role controls admin features (manage users, teams, sites). It does not restrict per-application access — a viewer with operate permission on an app can still start it. See Permissions — Platform Roles.

docs.title: PKI
docs.text: The certificate authority and certificate-issuance flow used for mTLS. AppControl supports per-organization PKI (auto-initialized), enterprise PKI (bring-your-own CA), and cert-manager (Kubernetes). See Configuration — TLS.

docs.title: Permission level
docs.text:
The granular access level a user (or team) has on a specific application:

view < operate < edit < manage < owner
Level Numeric Capability view 1 Read map, status, logs operate 2 Start, stop, restart, run diagnostics edit 3 Modify components, commands, dependencies manage 4 Grant permissions, share links owner 5 Delete app, transfer ownership

The effective level is MAX(direct, all_team_grants). Org admins are implicit owners on everything. See Permissions.

docs.title: Pink branch
docs.text: See Error branch. The visual color used to highlight failed components and their dependents in the map view.

docs.title: PR-only mode
docs.text: Optional mode in which start/stop operations are gated behind a merged Pull Request. The map (components, commands, dependencies) is versioned as code and operations are bound to git history. Used in highly regulated environments. See README — Garde-fous par conception.

docs.title: Quorum
docs.text: Cluster health policy in which the parent component is RUNNING if strictly more than half its enabled members are RUNNING.

docs.title: Rebuild
docs.text:
The targeted reconstruction operation that follows a diagnostic. Two flavors:

  • App rebuild — uses rebuild_cmd; reinstalls the application layer, keeps the host.
  • Infra rebuild — uses rebuild_infra_cmd; reinstalls the infrastructure (OS, filesystem). Executed by a bastion agent (rebuild_agent_id).

Rebuild respects DAG order and skips components flagged with rebuild_protected = true. See Architecture — 3-Level Diagnostic + Rebuild.

docs.title: Rebuild protection
docs.text: The rebuild_protected = true flag on a component prevents the rebuild engine from touching it. Used for components whose data must never be regenerated by AppControl (databases of record, archive storage). A rebuild against a protected component returns HTTP 409. See Backend CLAUDE.md — Rebuild Engine.

docs.title: Referenced app
docs.text: A component of type application with a referenced_app_id pointing to another application. When the parent app starts, the referenced app is recursively started first; its state is derived from its components' aggregate state, not its own cached column. See Backend CLAUDE.md — Application-Type Components.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
The configurable lifetime of audit rows. Two knobs:

  • RETENTION_ACTION_LOG_DAYS — default 0 (unlimited). Deletes action_log rows older than N days.
  • RETENTION_CHECK_EVENTS_DAYS — default 0 (unlimited). Drops check_events partitions older than N days.

DORA requires 5 years minimum for incident records. See Hardening.

docs.title: RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
docs.text: The maximum acceptable data loss in time. For AppControl audit data, the RPO depends on your PostgreSQL backup cadence: typical RPO is 5–15 minutes if WAL archiving is configured, 1–24 hours otherwise. See Disaster Recovery.

docs.title: RTO (Recovery Time Objective)
docs.text: The maximum acceptable downtime. For AppControl-managed applications, the RTO is measured end-to-end through switchover_log (time from FREEZE to COMMIT phase). See Disaster Recovery.

docs.title: RTR (Recovery Time for Rebuild)
docs.text: The total elapsed time of a rebuild operation, measured by the rebuild engine and stored in action_log. Tracked over time to identify regression in reconstruction speed (DORA Article 11). See Architecture — 3-Level Diagnostic + Rebuild.

docs.title: SAML
docs.text: Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0 — alternative SSO mechanism, tested with ADFS, Azure AD, Okta. AppControl supports group-to-team auto-sync via saml_group_mappings. Configured via SAML_IDP_SSO_URL, SAML_IDP_CERT, SAML_SP_ENTITY_ID. See Configuration — SAML.

docs.title: Scheduler integration
docs.text: The REST API and appctl CLI exposed for use by enterprise schedulers (Control-M, AutoSys, Dollar Universe, TWS). Standard exit codes (0 success, 1 failure, 2 timeout, 3 auth, 4 not found, 5 permission denied) make integration straightforward. AppControl is not itself a scheduler. See Configuration — CLI.

docs.title: Site
docs.text: A physical or logical location: a datacenter, a DR site, a staging environment. Stored in the sites table. Every application and gateway belongs to a site. Sites are grouped by hosting. See User Guide — Sites.

docs.title: Site override
docs.text: Per-site customization of a component, stored in site_overrides. Lets the same component run on PRD and DR with different start_cmd, agent_id, env_vars, etc. The active site at any time is determined by applications.active_site_id.

docs.title: State transition
docs.text: A row in the append-only state_transitions table recording a change of a component's FSM state. Includes previous_state, next_state, trigger (e.g. health_check, sequencer, heartbeat_timeout), and a JSON details blob. Used for DORA Article 16 audit. See migrations/V005.

docs.title: Strong dependency
docs.text: A dependency that gates start/stop sequencing. The parent must reach RUNNING before the dependent starts; the dependent must reach STOPPED before the parent stops. AppControl currently treats every edge in the dependencies table as a strong dependency. The "weak dependency" concept is discussed in the user-guide narrative but does not yet have a dedicated column.

docs.title: Switchover
docs.text: The DR operation that migrates an application from its current site to another site. Executed in six phases (see Switchover phases). Tracked end-to-end in switchover_log. See User Guide — DR Switchover.

docs.title: Switchover phases
docs.text:
The six phases of a switchover:

Phase Name Description 1 Prepare Verify DR agents connected and resources available 2 Validate Run pre-flight health checks on the target site 3 StopSource Stop all components on the source site (reverse DAG) 4 Sync Verify data replication is complete 5 StartTarget Start all components on the target site (DAG order) 6 Commit Update applications.active_site_id — point of no return

Rollback is available up to phase 5. See Disaster Recovery.

docs.title: Switchover mode
docs.text:
The flavor of switchover:

  • FULL — every component is migrated.
  • SELECTIVE — only operator-chosen components are migrated.
  • PROGRESSIVE — components are migrated in DAG levels, with a pause between each level for validation.

Stored in switchover_log.mode.

docs.title: Team
docs.text: A named group of users in the teams table. Teams are granted application permissions; members inherit those grants. Teams can be auto-synced from SAML groups via saml_group_mappings. See Permissions — Teams.

docs.title: TcpConnect
docs.text: A native command kind that attempts a TCP connect to a host:port. Used for simple liveness probes when no shell utility is available on the host. The agent reports exit code 0 on successful connect, non-zero otherwise.

docs.title: UNREACHABLE
docs.text: The FSM state assigned to a component when its agent fails to send 3 consecutive heartbeats. The component's previous state is preserved in state_transitions.details.previous_state so the FSM can restore it on reconnect. See Backend CLAUDE.md — Heartbeat Monitor.

docs.title: Vault
docs.text: External credential store (HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) that holds secret variable values. AppControl never sees the plaintext: it sends a placeholder ($(secret:NAME)) in the command, the agent resolves it from the vault at execution time, and zeroes the memory after exec. See Security Architecture §11.

docs.title: Weak dependency
docs.text: A dependency edge that is not gated by the DAG sequencer: both endpoints start in parallel, but the edge is still drawn in the map and exported in reports. Useful for documenting "B reads from A, but B must not block on A at start-up". Stored as dependencies.dependency_type = 'weak' (introduced in migration V056) and exposed via the POST /api/v1/apps/:id/dependencies API as {"dependency_type": "weak"}. Defaults to strong so pre-V056 rows and older clients see no behaviour change.

docs.title: WebSocket hub
docs.text: The backend component that manages per-user WebSocket subscriptions. On every Subscribe(app_id), the hub computes the user's effective permission and rejects the subscription if it is below view. State change events are fan-out only to subscribers who pass the permission filter. See Security Architecture §7.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text:
A site-scoped access boundary. A workspace binds users (directly or via teams) to a set of sites. When workspaces are configured, a user can only access components whose site is included in at least one of their workspaces. Without workspaces, all sites are accessible (the feature is opt-in). Defined in workspace_sites and workspace_members (migration V011).

Last updated alongside the codebase. To report a missing or stale entry, open a documentation issue.

docs.title: Production Hardening Checklist
docs.text:
This page is a literal checklist to walk through before promoting an AppControl deployment to production. Each item gives the rationale and the verification command so you can prove compliance.

For the architectural background, see Security Architecture. For the regulatory mapping, see Compliance — DORA / NIS2.

Default config is for development

Out of the box, AppControl ships with developer-friendly defaults (JWT_SECRET=dev-secret-..., no CORS restriction, APP_ENV=development). Production deployments must explicitly opt out of every dev convenience.

docs.title: JWT_SECRET set to ≥ 32 random characters
docs.text:
Rationale. JWTs sign every API call. A weak or default secret lets any attacker forge admin tokens. The backend panics on startup in production when the secret is short or matches known dev values.

Set.

NEW=$(openssl rand -base64 48)
kubectl create secret generic appcontrol-jwt \
  --namespace appcontrol \
  --from-literal=jwt-secret="$NEW" \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl rollout restart -n appcontrol deployment/appcontrol-backend

Verify.

# Length ≥ 32
kubectl get secret -n appcontrol appcontrol-jwt -o jsonpath='{.data.jwt-secret}' | base64 -d | wc -c

# Not in known-bad list
SEC=$(kubectl get secret -n appcontrol appcontrol-jwt -o jsonpath='{.data.jwt-secret}' | base64 -d)
[[ "$SEC" =~ (dev|change|secret|password) ]] && echo "FAIL: insecure" || echo "OK"
  • Set and verified.

docs.title: APP_ENV=production
docs.text:
Rationale. Setting APP_ENV=production toggles strict mode: insecure-default warnings become fatal errors, dev login endpoints are disabled, CORS becomes restrictive.

Verify.

kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- env | grep APP_ENV
# APP_ENV=production
  • APP_ENV=production confirmed in every backend replica.

docs.title: CORS_ORIGINS restricted to known frontends
docs.text:
Rationale. A permissive CORS policy lets any malicious site script the API on behalf of a logged-in user.

Set.

backend:
  env:
    CORS_ORIGINS: "https://appcontrol.example.com,https://admin.example.com"

Verify.

# Confirm the env is set
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- env | grep CORS_ORIGINS

# Attempt a cross-origin request — must be rejected
curl -i -H "Origin: https://attacker.example" https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps
# Expect: 403 or missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin
  • CORS restricted and verified.

docs.title: OIDC or SAML configured; local auth disabled in production
docs.text:
Rationale. Local-password authentication is appropriate for development but should not be the production door. SSO centralizes account lifecycle, MFA enforcement, and SSO-level auditing.

Set. Configure OIDC or SAML per Configuration §Users.

Verify.

# In production, /auth/login returns 404
curl -is https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/auth/login -X POST -d '{}'
# Expect: HTTP/2 404
  • SSO configured, local auth disabled.

docs.title: API key rotation policy
docs.text:
Rationale. Stale API keys widen the attack surface. Rotate every 90 days (industry standard for high-privilege machine credentials).

Set. When creating an API key, set expires_in_days: 90. Document the rotation procedure in your runbook.

Verify.

-- Keys older than 90 days should be < 5 % of total keys
SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days') AS stale,
  count(*) AS total
FROM api_keys WHERE revoked_at IS NULL;
  • Rotation policy documented; stale keys identified and rotated.

docs.title: Enrollment tokens: limited max_uses and short valid_hours
docs.text:
Rationale. An enrollment token grants permanent identity to whoever uses it first. A token with max_uses: 1000 and valid_hours: 8760 is effectively a permanent credential.

Set. Recommended defaults:

Use case max_uses valid_hours Onboarding a single agent 1 4 Onboarding a batch of agents (Ansible playbook) N (exactly) 4 Long-running automation not recommended n/a — prefer per-host tokens

Verify.

SELECT name, max_uses, expires_at FROM enrollment_tokens
WHERE revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
ORDER BY expires_at DESC;
  • All active tokens have bounded max_uses and expires_at ≤ 7 days.

docs.title: mTLS enabled
docs.text:
Rationale. Plaintext between agent and gateway exposes commands, credentials, and check output. mTLS provides mutual authentication and forward-secret encryption.

Set. Ensure TLS_ENABLED=true on every gateway and agent. Certificates come from the per-org CA (auto-PKI) or your enterprise PKI. See Configuration — TLS.

Verify.

# Gateway
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-gateway -- env | grep TLS_ENABLED
# TLS_ENABLED=true

# Agent
grep enabled /etc/appcontrol/agent.yaml
# enabled: true

# Probe the gateway with no cert — must be rejected
curl -k https://gateway.example.com:4443/health 2>&1 | grep -i "alert.*certificate"
# Or simulate a full handshake without client cert — should fail
openssl s_client -connect gateway.example.com:4443 < /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -i "alert"
  • mTLS enabled end-to-end.

docs.title: Rate limits reviewed
docs.text:
Rationale. Defaults are reasonable for moderate fleets. Larger or smaller installs need to tune.

Variable Default Rationale RATE_LIMIT_AUTH 10/min/IP Prevents brute-force login RATE_LIMIT_OPERATIONS 5/min/user Throttles per-user start/stop spam RATE_LIMIT_READS 200/min/user Tolerates dashboard polling

Verify.

kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- env | grep RATE_LIMIT

# Trigger a 429
for i in $(seq 1 12); do
  curl -is -X POST https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/auth/login -d '{}' | head -1
done
# Expect: 429 after the 10th request
  • Rate limits set appropriate for fleet size.

docs.title: CA private key not on disk where the backend runs
docs.text:
Rationale. The CA private key is the master credential. If the backend host is compromised, the attacker can sign any cert.

Set. Two options:

  • Sealed secret with strict RBAC (supported today). Keep the CA in a Kubernetes secret with only the backend ServiceAccount as reader; encrypt the secret at rest with a KMS-backed key.
  • HSM / KMS-backed CA (roadmap, not yet implemented). Delegating CA signing to HashiCorp Vault PKI, AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault is planned. Today the backend signs in-process with the CA private key loaded from the database (column organizations.ca_private_key, encrypted at rest by PostgreSQL TDE or LUKS at the volume layer). Tracking item: hsm-ca-signing.

Verify.

# Verify the backend cannot read the CA from disk
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- ls -la /etc/appcontrol/pki/ca.key 2>&1
# Expect: No such file or directory
  • CA private key not stored on the backend filesystem.

docs.title: Database credentials are not the default appcontrol:appcontrol@localhost
docs.text:
Rationale. A default-password database is a common entry point for lateral movement.

Set. Use a strong, randomly-generated password. Restrict source IPs at the DB level.

Verify.

# Inspect the database URL — must not contain default password
URL=$(kubectl get secret -n appcontrol appcontrol-db -o jsonpath='{.data.database-url}' | base64 -d)
[[ "$URL" =~ appcontrol:appcontrol@ ]] && echo "FAIL: default creds" || echo "OK"

# Also verify pg_hba.conf accepts only the backend's source
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SHOW listen_addresses;"
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SELECT * FROM pg_hba_file_rules WHERE type = 'host';"
  • Database credentials hardened.

docs.title: RETENTION_ACTION_LOG_DAYS and RETENTION_CHECK_EVENTS_DAYS set per regulation
docs.text:
Rationale. DORA Article 16 requires incident records for at least 5 years. NIS2 has similar expectations. Defaults are 0 (unlimited) which technically satisfies the rule but exposes you to storage exhaustion. Set explicit values.

Set.

backend:
  env:
    RETENTION_ACTION_LOG_DAYS:   "1825"   # 5 years
    RETENTION_CHECK_EVENTS_DAYS: "90"     # 3 months hot, then offloaded to archive

For check events older than 90 days, archive partitions to cold storage before the retention task drops them (see Backup & Restore — Partitioned check_events).

Verify.

kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- env | grep RETENTION
  • Retention values set and reviewed with compliance team.

docs.title: Logs go to a centralized SIEM in JSON format
docs.text:
Rationale. Per-pod log files are insufficient evidence for a regulator. Structured logs let you correlate access patterns and detect anomalies.

Set.

backend:
  env:
    LOG_FORMAT: "json"
    RUST_LOG:   "info,appcontrol_backend=info,tower_http=info"

Forward stdout/stderr to your SIEM (Splunk, Datadog, Elastic, Loki).

Verify.

# Recent logs must be valid JSON
kubectl logs -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend --tail=10 | jq -c '.'
  • JSON logs forwarded to SIEM.

docs.title: Backups encrypted at rest, with an off-site copy
docs.text:
Rationale. Production backups containing the action log are themselves sensitive. They must be encrypted at rest, and an off-site copy must exist for the doomsday scenario.

Set. See Backup & Restore — Encryption at rest for aws s3 cp --sse aws:kms example and cross-region replication.

Verify.

# Confirm KMS encryption on the most recent backup
LATEST=$(aws s3 ls s3://appcontrol-backups/daily/ --recursive | sort | tail -1 | awk '{print $4}')
aws s3api head-object --bucket appcontrol-backups --key "$LATEST" | jq '.ServerSideEncryption, .SSEKMSKeyId'

# Confirm cross-region replication
aws s3api get-bucket-replication --bucket appcontrol-backups
  • Backups encrypted; off-site copy verified.

docs.title: Agents → gateway only; gateway → backend only; no direct agent → backend
docs.text:
Rationale. Defense in depth: even if an agent is compromised, it should not be able to talk directly to the database or to other agents.

Set. Kubernetes NetworkPolicies (the Helm chart ships sensible defaults — verify they are enabled).

networkPolicy:
  enabled: true

This restricts:

Source Destination Ports allowed Frontend pods Backend pods 3000 Ingress controller Frontend pods 8080 Backend pods PostgreSQL 5432 Backend pods Gateway pods 3000 (WS) External (any) Gateway pods 4443 Gateway pods Backend pods 3000 All others denied

Verify.

kubectl get networkpolicy -n appcontrol
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n appcontrol

# From an agent host, try the backend directly — must fail
nc -vz appcontrol-backend.appcontrol.svc.cluster.local 3000
# Expect: connection refused / blocked
  • NetworkPolicies enabled and tested.

docs.title: Backend / gateway / agent run as non-root
docs.text:
Rationale. A privilege-escalation bug becomes far more dangerous if the process is already root.

Set. Helm chart uses runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser: 65532 for backend / gateway / frontend. Agent runs as root by default on hosts because it executes user-defined commands; restrict to a dedicated appcontrol user where you can.

Verify.

# Container UID
kubectl get pod -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=backend -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.securityContext.runAsUser}'
# Expect: 65532 or similar non-zero

# Agent user (on host)
ps -o user= -p $(pidof appcontrol-agent)
  • Non-root verified for backend, gateway, frontend.

docs.title: PostgreSQL: ssl=require, scram-sha-256 auth
docs.text:
Rationale. Plaintext SQL on a public network leaks every query (and the JWT in some). SCRAM-SHA-256 is the strongest standard PostgreSQL auth mechanism.

Set.

# pg_hba.conf
hostssl appcontrol appcontrol 10.0.0.0/16 scram-sha-256

# postgresql.conf
password_encryption = scram-sha-256
ssl = on

# In DATABASE_URL
postgres://appcontrol:PASSWORD@db.internal:5432/appcontrol?sslmode=require

Verify.

psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SHOW ssl; SHOW password_encryption;"
# ssl                       | on
# password_encryption       | scram-sha-256
  • PostgreSQL TLS + SCRAM enabled.

docs.title: OS hardening: SELinux/AppArmor enforcing; recent patches
docs.text:
Rationale. Standard infrastructure hygiene. Mandatory Access Control limits the blast radius of any process compromise.

Set. Distribution-dependent. RHEL: setenforce 1; Ubuntu: aa-status enforcing on appcontrol-agent. Apply security errata weekly.

Verify.

# RHEL
getenforce
# Expect: Enforcing

# Ubuntu
sudo aa-status | head -3
# Expect: profiles loaded

# Patches
sudo dnf updateinfo summary security  # RHEL
sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run     # Ubuntu
  • MAC enforcing; security patches current.

docs.title: No debug toolchain on production hosts
docs.text:
Rationale. Compilers, package managers, and debugging tools are the first thing an intruder reaches for. Strip them from production images.

Verify.

# Inside the backend container
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- sh -c 'which gcc gdb strace tcpdump apt yum 2>&1' | grep -v 'not found' && echo "FAIL" || echo "OK"
  • Debug tooling absent from production images.

docs.title: SAML_WANT_ASSERTIONS_SIGNED=true
docs.text:
Rationale. Unsigned SAML assertions can be tampered with. Without signature verification, an attacker who can MITM the assertion can impersonate any user.

Set. This is the default in production; verify it is not overridden.

Verify.

kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- env | grep SAML_WANT_ASSERTIONS_SIGNED
# SAML_WANT_ASSERTIONS_SIGNED=true
  • Signed assertions enforced.

docs.title: Approval workflow enabled for high-risk operations
docs.text:
Rationale. A single operator should not be able to switch over a critical application without a second pair of eyes. See Security Architecture §9.

Set. Per application, configure the approval policy in Settings > Application > Approvals:

Risk Operations Approvers needed Low diagnose, custom commands 0 Medium start, stop, restart configurable (0 or 1) High switchover, rebuild 1 Critical DR commit, break-glass 2

Verify.

SELECT name, settings->'approvals' AS approvals FROM applications;
  • Approval policy configured for production apps.

docs.title: Break-glass accounts pre-provisioned
docs.text:
Rationale. When OIDC is down or all tokens have expired, you still need a way in. Pre-provisioned break-glass accounts with passwords sealed in an external vault meet this need.

Set. See Security Architecture §10.

Verify.

SELECT username, is_active FROM break_glass_accounts;
-- Expect: at least 2 active accounts
  • Break-glass procedure tested annually.

docs.title: Verification summary script
docs.text:
Run this against your production install at any time:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/hardening-check.sh
set -e
NS=${NAMESPACE:-appcontrol}

echo "== JWT_SECRET length"
LEN=$(kubectl get secret -n $NS appcontrol-jwt -o jsonpath='{.data.jwt-secret}' | base64 -d | wc -c)
[[ $LEN -ge 32 ]] && echo "OK ($LEN bytes)" || echo "FAIL ($LEN bytes)"

echo "== APP_ENV"
ENV=$(kubectl exec -n $NS deploy/appcontrol-backend -- printenv APP_ENV)
[[ "$ENV" == "production" ]] && echo "OK" || echo "FAIL (got '$ENV')"

echo "== CORS_ORIGINS"
CORS=$(kubectl exec -n $NS deploy/appcontrol-backend -- printenv CORS_ORIGINS)
[[ -n "$CORS" ]] && echo "OK ($CORS)" || echo "FAIL"

echo "== TLS on gateway"
TLS=$(kubectl exec -n $NS deploy/appcontrol-gateway -- printenv TLS_ENABLED)
[[ "$TLS" == "true" ]] && echo "OK" || echo "FAIL"

echo "== NetworkPolicies"
COUNT=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n $NS --no-headers | wc -l)
[[ $COUNT -ge 3 ]] && echo "OK ($COUNT policies)" || echo "FAIL ($COUNT policies)"

echo "== Backend non-root"
UID=$(kubectl get pod -n $NS -l app.kubernetes.io/component=backend -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.securityContext.runAsUser}')
[[ "$UID" != "0" && -n "$UID" ]] && echo "OK (UID=$UID)" || echo "FAIL"

echo "== Retention"
RET=$(kubectl exec -n $NS deploy/appcontrol-backend -- printenv RETENTION_ACTION_LOG_DAYS)
[[ -n "$RET" && "$RET" != "0" ]] && echo "OK (retention=$RET days)" || echo "FAIL"

echo "== JSON logs"
FMT=$(kubectl exec -n $NS deploy/appcontrol-backend -- printenv LOG_FORMAT)
[[ "$FMT" == "json" ]] && echo "OK" || echo "FAIL"

Schedule this in your CI / CronJob to alert on drift.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Security Architecture — design rationale for each control
  • Configuration — full env var reference
  • Compliance — DORA / NIS2 — regulatory mapping for each item
  • PRODUCTION_DEPLOYMENT.md — initial deployment steps

docs.title: High Availability
docs.text:
This page distinguishes the current reconstruction deployment from HA patterns that still require implementation and qualification. For DR scenarios, see Disaster Recovery.

Current reconstruction boundary — 12 September 2026

Use one backend, disable backend autoscaling, and schedule backend upgrades with an interruption. The Helm defaults use replicaCount: 1 and strategy.type: Recreate. Command routing and WebSocket subscribers are local to the backend process; cross-backend routing and durable resumption of interrupted reconstruction operations are not implemented. A shared database, an ownership lease or HA_MODE=true does not supply these guarantees. See the reconstruction improvement plan, R01–R04.

docs.title: Table of contents
docs.text:
• HA topology overview
  • Backend HA
  • Gateway HA
  • Database HA
  • Agent reconnect semantics
  • WebSocket affinity
  • Example load balancer configurations
  • Example Helm values overlay
  • What survives, what does not

docs.title: HA topology overview
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────┐
                │ External LB / Ingress    │  L7, TLS, one backend target
                │   appcontrol.example.com │
                └────────┬─────────────────┘
                         │
        ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
        │                                 │
   ┌────▼─────┐                      ┌────▼─────┐
   │ Frontend │  x N (nginx)         │ Backend  │  x 1 (Rust + Axum)
   │  pods    │                      │  pods    │
   └──────────┘                      └────┬─────┘
                                          │ sqlx pool (TCP+TLS)
                                          ▼
                                  ┌───────────────┐
                                  │ PostgreSQL 16 │  Primary + sync replica
                                  │   Patroni /   │  (or managed: RDS Multi-AZ,
                                  │   pgBouncer   │   CloudSQL HA, Azure HA)
                                  └───────────────┘

                ┌──────────────────────────┐
                │ External LB (TCP)         │
                │  gateway.example.com:4443 │  Layer 4, NLB
                └────────┬─────────────────┘
                         │
        ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
        │                                 │
   ┌────▼──────┐                     ┌────▼──────┐
   │ Gateway 1 │ (PRD zone)          │ Gateway 2 │ (DR zone)
   └────┬──────┘                     └────┬──────┘
        │ WSS mTLS                        │ WSS mTLS
        ▼                                 ▼
    Agents in PRD                     Agents in DR

Three failure domains are independent:

  • Backend persists application/audit records in the database, but keeps connections and active execution tasks in process memory. Do not scale it horizontally for reconstruction yet.
  • Gateway has no database dependency. Agent reconnection to another gateway is separate from backend HA and must be qualified with the configured endpoints.
  • Database uses PostgreSQL native replication (managed or self-hosted with Patroni).

docs.title: Backend HA
docs.text: Persistent records survive a backend restart when the database survives. Live gateway routes, browser subscriptions and executing reconstruction tasks do not become available to another backend merely because it shares that database.

docs.title: Shared settings do not implement backend HA
docs.text:
Environment variable Required for HA Notes HA_MODE=true Rate limiting only Uses PostgreSQL counters; does not route commands/events between backends or resume operations. DATABASE_URL Yes All replicas point at the same DB (or a load-balanced read-write endpoint). JWT_SECRET Yes Must be identical across replicas; JWTs signed by replica A must validate on replica B. JWT_ISSUER Yes Must be identical across replicas. DB_POOL_SIZE Tune Each replica opens its own pool. Total connections = replicas × DB_POOL_SIZE. Don't exceed PostgreSQL's max_connections. SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_SECS Shutdown setting Must fit within the pod termination grace period; it is not an operation completion or recovery guarantee.

See Configuration — Backend HA.

docs.title: Replica count
docs.text:
Use one backend for the current reconstruction pilot. The chart generates no HPA; do not attach an external autoscaler or override the count above one. Size and load-test this instance against the client's workload.

The backend PDB uses minAvailable: 1; with one replica this can block a voluntary node drain. It does not provide redundancy or preserve an operation during a Deployment update. Recreate prevents old/new replicas from overlapping during that update and causes a planned control-plane interruption. Finish or reconcile operations before maintenance.

Multiple backend replicas are a future qualification target: gateway connected to B, command submitted to A, browser on another backend, followed by loss of the connection owner. These cases require cross-backend routing and a defined interruption/reconciliation contract before an HA claim.

docs.title: Load-balancer health checks
docs.text:
Probe Endpoint Frequency Treats as unhealthy if Liveness /health 10 s Pod fails the probe — Kubernetes restarts it Readiness /ready 5 s Pod removed from Service endpoints (DB unreachable, migrations in progress) LB pool health /ready 5 s LB stops routing new requests to the pod 
# Illustrative probes; inspect the rendered chart for its actual timings
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 3000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3

docs.title: Sticky sessions
docs.text: A single backend needs no affinity between backend replicas. With multiple backends, JWT validation alone is insufficient: the gateway connection and its command route may belong to another process. HTTP cookie/IP affinity does not align independently established gateway and browser connections. See WebSocket affinity.

docs.title: Drain behavior
docs.text: The backend has a shutdown signal handler and an HTTP graceful-shutdown path. They do not checkpoint reconstruction tasks or transfer them to another process. Do not use a timeout or pod readiness as proof that an operation completed. Stop new operation submissions, await terminal results and resolve ambiguous external jobs before a planned restart. After an unexpected restart, obtain fresh checks and reconcile recorded operations before retrying; an external command may have continued running.

docs.title: Gateway HA
docs.text: Gateways are stateless WebSocket relays. They hold no database connection and no agent state — each agent's (agent_id, gateway_id) mapping is tracked by the backend in agents.last_gateway_id for routing.

docs.title: Why server-side gateway clustering is not needed
docs.text:
The gateway-failover problem is solved on the agent side: each agent is configured with multiple gateway.urls and falls over automatically. This is the same pattern Consul uses for client → server failover.

# /etc/appcontrol/agent.yaml
gateway:
  urls:
    - wss://gateway-prd-01.example.com:4443/ws
    - wss://gateway-prd-02.example.com:4443/ws
  failover_strategy: ordered     # try first, fall through on failure
  primary_retry_secs: 300        # return to primary every 5 min once it recovers
  reconnect_interval_secs: 10

docs.title: Behind a TCP load balancer
docs.text:
If you want a single DNS entry, place a Layer-4 LB (AWS NLB, GCP TCP LB, HAProxy) in front of your gateway pool:

gateway:
  urls:
    - wss://gateway.example.com:4443/ws       # NLB VIP

In this case, you do not need the multi-URL agent config. However:

  • An NLB conceals the actual gateway pod identity; agents.last_gateway_id may be incorrect during a brief failover window.
  • The agent does not know which pod it lands on; if the pod has a stale cert, the agent gets a TLS error and retries.
  • Mixing NLB + multi-URL gives the best of both — if the NLB itself is down, agents try the individual gateway URLs.

docs.title: How many gateways
docs.text:
Zone size Recommended gateway count Why < 500 agents 2 N+1 redundancy 500–5000 agents 3 Load distribution + N+1 > 5000 agents ≥ 4 Distribute connection count

Each gateway can handle thousands of WebSocket connections. The practical limit is the host's file-descriptor ulimit and memory (one connection ~ 64 KB resident).

docs.title: Maintenance workflow
docs.text:
1. Mark the gateway inactive in the backend: 
    curl -X PATCH https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/gateways/<id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"is_active": false}'
  2. Agents detect the disconnection, fail over to the next gateway in their list.
  3. Perform maintenance (kernel patch, upgrade, cert rotation).
  4. Re-enable the gateway: 
    curl -X PATCH https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/gateways/<id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"is_active": true}'
  5. With failover_strategy: ordered and primary_retry_secs: 300, agents return to the primary within 5 min.

docs.title: Database HA
docs.text: AppControl supports any production-grade PostgreSQL 16 HA setup.

docs.title: Managed services (recommended)
docs.text: Provider Service HA option AWS RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ standby (sync), automatic failover GCP CloudSQL HA with failover replica (sync) Azure Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server Zone-redundant HA Generic CrunchyData PGO, Zalando Patroni Streaming replication + Etcd consensus

docs.title: Recommended PostgreSQL config
docs.text:
# postgresql.conf
max_connections = 200                # replicas × DB_POOL_SIZE + headroom
shared_buffers = 4GB                 # 25 % of host RAM
effective_cache_size = 12GB          # 75 % of host RAM
work_mem = 16MB
maintenance_work_mem = 1GB
wal_level = replica
synchronous_commit = on              # required: lose less than 1 commit on failover
synchronous_standby_names = 'replica-1'
checkpoint_timeout = 15min
max_wal_size = 4GB
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'your-wal-archive-command'  # see BACKUP_RESTORE.md

docs.title: Failover handling
docs.text:
The backend uses a sqlx connection pool. On primary loss, requests can fail while connections and the read-write endpoint recover. DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECS is a connection timeout, not an end-to-end failover guarantee. Verify the provider's promotion, DNS/LB behavior and recovery of the pool in the deployment being qualified. An interrupted operation still requires reconciliation.

An optional PgBouncer layer can manage database connections; it does not guarantee error-free failover or resume an interrupted reconstruction:

backend pods ─── (sqlx) ──▶ pgbouncer ──▶ PostgreSQL primary

Size connection pools against PostgreSQL's limits and test database failover with an active operation. Database redundancy does not remove the single-backend reconstruction boundary.

docs.title: Read replicas
docs.text:
AppControl does not currently route any query to a read replica. The backend uses a single DATABASE_URL (set in crates/backend/src/config.rs::AppConfig::database_url) for both reads and writes, and every repository implementation in crates/backend/src/repository/ is wired against that one pool.

Adding read-replica routing — a separate DATABASE_REPLICA_URL pool that report endpoints (/api/v1/reports/*) and the heavier audit queries could opt into — is on the roadmap. It is not yet implemented and is not exposed as a configuration knob.

docs.title: Agent reconnect semantics
docs.text: Agents can reconnect after a gateway or backend failure. Reconnection does not prove completion of commands that were in flight or resume a backend reconstruction task.

docs.title: State at the agent
docs.text:
The agent maintains:

  • Component config snapshot — last UpdateConfig from the backend, kept in memory.
  • Local scheduler — runs checks autonomously based on the snapshot; does not poll the backend.
  • Delta tracking — for each component, the last exit_code sent. A new CheckResult is only sent when the exit code changes.
  • Offline buffer — sled DB at /var/lib/appcontrol/buffer-{agent-id}, ≤ 100 MB, FIFO rotation.

docs.title: Reconnect sequence
docs.text:
1. WebSocket close detected.
  2. Agent enters reconnect loop:
  3. Try gateway.urls[0]. If failure, wait reconnect_interval_secs and try [1], etc.
  4. Exponential backoff on repeated failure: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 60 (max) seconds.
  5. On successful connect, agent sends Register { agent_id, hostname, ip_addresses, labels, version }.
  6. Agent replays the offline buffer in chronological order before resuming real-time deltas.

docs.title: Results and ACKs
docs.text: Command results are correlated by request UUID; real backend/gateway/agent tests verify matching results and ACKs. This is a transport/persistence proof, not an exactly-once guarantee for an external effect or a durable reconstruction-resume mechanism. Inspect the recorded command and provider job before repeating an ambiguous action. See the process and ACK evidence and improvement-plan R02/R03.

docs.title: Buffer-on-disk during disconnect
docs.text:
While disconnected:

  • Agent continues running checks.
  • Each CheckResult is written to the local sled DB with a nanosecond-precision timestamp key.
  • Buffer is FIFO bounded at 100 MB by default (override with the BUFFER_MAX_BYTES environment variable on the agent process; value in bytes, 0 or unparseable value falls back to the default). When the cap is exceeded, the oldest entries are evicted in order until the buffer fits again.
  • On reconnect, the buffer is drained in order, then the agent resumes real-time mode.

This means a 1 h disconnect on a 50-component agent at 30 s check interval produces ≈ 6000 buffered events × 200 bytes = ~1.2 MB — well under the buffer cap.

docs.title: WebSocket affinity
docs.text:
The backend exposes two WebSocket endpoints:

  • /ws for the frontend (browsers + CLI watch operations).
  • /ws/gateway for gateways (one persistent connection per gateway).

docs.title: Hub model — process-local routing
docs.text: The hub keeps gateway routes and WebSocket senders in process memory. The reconstruction path calls that local hub. A PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY bridge for cross-backend commands/events is not implemented in this path. Database persistence alone does not deliver a command to a gateway owned by another backend or publish an event to that backend's browser subscribers.

docs.title: Implication for load balancing
docs.text:
• Route browser/API and gateway connections to the same single backend for the current pilot.
  • Sticky HTTP sessions are not a substitute for cross-backend routing.
  • A browser can reconnect after restart; an in-flight operation does not automatically resume. Inspect its persisted status and reconcile external effects before a fresh assessment and approved retry.

docs.title: Implication for monitoring
docs.text: Monitor backend readiness, gateway/agent connectivity and operation/command results separately. A healthy pod or an open WebSocket is not proof that the requested application recovery completed.

docs.title: HAProxy — backend (HTTP/HTTPS + WebSocket)
docs.text:
global
