docs.title: Integration Cookbook
docs.text: Concrete, copy-paste recipes for integrating AppControl with common enterprise tools.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: All recipes assume: - AppControl backend is running at https://appcontrol.example.com - You have an API key: ac_your-api-key-here - The target application is already modeled in AppControl with ID APP_ID

docs.title: Create an API Key
docs.text:
Create a key in Settings → API Keys, or use the API with an authenticated account. For a single application's lifecycle operations:

jq -n --arg app "$APP_ID" '{name: "control-m-integration", allowed_actions: [("app:" + $app + ":read"), ("app:" + $app + ":start"), ("app:" + $app + ":stop")]}' > key-request.json
curl -X POST https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/api-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $JWT_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @key-request.json

Keys are a ceiling on the account's application permissions. They default to read-only with a 30-day expiry when omitted. Restricted keys deny unclassified routes; the recipes below need capabilities matching their actual endpoints. Recovery planning requires plan, diagnosis diagnose, and recovery execution execute, alongside the account's required RBAC. Legacy * keys retain full account permissions and should not be used for analysis-only AI integrations.

Save the returned key — it's shown only once.

docs.title: Start an Application from a Control-M Job
docs.text:
Create a Control-M job that calls the AppControl CLI:

Job Name: START_BILLING_APP
Command: /usr/local/bin/appctl start billing-prod --wait --timeout 300
Run As: appcontrol-svc
Exit Codes: 0=OK, 1=FAIL, 2=TIMEOUT

AppControl CLI exit codes: | Code | Meaning | |------|---------| | 0 | Success | | 1 | Failure | | 2 | Timeout | | 3 | Auth error | | 4 | Not found | | 5 | Permission denied |

docs.title: Check Application Status Before a Job
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# pre-condition.sh — use as Control-M pre-condition
STATUS=$(appctl status billing-prod --format short)
if [ "$STATUS" != "RUNNING" ]; then
  echo "Application not running, aborting job"
  exit 1
fi
exit 0

docs.title: Stop After a Batch Window
docs.text:
Job Name: STOP_BILLING_APP
Command: /usr/local/bin/appctl stop billing-prod --wait --timeout 180
Condition In: END_OF_BATCH_WINDOW

docs.title: JIL Definition for AppControl Start
docs.text:
insert_job: start_billing_app
job_type: CMD
command: /usr/local/bin/appctl start billing-prod --wait --timeout 300
machine: appcontrol-host
owner: autosys_svc
permission: gx,ge
alarm_if_fail: 1
std_out_file: /var/log/autosys/appcontrol_start.log
std_err_file: /var/log/autosys/appcontrol_start.err

docs.title: Conditional Start Based on AppControl State
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# autosys_wrapper.sh
APP_ID="billing-prod"
ACTION="$1"

# Check current state via API
STATE=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
  "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/orchestration/apps/$APP_ID/status" \
  | jq -r '.all_running')

if [ "$ACTION" = "start" ] && [ "$STATE" = "true" ]; then
  echo "Already running, skipping"
  exit 0
fi

appctl "$ACTION" "$APP_ID" --wait --timeout 300
exit $?

docs.title: Creating a Dollar Universe Task
docs.text:
# DU task script
#!/bin/bash
# u_start_app.sh — Dollar Universe uproc

AC_API_KEY="${AC_API_KEY}"
APP_ID="${U_APP_ID}"
TIMEOUT="${U_TIMEOUT:-300}"

# Start via REST API (Dollar Universe prefers API calls over CLI)
RESPONSE=$(curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}" \
  -X POST "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/orchestration/apps/$APP_ID/start" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"dry_run": false}')

HTTP_CODE=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | tail -1)
if [ "$HTTP_CODE" != "200" ]; then
  echo "Start failed with HTTP $HTTP_CODE"
  exit 1
fi

# Wait for completion
WAIT_RESPONSE=$(curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}" \
  "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/orchestration/apps/$APP_ID/wait-running?timeout=$TIMEOUT" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY")

STATUS=$(echo "$WAIT_RESPONSE" | head -1 | jq -r '.status')
case "$STATUS" in
  running) exit 0 ;;
  timeout) exit 2 ;;
  failed)  exit 1 ;;
  *)       exit 1 ;;
esac

docs.title: HTTP Task: Start Application
docs.text:
In your XL Release template, add an HTTP Request task:

Field Value URL https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/orchestration/apps/${app_id}/start Method POST Headers Authorization: ApiKey ${api_key}, Content-Type: application/json Body {"dry_run": false}

docs.title: HTTP Task: Wait for Running
docs.text:
Add a second HTTP Request task:

Field Value URL https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/orchestration/apps/${app_id}/wait-running?timeout=300 Method GET Headers Authorization: ApiKey ${api_key} Expected Status 200

docs.title: Validate Your XL Release Sequence
docs.text:
Before migrating, validate that your XL Release template's restart order matches AppControl's DAG:

curl -X POST "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/validate-sequence" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sequence": ["redis-cache", "postgres-db", "api-server", "web-frontend"],
    "operation": "start"
  }'

Response: 

{
  "valid": true,
  "conflicts": [],
  "expected_order": [["redis-cache", "postgres-db"], ["api-server"], ["web-frontend"]]
}

If there are conflicts, the response tells you exactly what's wrong: 

{
  "valid": false,
  "conflicts": [
    {
      "type": "dependency_order_violation",
      "dependent": "api-server",
      "dependency": "postgres-db",
      "message": "'api-server' depends on 'postgres-db' but starts at position 0 while postgres-db is at position 1"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Replace XL Release Restart Templates
docs.text:
Before (XL Release manages dependencies): 

Phase: Restart Application
  Task 1: Start Redis (SSH)
  Task 2: Start PostgreSQL (SSH)
  Task 3: Wait 30s
  Task 4: Start API Server (SSH)
  Task 5: Wait 10s
  Task 6: Start Web Frontend (SSH)
  Task 7: Health check (HTTP)

After (AppControl manages dependencies): 

Phase: Restart Application
  Task 1: POST /api/v1/orchestration/apps/{id}/start
  Task 2: GET /api/v1/orchestration/apps/{id}/wait-running?timeout=300

docs.title: Post-Deploy Restart via Jenkinsfile
docs.text:
pipeline {
    agent any
    environment {
        AC_API_KEY = credentials('appcontrol-api-key')
        AC_URL = 'https://appcontrol.example.com'
        APP_ID = 'your-app-id'
    }
    stages {
        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                // Your deployment steps here
                sh 'helm upgrade myapp ./helm/myapp'
            }
        }
        stage('Restart via AppControl') {
            steps {
                sh """
                    curl -f -X POST ${AC_URL}/api/v1/orchestration/apps/${APP_ID}/start \
                      -H "Authorization: ApiKey ${AC_API_KEY}" \
                      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
                      -d '{"dry_run": false}'
                """
                // Wait for all components to be running
                sh """
                    STATUS=\$(curl -s ${AC_URL}/api/v1/orchestration/apps/${APP_ID}/wait-running?timeout=300 \
                      -H "Authorization: ApiKey ${AC_API_KEY}" | jq -r '.status')
                    if [ "\$STATUS" != "running" ]; then
                      echo "Application failed to start: \$STATUS"
                      exit 1
                    fi
                """
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: .gitlab-ci.yml
docs.text:
restart_application:
  stage: post-deploy
  image: curlimages/curl:latest
  variables:
    AC_URL: "https://appcontrol.example.com"
    APP_ID: "your-app-id"
  script:
    - |
      # Trigger restart
      curl -f -X POST "$AC_URL/api/v1/orchestration/apps/$APP_ID/start" \
        -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"dry_run": false}'

      # Wait for running
      STATUS=$(curl -s "$AC_URL/api/v1/orchestration/apps/$APP_ID/wait-running?timeout=300" \
        -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" | jq -r '.status')

      if [ "$STATUS" != "running" ]; then
        echo "Restart failed: $STATUS"
        exit 1
      fi
      echo "Application is running"
  only:
    - main

docs.title: Webhook Notification Setup
docs.text:
Configure AppControl to send webhooks on FAILED state transitions:

# Subscribe to failure events via API
curl -X POST "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/notification-preferences" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $JWT_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "event_type": "failure",
    "channel": "webhook",
    "webhook_url": "https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue",
    "webhook_headers": {
      "Content-Type": "application/json"
    }
  }'

docs.title: PagerDuty Webhook Payload Transform
docs.text:
AppControl webhook payload: 

{
  "event_type": "state_change",
  "component_id": "...",
  "component_name": "api-server",
  "application_name": "billing-prod",
  "from_state": "RUNNING",
  "to_state": "FAILED",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-24T10:30:00Z"
}

Use a PagerDuty integration or middleware to transform this into PagerDuty's event format.

docs.title: Change Request on Operations
docs.text:
Use AppControl's audit trail to feed ServiceNow change records:

# Export audit trail for a time range
curl -s "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/reports/audit?from=2026-02-23&to=2026-02-24" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
  | jq '.entries[] | {
      type: .action,
      target: .entity_type,
      user: .user_id,
      timestamp: .created_at
    }'

docs.title: Export DAG as Graphviz
docs.text:
# Get DOT format for Graphviz rendering
curl -s "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/topology?format=dot" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
  | jq -r '.content' > app_topology.dot

# Render to PNG
dot -Tpng app_topology.dot -o app_topology.png

docs.title: Export as YAML for Config Management
docs.text:
curl -s "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/topology?format=yaml" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
  | jq -r '.content' > app_topology.yaml

docs.title: Export as JSON for CMDB Ingestion
docs.text:
curl -s "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/topology?format=json" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" > app_topology.json

docs.title: Get Execution Plan Before Any Operation
docs.text:
# What would a start do?
curl -s "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/plan?operation=start" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" | jq '.plan'

# What would a stop do?
curl -s "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/plan?operation=stop" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" | jq '.plan'

# Plan for a specific component and its dependencies
curl -s "https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/plan?operation=start&scope=$COMPONENT_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" | jq '.plan'

Response example: 

{
  "levels": [
    {
      "level": 0,
      "components": [
        {"name": "redis", "current_state": "RUNNING", "predicted_action": "skip"},
        {"name": "postgres", "current_state": "STOPPED", "predicted_action": "start"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "level": 1,
      "components": [
        {"name": "api-server", "current_state": "STOPPED", "predicted_action": "start"}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "total_actions": 2
}

docs.title: Limits and Quotas
docs.text:
This page documents the limits enforced by AppControl, along with the configurable knobs and what happens when each limit is reached. Numbers come from the code; treat the recommended values as guidance, not hard guarantees.

For sizing the deployment to stay within these limits, see Capacity Planning.

docs.title: Table of contents
docs.text:
• Per-entity limits
  • Storage limits
  • Rate limits
  • Connection and pool limits
  • Agent-side limits
  • Token and credential limits
  • HTTP and WebSocket limits
  • Cluster limits
  • DAG limits

docs.title: Components per application
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none. The schema accepts any number of components rows linked to one applications row.
  • Recommended: ≤ 500 for a usable DAG visualization. Above this, the Map View becomes hard to navigate even with React Flow's optimizations.
  • What happens at the limit: No technical failure — performance degrades. The map's auto-layout step grows roughly O(n²); a 1000-node application takes several seconds to render initially.
  • Workaround for large apps: Split into multiple applications and reference one from another via a referenced app component type.

docs.title: Applications per organization
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • Recommended: plan capacity per Capacity Planning. The list endpoint (GET /apps) loads all applications the user has access to; for very large orgs this becomes a Postgres heavy-read.
  • What happens at the limit: Above ~5000 apps per user, the dashboard's initial load slows visibly. The user can filter by tag or site to recover responsiveness.

docs.title: Components per agent
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • Recommended: ≤ 500 per agent. The agent runs every component's checks on its local scheduler; CPU rises proportionally with the count.
  • What happens at the limit: The agent may exceed its RLIMIT_CPU for the host. Splitting work across multiple agents on the same host is supported via explicit AGENT_ID overrides.

docs.title: Sites and hostings per organization
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • Recommended: ≤ 50 sites, ≤ 20 hostings. Beyond that, the site picker in the UI becomes unwieldy.

docs.title: Users, teams, workspaces
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • Recommended: ≤ 5000 users, ≤ 1000 teams, ≤ 100 workspaces per organization.

docs.title: Action log row size
docs.text:
• stdout field truncation: the agent truncates both stdout and stderr to 4 KB per check before sending (see crates/agent/src/executor.rs). The same 4 KB-truncated payload is what ultimately lands in command_executions.stdout for sync commands.
  • Why 4 KB: A larger payload would dominate the WebSocket frame; check outputs are intended to be summaries, not full logs. If you need to inspect the full output of a one-off command, run it via the live terminal session feature (POST /api/v1/components/:id/terminal/open) which streams stdout/stderr in real time without truncation. A command_executions.stdout_chunks streaming table is on the roadmap; it is not yet implemented.

docs.title: action_log retention
docs.text:
• Default: RETENTION_ACTION_LOG_DAYS=0 (unlimited).
  • Recommended: 1825 (5 years) for DORA compliance.
  • What happens at the limit: When the daily retention task runs, rows older than the cutoff are archived to action_log_archive (not deleted — respects the append-only rule, see Phase 10 CHANGELOG entry).

docs.title: check_events retention
docs.text:
• Default: RETENTION_CHECK_EVENTS_DAYS=0 (unlimited).
  • Recommended: 90 for production (3 months of hot health-check history).
  • Mechanism: check_events is partitioned by month. The retention task drops entire partitions older than the cutoff. This is O(1) per partition — no row scan.
  • What happens at the limit: Older partitions are no longer queryable from PostgreSQL. If you need long-term retention for regulatory reasons, archive monthly partitions to cold storage before they are dropped. See Backup & Restore — Partitioned check_events.

docs.title: state_transitions, switchover_log, config_versions
docs.text:
• Retention: no separate knob; growth is moderate (state transitions are ~ 5 % of check rates).
  • Cleanup: none by default. These tables are essential audit; design for permanent retention.
  • What happens at the limit: Disk fills up. Plan storage growth from day one (see Capacity Planning — PostgreSQL).

docs.title: Rate limits
docs.text: All rate limits are configurable per organization via environment variables on the backend. Defaults below.

docs.title: Authentication endpoints
docs.text:
Variable Default Scope Endpoints RATE_LIMIT_AUTH 10 req / minute per IP Per source IP /auth/oidc/callback, /auth/saml/acs, /auth/login, /api-keys

What happens at the limit: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Response headers:

HTTP/2 429
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 32
Retry-After: 32

docs.title: Operation endpoints
docs.text:
Variable Default Scope Endpoints RATE_LIMIT_OPERATIONS 5 req / minute per user Per authenticated user POST /apps/:id/start, /stop, /switchover, /rebuild, etc.

The lower per-user limit is intentional: a single operator rarely needs more than 5 start/stop operations per minute. Schedulers using API keys are subject to the same per-user limit (where the API key counts as one user).

docs.title: Read endpoints
docs.text:
Variable Default Scope Endpoints RATE_LIMIT_READS 200 req / minute per user Per authenticated user All GET /api/v1/*

This is high enough to support live dashboards that poll the API. The frontend's React Query layer further reduces calls via caching.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
To raise limits, set the env var on the backend:

backend:
  env:
    RATE_LIMIT_AUTH:       "20"
    RATE_LIMIT_OPERATIONS: "10"
    RATE_LIMIT_READS:      "500"

To disable rate limiting (not recommended in production), set the value to 0. The limiter short-circuits before touching its counter, so RATE_LIMIT_AUTH=0, RATE_LIMIT_OPERATIONS=0 and RATE_LIMIT_READS=0 all behave as "unlimited". Disabling applies in both single-instance and HA_MODE=true deployments.

docs.title: HA mode
docs.text: When HA_MODE=true, rate-limit counters move from in-process DashMap to PostgreSQL (INCR + EXPIRE pattern). This is critical for multi-replica deployments — otherwise the limits are per-replica, not global.

docs.title: Backend DB pool
docs.text:
Variable Default Description DB_POOL_SIZE 20 Maximum connections per replica DB_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECS 600 Close idle connections after N seconds DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECS 30 Timeout for acquiring a connection from the pool

What happens at the limit:

  • Pool exhausted → new requests wait up to DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECS for a connection.
  • Timeout reached → backend returns 503 Service Unavailable with acquire timeout in the log.
  • See Troubleshooting — DB pool exhausted for the diagnosis flow.

docs.title: PostgreSQL max_connections
docs.text:
PostgreSQL itself has a global max_connections (default 100 in upstream, often 200 in managed services). Plan:

max_connections ≥ (replicas × DB_POOL_SIZE) + admin_headroom

Run PgBouncer in front of PostgreSQL if you need many replicas — see High Availability — Database HA.

docs.title: WebSocket: 1 connection per agent → gateway
docs.text: By design. Each agent maintains exactly one persistent WebSocket to its currently-selected gateway. Failover replaces the connection, never duplicates it.

docs.title: Gateway → Backend: 1 multiplexed WebSocket
docs.text:
Each gateway opens one WebSocket to the backend over which all agents' traffic is multiplexed. This means N gateways → N WebSockets at the backend, regardless of the agent count.

What happens at the limit: N is small (typically ≤ 10 gateways per install), so this is rarely a limit. If a gateway's WS is saturated, the gateway uses backpressure: when its 1024-message send buffer to an agent or 4096-message buffer to the backend fills, it drops messages with a warning log (see CHANGELOG Phase 8 "Bounded channels with backpressure").

docs.title: Per-gateway file descriptor limit
docs.text:
Each agent connection consumes one file descriptor on the gateway host. Defaults are:

  • Linux: ulimit -n 1024 by default — too tight for > 1024 agents.
  • Recommended: LimitNOFILE=65536 in the systemd unit or securityContext.sysctls in Kubernetes.

What happens at the limit: Accept fails with EMFILE; agents see "connection refused" and fail over.

docs.title: Disk buffer
docs.text:
• Storage backend: sled embedded KV store.
  • Path: /var/lib/appcontrol/buffer-{agent_id} (Linux), %PROGRAMDATA%\AppControl\buffer-{id} (Windows).
  • Default cap: ~ 100 MB (FIFO rotation).
  • What happens at the limit: Oldest entries are evicted to make room. The agent does not block check execution.

docs.title: Per-command resource limits
docs.text:
The agent today enforces a wall-clock timeout only on sync commands; it does not call setrlimit(2) on child processes. Hardening the child via RLIMIT_CPU, RLIMIT_AS, RLIMIT_NOFILE, RLIMIT_NPROC etc. is the responsibility of the system service manager that supervises the agent (systemd unit, Windows service).

Mechanism Value Notes Sync check timeout per-component check_interval_seconds (default 120 s) When the deadline is hit, the agent kills the process group (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 5 s grace) and reports exit_code = -1. Async start/stop/rebuild no agent-enforced timeout These commands are double-forked and intentionally inherit the parent shell context to support long-running services.

If you need OS-level resource caps on the agent itself or on the commands it spawns, configure them in your systemd unit (e.g. LimitCPU=, MemoryMax=, LimitNOFILE=, LimitNPROC=) — those are inherited by every child the agent forks. Per-command resource limits inside the agent are on the roadmap; this page will be updated if and when they ship.

docs.title: Check command deduplication
docs.text:
If multiple components on the same agent share the same check_cmd (verbatim), the agent executes it once per scheduling tick and shares the result. Key: SHA-256 of the command string.

  • Hard limit: none.
  • Implication: changing the command (even whitespace) invalidates the dedup key.

docs.title: Enrollment tokens
docs.text:
Field Default Hard limit max_uses 1 none valid_hours 24 none (but recommended ≤ 168 / 7 days) Token format ac_enroll_<28 random chars> n/a
  • What happens at max_uses: Next enrollment request returns HTTP 409 Conflict. The token must be regenerated.
  • What happens at expiry: HTTP 410 Gone. Same fix.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Field Default Hard limit expires_in_days none (caller-supplied) none name length 1–100 chars varchar(100) in api_keys table Rate of use n/a — only the API-level rate limit applies n/a Number of keys per user none none

Recommendation: set expires_in_days: 90 for production. See Hardening — API key rotation.

docs.title: Share links
docs.text: Field Default Hard limit max_uses unlimited none expires_at unlimited none Permission level granted configurable up to manage (cannot grant owner via a link)

docs.title: JWT tokens
docs.text:
• Expiry: 24 hours.
  • Refresh: the frontend silently refreshes when < 5 min remain.
  • Revocation: entries in the revoked_tokens table block reuse until natural expiry.

docs.title: HTTP request size
docs.text:
• Default: Axum's default body limit is 2 MB. Configurable in code, not via env var.
  • What happens at the limit: HTTP 413 Payload Too Large.
  • Relevant endpoints:
  • POST /apps/:id/import — YAML/JSON application import. The 2 MB ceiling allows ~ 5000 components per import.
  • POST /admin/agent-binaries — agent binary upload. Increased to 50 MiB via a per-route DefaultBodyLimit::max(50 MiB) layer (see crates/backend/src/api/mod.rs::AGENT_BINARY_UPLOAD_LIMIT_BYTES). Sized for a base64-encoded Rust agent binary plus its JSON envelope.

docs.title: Request timeout
docs.text:
• Default: no global timeout (axum); per-route timeouts vary.
  • WebSocket idle timeout: 60 s heartbeat + 30 s grace = ~ 90 s before the server forcibly closes a silent socket.
  • Long operations: operations that take > 60 s return an operation_id immediately; the client polls or watches a WebSocket for progress.

docs.title: WebSocket message size
docs.text:
• Default: 64 MB per frame (tokio-tungstenite default).
  • Practical limit: most frames are < 1 KB; large ones come from UpdateConfig snapshots with many components.

docs.title: CORS preflight
docs.text: • Cache: Access-Control-Max-Age: 600 (10 min). Browsers cache the preflight result.

docs.title: Members per fan-out cluster
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • Recommended: ≤ 100. Each member is an independently-monitored entity; the parent state is computed by the cluster health policy over all members.
  • What happens at the limit: Performance degrades. The state-rollup query (SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE current_state = 'RUNNING') ... FROM cluster_member_state) scales linearly. At 1000+ members, expect 50–100 ms rollup latency.

docs.title: Aggregate clusters
docs.text: Aggregate clusters have no native limit because they are represented by a single component — the user-defined check_cmd handles cluster-wide aggregation externally.

docs.title: Cluster member overrides
docs.text: Each cluster_members row may override check_cmd, start_cmd, stop_cmd, env_vars. Overrides are unbounded in count.

docs.title: Depth (longest dependency chain)
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • Tested up to: 50 levels deep.
  • What happens at the limit: Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) is O(V + E). Operations on very deep DAGs serialize sequentially because each level must complete before the next starts.

docs.title: Width (parallelism per level)
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • Tested up to: 200 components in parallel.
  • What happens at the limit: All components at the same level are dispatched in parallel via tokio::join!. Bottleneck becomes the agent's ability to handle concurrent ExecuteCommand frames.

docs.title: Total edges
docs.text:
• Hard limit: none.
  • What happens at the limit: Cycle detection in import / edit becomes slower (O(V + E) per check). For 10 000+ edges, this may take seconds.

docs.title: Cycle detection
docs.text:
• AppControl rejects cycles at write time (import, edit). The check uses Kahn's algorithm: if the topological sort fails (count < |V|), a cycle exists.
  • HTTP 400 Bad Request is returned with the offending cycle nodes in the error body.

docs.title: HTTP probes
docs.text:
For check_native = { "kind": "http", ... }:

  • Default timeout: 5 s (in the spec).
  • Max URL length: 8 KB (curl's limit).
  • Max response inspected: 64 KB (then truncated).
  • Headers: any user-provided headers.

docs.title: TCP probes (planned)
docs.text: • Default timeout: 3 s.

docs.title: Process probes (planned)
docs.text: • Implementation: name-matching via sysinfo — no limit on process count scanned.

docs.title: What happens at the limit — summary table
docs.text: Limit Default At the limit Rate limit 10/200/5 per min HTTP 429 DB pool 20 conns HTTP 503 after 30 s wait action_log retention unlimited rows archived check_events retention unlimited oldest partition dropped Agent disk buffer 100 MB FIFO eviction RLIMIT_CPU (checks) 30 s process killed Enrollment token max_uses 1 HTTP 409 Enrollment token validity 24 h HTTP 410 API key expiry none set HTTP 401 HTTP body 2 MB HTTP 413 Gateway agent connections open fds accept fails (EMFILE) DAG cycle in edit/import n/a HTTP 400

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Capacity Planning — how to size the install to stay within limits
  • High Availability — pool sizing for multi-replica deployments
  • Troubleshooting — diagnostic flows when a limit is hit
  • Hardening — recommended retention and rate-limit values for production
  • migrations/V005__event_tables.sql — check_events partition definition
  • migrations/V016__fsm_cache_notifications_locks.sql — operation lock schema

docs.title: Component logs
docs.text: AppControl can retrieve logs from the agent assigned to a component. Open an application map, select a component, then open Logs.

docs.title: Choose the right source
docs.text:
Source Configuration Persistence Best use Command output None Stored by AppControl Inspect stdout/stderr and status returned by start, stop and custom commands Live process output None In-memory agent buffer Inspect recent stdout/stderr emitted while the agent is connected Log file Absolute path on the agent machine Stored by the application Tail Linux or Windows application logs Windows Event Log Log name, with optional source and level Stored by Windows Inspect Application, System or Security events Diagnostic command A read-only command Result shown on demand Query application or operating-system status through the agent

Command output and live process output are different. Command output is the audited history of commands executed by AppControl. The live process source is the agent's bounded, in-memory buffer and is cleared when the agent restarts.

docs.title: Add a source in the UI
docs.text:
1. Assign an enrolled agent to the component.
  2. Open the component's Logs tab.
  3. Select +.
  4. Choose Log File, Windows Event Log or Diagnostic Command.
  5. Enter a display name and the source-specific values.

For a file source, use an absolute path that exists on the agent machine, such as /var/log/my-application/application.log or C:\ProgramData\MyApplication\logs\application.log.

For a Windows event source:

  • Event Log Name is normally Application, System or Security.
  • Event Source is optional and restricts results to one Windows provider.
  • The agent service account must have permission to read the selected log.

The Logs tab supports a line limit, a time range and a text filter. Requests are limited to 1,000 lines to protect the agent and backend.

Diagnostic commands run synchronously through the assigned agent and display their exit code, duration, stdout and stderr in the same tab. Start and stop commands use detached execution; their persisted return confirms whether the process was launched, while subsequent application output must be read from the application's file, Windows Event Log, or another configured source.

docs.title: Add a source with the API
docs.text:
Set the connection values once:

export APPCONTROL_URL="https://appcontrol.example.com"
export APPCONTROL_TOKEN="<access-token>"
export COMPONENT_ID="<component-uuid>"

Create a Linux file source from the supplied example:

curl --fail-with-body \
  -X POST "$APPCONTROL_URL/api/v1/components/$COMPONENT_ID/log-sources" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APPCONTROL_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data @examples/log-source-file.json

For Windows Event Log, adapt examples/log-source-windows-event.json, especially event_log_source, then send it to the same endpoint.

Retrieve live process output:

curl --fail-with-body \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APPCONTROL_TOKEN" \
  "$APPCONTROL_URL/api/v1/components/$COMPONENT_ID/logs?source=process&lines=100&since=1h"

Retrieve a configured file or event source by using the source UUID returned when it was created:

SOURCE_ID="<log-source-uuid>"
curl --fail-with-body \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $APPCONTROL_TOKEN" \
  "$APPCONTROL_URL/api/v1/components/$COMPONENT_ID/logs?source=$SOURCE_ID&lines=200&filter=ERROR&since=24h"

docs.title: Permissions and sensitive logs
docs.text:
• Viewing logs requires Operate permission on the component.
  • Creating, changing or deleting a source requires Edit permission.
  • Mark a source as sensitive when it can expose credentials, personal data or business data. Sensitive sources require Edit permission even for reads.
  • Every log access is written to the AppControl audit trail.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check No agent is assigned Assign an enrolled agent to the component HTTP 503 Confirm that the agent and its gateway are connected File cannot be read Verify the absolute path and agent service-account permissions Windows Event Log is empty Verify the log name, provider filter, level and service-account permissions Live process output is empty Run a component command and confirm the agent has not restarted

Log retrieval times out after 30 seconds. File and event-log errors returned by the agent are surfaced by the API rather than replaced with empty results.

docs.title: Component Metrics
docs.text: AppControl supports generic metrics extraction from check commands. Any check script (health, integrity, infrastructure) can return structured JSON data that gets stored, visualized, and used for dashboards.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When a check command runs, AppControl inspects its stdout for JSON data. If found, the metrics are:

  1. Stored in the check_events table alongside the check result
  2. Displayed in the component detail panel
  3. Available for historical charts and dashboards
  4. Accessible via API for external integrations

This approach is non-intrusive: existing scripts continue to work unchanged. Simply add JSON output to enable metrics.

docs.title: Output Formats
docs.text: AppControl supports four detection strategies, tried in order:

docs.title: 1. Pure JSON (Recommended for new scripts)
docs.text:
The entire stdout is a valid JSON object:

#!/bin/bash
# health_check.sh - Pure JSON output

CONNECTIONS=$(netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED | wc -l)
MEMORY_MB=$(free -m | awk '/^Mem:/{print $3}')
UPTIME_HOURS=$(awk '{print int($1/3600)}' /proc/uptime)

cat <<EOF
{
  "connections": $CONNECTIONS,
  "memory_mb": $MEMORY_MB,
  "uptime_hours": $UPTIME_HOURS,
  "status": "healthy"
}
EOF

exit 0

docs.title: 2. Tagged Format (<appcontrol>...</appcontrol>)
docs.text:
Embed metrics within normal log output using XML-style tags:

#!/bin/bash
# health_check.sh - Tagged format

echo "[INFO] Starting health check..."
echo "[INFO] Checking database connections..."

CONNECTIONS=$(netstat -an | grep :5432 | grep ESTABLISHED | wc -l)
QUERIES_PER_SEC=$(psql -t -c "SELECT xact_commit FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname='mydb'")

echo "[INFO] Health check complete"

# Metrics embedded in tags (ignored by normal log processing)
echo "<appcontrol>{\"connections\": $CONNECTIONS, \"qps\": $QUERIES_PER_SEC}</appcontrol>"

exit 0

docs.title: 3. Marker Format (---METRICS---)
docs.text:
Use a clear marker to separate logs from metrics:

#!/bin/bash
# health_check.sh - Marker format

echo "Checking service health..."
systemctl is-active myservice || exit 1

RESPONSE_TIME=$(curl -w "%{time_total}" -o /dev/null -s http://localhost:8080/health)
ACTIVE_SESSIONS=$(redis-cli GET active_sessions)

echo "Service is healthy"
echo "---METRICS---"
cat <<EOF
{
  "response_time_ms": $(echo "$RESPONSE_TIME * 1000" | bc),
  "active_sessions": $ACTIVE_SESSIONS
}
EOF

exit 0

docs.title: 4. Auto-Detect (Last JSON Line)
docs.text:
AppControl scans stdout backwards for the last line that is a valid JSON object:

#!/bin/bash
# health_check.sh - Auto-detect (last JSON line)

echo "[2024-01-15 10:30:45] Starting health check"
echo "[2024-01-15 10:30:45] Checking process status..."
echo "[2024-01-15 10:30:46] Process myapp is running (PID 12345)"
echo "[2024-01-15 10:30:46] Checking memory usage..."
echo "[2024-01-15 10:30:46] Memory: 1.2GB / 4GB"
echo "[2024-01-15 10:30:46] Health check passed"

# Last line is JSON - automatically detected
echo '{"memory_gb": 1.2, "memory_percent": 30, "pid": 12345}'

exit 0

docs.title: Metric Data Structure
docs.text: Metrics can contain any valid JSON object. Common patterns:

docs.title: Simple Key-Value Metrics
docs.text:
{
  "cpu_percent": 45.2,
  "memory_mb": 2048,
  "disk_percent": 67,
  "connections": 150
}

docs.title: Nested Structures
docs.text:
{
  "database": {
    "connections": 50,
    "queries_per_sec": 1200,
    "cache_hit_ratio": 0.95
  },
  "http": {
    "requests_per_sec": 500,
    "avg_response_ms": 45,
    "error_rate": 0.02
  }
}

docs.title: With Widget Hints
docs.text:
Add _widget suffix to suggest display type:

{
  "cpu_percent": 78,
  "cpu_percent_widget": "gauge",
  "memory_breakdown": {
    "heap": 512,
    "stack": 64,
    "native": 128
  },
  "memory_breakdown_widget": "pie",
  "recent_requests": [100, 120, 95, 140, 130],
  "recent_requests_widget": "sparkline"
}

docs.title: Widget Types
docs.text:
The UI supports multiple widget types for metric visualization:

Widget Use Case Data Format number Single value display 42, "1.5GB" gauge Percentage/progress 0-100 number status OK/Warning/Error indicator "ok", "warning", "error" sparkline Mini trend chart Array of numbers bars Horizontal bar chart {"label": value, ...} pie Pie/donut chart {"label": value, ...} table Tabular data Array of objects list Simple list Array of strings text Formatted text String

docs.title: Widget Examples
docs.text:
Gauge (CPU/Memory usage): 

{
  "cpu_percent": 72,
  "cpu_percent_widget": "gauge"
}

Sparkline (Request trend): 

{
  "requests_1h": [120, 145, 132, 198, 176, 154],
  "requests_1h_widget": "sparkline"
}

Pie (Memory breakdown): 

{
  "memory": {
    "Java Heap": 2048,
    "Native": 512,
    "Metaspace": 256
  },
  "memory_widget": "pie"
}

Table (Top processes): 

{
  "top_processes": [
    {"name": "java", "cpu": 45, "memory": 2048},
    {"name": "nginx", "cpu": 12, "memory": 128},
    {"name": "redis", "cpu": 8, "memory": 512}
  ],
  "top_processes_widget": "table"
}

Bars (Resource distribution): 

{
  "disk_usage": {
    "/data": 75,
    "/logs": 45,
    "/tmp": 20
  },
  "disk_usage_widget": "bars"
}

docs.title: Display Locations
docs.text: Metrics appear in multiple places in the UI:

docs.title: 1. Component Detail Panel
docs.text: When you click a component, the detail panel shows: - Latest metrics with appropriate widgets - Historical chart for numeric values - Last updated timestamp

docs.title: 2. Node Tooltips
docs.text: Hovering over a component node shows key metrics as a quick summary.

docs.title: 3. Dashboard Cards
docs.text: Create dashboard cards that aggregate metrics across components: - Application-level summaries - Cross-component comparisons - Alert thresholds

docs.title: 4. Fullscreen View
docs.text: Expand any metric to fullscreen for detailed analysis with historical data.

docs.title: Get Latest Metrics
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/components/{id}/metrics

Response:
{
  "component_id": "uuid",
  "metrics": {
    "cpu_percent": 45,
    "memory_mb": 2048
  },
  "at": "2024-01-15T10:30:46Z"
}

docs.title: Get Metrics History
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/components/{id}/metrics/history?limit=100

Response:
{
  "component_id": "uuid",
  "history": [
    {
      "metrics": {"cpu_percent": 45, "memory_mb": 2048},
      "at": "2024-01-15T10:30:46Z"
    },
    {
      "metrics": {"cpu_percent": 42, "memory_mb": 2010},
      "at": "2024-01-15T10:30:16Z"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Database Health Check (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

DB_NAME="${1:-mydb}"
HOST="${2:-localhost}"

# Check connection
pg_isready -h "$HOST" -d "$DB_NAME" > /dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1

# Gather metrics
read CONNECTIONS ACTIVE_QUERIES <<< $(psql -h "$HOST" -d "$DB_NAME" -t -A -c "
  SELECT
    (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity),
    (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active')
")

CACHE_HIT=$(psql -h "$HOST" -d "$DB_NAME" -t -A -c "
  SELECT round(100.0 * sum(blks_hit) / nullif(sum(blks_hit + blks_read), 0), 2)
  FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = '$DB_NAME'
")

DB_SIZE=$(psql -h "$HOST" -d "$DB_NAME" -t -A -c "
  SELECT pg_database_size('$DB_NAME') / 1024 / 1024
")

cat <<EOF
{
  "connections": $CONNECTIONS,
  "active_queries": $ACTIVE_QUERIES,
  "cache_hit_ratio": $CACHE_HIT,
  "cache_hit_ratio_widget": "gauge",
  "database_size_mb": $DB_SIZE
}
EOF

exit 0

docs.title: Java Application Health Check
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

PID_FILE="${1:-/var/run/myapp.pid}"
JMX_PORT="${2:-9999}"

# Check process
if [ ! -f "$PID_FILE" ]; then
  echo '{"status": "error", "message": "PID file not found"}'
  exit 1
fi

PID=$(cat "$PID_FILE")
if ! kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo '{"status": "error", "message": "Process not running"}'
  exit 1
fi

# Get JVM metrics via jstat
HEAP_USED=$(jstat -gc "$PID" | tail -1 | awk '{print ($3+$4+$6+$8)/1024}')
HEAP_MAX=$(jstat -gc "$PID" | tail -1 | awk '{print ($1+$2+$5+$7)/1024}')
GC_COUNT=$(jstat -gc "$PID" | tail -1 | awk '{print $13+$15}')
GC_TIME=$(jstat -gc "$PID" | tail -1 | awk '{print $14+$16}')

# Get thread count
THREADS=$(jstack "$PID" 2>/dev/null | grep -c "^\"" || echo 0)

cat <<EOF
{
  "heap_used_mb": $(printf "%.0f" $HEAP_USED),
  "heap_max_mb": $(printf "%.0f" $HEAP_MAX),
  "heap_percent": $(echo "scale=1; $HEAP_USED * 100 / $HEAP_MAX" | bc),
  "heap_percent_widget": "gauge",
  "gc_count": $GC_COUNT,
  "gc_time_ms": $(printf "%.0f" $GC_TIME),
  "thread_count": $THREADS
}
EOF

exit 0

docs.title: Web Service Health Check
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
set -e

URL="${1:-http://localhost:8080/health}"
TIMEOUT="${2:-5}"

# Make request and capture timing
RESPONSE=$(curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}\n%{time_total}" \
  --connect-timeout "$TIMEOUT" \
  -o /tmp/health_response.txt \
  "$URL" 2>/dev/null)

HTTP_CODE=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | tail -2 | head -1)
RESPONSE_TIME=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | tail -1)

if [ "$HTTP_CODE" != "200" ]; then
  echo "{\"status\": \"error\", \"http_code\": $HTTP_CODE}"
  exit 1
fi

# Parse response if JSON
BODY=$(cat /tmp/health_response.txt 2>/dev/null || echo "{}")

cat <<EOF
{
  "http_code": $HTTP_CODE,
  "response_time_ms": $(echo "$RESPONSE_TIME * 1000" | bc | cut -d. -f1),
  "response_time_ms_widget": "number",
  "upstream_status": $(echo "$BODY" | jq -c '.checks // {}')
}
EOF

exit 0

docs.title: Windows Service Health Check (PowerShell)
docs.text:
# health_check.ps1
param(
    [string]$ServiceName = "MyService"
)

$service = Get-Service -Name $ServiceName -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

if (-not $service) {
    @{status = "error"; message = "Service not found"} | ConvertTo-Json
    exit 1
}

if ($service.Status -ne "Running") {
    @{status = "error"; service_status = $service.Status} | ConvertTo-Json
    exit 1
}

# Get process metrics
$process = Get-Process -Name $ServiceName -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

$metrics = @{
    status = "ok"
    service_status = $service.Status.ToString()
}

if ($process) {
    $metrics["cpu_percent"] = [math]::Round($process.CPU, 2)
    $metrics["memory_mb"] = [math]::Round($process.WorkingSet64 / 1MB, 0)
    $metrics["memory_mb_widget"] = "number"
    $metrics["thread_count"] = $process.Threads.Count
    $metrics["handle_count"] = $process.HandleCount
}

$metrics | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
exit 0

docs.title: 1. Keep Metrics Small
docs.text:
Metrics are stored with every check execution (default: every 30 seconds). Keep the JSON payload small:

// Good - focused metrics
{"cpu": 45, "mem": 2048, "conns": 150}

// Avoid - too verbose
{"cpu_usage_percent_current": 45.234567, "memory_usage_megabytes": 2048.123456, ...}

docs.title: 2. Use Consistent Keys
docs.text:
Use the same metric keys across check runs to enable historical charting:

// Consistent - enables trending
{"qps": 1200}  // Run 1
{"qps": 1250}  // Run 2
{"qps": 1180}  // Run 3

// Avoid - breaks trending
{"queries_per_second": 1200}  // Run 1
{"qps": 1250}                 // Run 2
{"queryRate": 1180}           // Run 3

docs.title: 3. Include Status Indicators
docs.text:
Add status fields for quick visual assessment:

{
  "db_status": "ok",
  "cache_status": "warning",
  "queue_status": "ok",
  "overall_status": "warning"
}

docs.title: 4. Widget Hints are Optional
docs.text:
The UI auto-detects appropriate widgets based on data type. Add _widget hints only when you need specific visualization:

{
  "cpu": 75,           // Auto: gauge (0-100 range detected)
  "memory_mb": 2048,   // Auto: number
  "errors": [1,0,2,0,1] // Auto: sparkline (array of numbers)
}

docs.title: 5. Handle Errors Gracefully
docs.text:
Return error information in JSON format:

{
  "status": "error",
  "error_code": "DB_CONNECTION_FAILED",
  "message": "Could not connect to database",
  "last_successful_check": "2024-01-15T10:25:00Z"
}

docs.title: Storage and Retention
docs.text:
Metrics are stored in the check_events table:

CREATE TABLE check_events (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    component_id UUID NOT NULL,
    check_type VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- health, integrity, infrastructure
    exit_code SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    stdout TEXT,
    duration_ms INTEGER,
    metrics JSONB,                     -- Extracted JSON metrics
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Index for efficient metrics queries
CREATE INDEX idx_check_events_metrics
    ON check_events (component_id, created_at DESC)
    WHERE metrics IS NOT NULL;

Default retention: 30 days. Configure via CHECK_EVENTS_RETENTION_DAYS environment variable.

docs.title: Metrics Not Appearing
docs.text:
1. Check JSON validity: Use jq to validate your output 

    ./health_check.sh | jq .

  2. Verify extraction: Check agent logs for "extracted metrics" entries

  3. Check database: Query check_events directly 

    SELECT metrics FROM check_events
WHERE component_id = 'your-id'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;

docs.title: Large Metrics Causing Issues
docs.text: If metrics are too large (>64KB), they may be truncated. Solutions: - Reduce metric granularity - Remove verbose nested structures - Use summary statistics instead of raw data

docs.title: Mixed Output Parsing
docs.text: If auto-detect picks the wrong JSON line: - Use ---METRICS--- marker for explicit separation - Or output pure JSON (no log lines)

docs.title: Migration Guide: From Scripts & Templates to AppControl
docs.text: Step-by-step guide for teams migrating from shell scripts, XL Release templates, or scheduler-managed restarts to AppControl.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Most teams don't start from zero — they already have operational procedures encoded in scripts, templates, or schedulers. This guide helps you migrate progressively without disrupting existing operations.

docs.title: Migration Phases
docs.text:
Phase 1: Model      →  Import your application topology
Phase 2: Observe    →  Deploy agents in advisory mode
Phase 3: Validate   →  Compare existing procedures with AppControl's DAG
Phase 4: Integrate  →  Existing tools call AppControl instead of scripts
Phase 5: Operate    →  AppControl handles operations natively

docs.title: Step 1.1: Identify Components
docs.text:
List all processes/services that make up your application:

Component Host Type Start Command Stop Command Check Command PostgreSQL db-01.prod database systemctl start postgresql systemctl stop postgresql pg_isready -h localhost Redis cache-01.prod cache systemctl start redis systemctl stop redis redis-cli ping API Server app-01.prod application /opt/api/start.sh /opt/api/stop.sh curl -f http://localhost:8080/health Web Frontend web-01.prod webserver systemctl start nginx systemctl stop nginx curl -f http://localhost:80/

docs.title: Step 1.2: Identify Dependencies
docs.text:
Map which components depend on which (who must start first):

Component Depends On API Server PostgreSQL, Redis Web Frontend API Server PostgreSQL (none) Redis (none)

docs.title: Step 1.3: Import into AppControl
docs.text:
Option A: YAML Import

Create a YAML file matching AppControl's import format:

application:
  name: billing-prod
  description: Production billing application
  components:
    - name: PostgreSQL
      type: database
      host: db-01.prod
      start_cmd: "systemctl start postgresql"
      stop_cmd: "systemctl stop postgresql"
      check_cmd: "pg_isready -h localhost"
      check_interval_seconds: 30
    - name: Redis
      type: cache
      host: cache-01.prod
      start_cmd: "systemctl start redis"
      stop_cmd: "systemctl stop redis"
      check_cmd: "redis-cli ping"
      check_interval_seconds: 15
    - name: API Server
      type: application
      host: app-01.prod
      start_cmd: "/opt/api/start.sh"
      stop_cmd: "/opt/api/stop.sh"
      check_cmd: "curl -sf http://localhost:8080/health"
      start_timeout_seconds: 120
    - name: Web Frontend
      type: webserver
      host: web-01.prod
      start_cmd: "systemctl start nginx"
      stop_cmd: "systemctl stop nginx"
      check_cmd: "curl -sf http://localhost:80/"
  dependencies:
    - from: API Server
      to: PostgreSQL
    - from: API Server
      to: Redis
    - from: Web Frontend
      to: API Server

Upload via UI (Import page) or API: 

curl -X POST https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/import/yaml \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $JWT_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-yaml" \
  --data-binary @billing-prod.yaml

Option B: UI Wizard

Use the onboarding wizard at /onboarding to create components visually with drag-and-drop dependency mapping.

Option C: API Calls

Create components and dependencies programmatically: 

# Create application
APP_ID=$(curl -s -X POST /api/v1/apps \
  -d '{"name":"billing-prod","site_id":"..."}' | jq -r '.id')

# Create components
PG_ID=$(curl -s -X POST /api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/components \
  -d '{"name":"PostgreSQL","component_type":"database","host":"db-01.prod",...}' | jq -r '.id')

# Create dependencies
curl -X POST /api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/dependencies \
  -d '{"from_component_id":"'$API_ID'","to_component_id":"'$PG_ID'"}'

docs.title: Phase 2: Observe (Advisory Mode)
docs.text: Deploy AppControl agents on your servers in advisory mode. Agents will: - Run health check commands (check_cmd) on their normal schedule - Report component state (RUNNING/STOPPED/FAILED) to the backend - NOT execute any start/stop/rebuild commands

docs.title: Step 2.1: Install Agents
docs.text:
# On each server, install the agent
curl -LO https://releases.appcontrol.io/agent/latest/appcontrol-agent
chmod +x appcontrol-agent
mv appcontrol-agent /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: Step 2.2: Configure Advisory Mode
docs.text:
Create /etc/appcontrol/agent.yaml:

agent:
  id: auto
mode: advisory    # <-- observation only, no command execution
gateway:
  urls:
    - wss://gateway.example.com:4443/ws
tls:
  enabled: true
  cert_file: /etc/appcontrol/agent.pem
  key_file: /etc/appcontrol/agent-key.pem
  ca_file: /etc/appcontrol/ca.pem

Or via environment variable: 

export AGENT_MODE=advisory

docs.title: Step 2.3: Enroll and Start
docs.text:
# Enroll agent with gateway
appcontrol-agent --enroll https://gateway.example.com:4443 --token YOUR_TOKEN

# Start the agent
systemctl start appcontrol-agent

docs.title: Step 2.4: Verify Observation
docs.text: Open the AppControl UI → Map View. You should see components with real-time health states, all driven by check commands. The agents are monitoring but not controlling.

docs.title: Step 3.1: Compare Existing Procedures
docs.text:
If you have an XL Release template or script that defines a restart order, validate it:

# Your current script restarts in this order:
# 1. PostgreSQL  2. Redis  3. API Server  4. Web Frontend

curl -X POST https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/validate-sequence \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sequence": ["PostgreSQL", "Redis", "API Server", "Web Frontend"],
    "operation": "start"
  }'

If valid: 

{"valid": true, "conflicts": []}

If conflicts found: 

{
  "valid": false,
  "conflicts": [
    {
      "dependent": "API Server",
      "dependency": "Redis",
      "message": "'API Server' depends on 'Redis' but starts at position 1 while Redis is at position 2"
    }
  ]
}

Fix the conflict in AppControl's DAG (or in your script, if the script was actually correct).

docs.title: Step 3.2: Get the Correct Execution Plan
docs.text:
curl -s https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/plan?operation=start \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY" | jq '.plan.levels'

This shows exactly what AppControl would do, level by level.

docs.title: Step 3.3: Dry Run
docs.text:
Test the actual start logic without executing commands:

appctl start billing-prod --dry-run

docs.title: Step 4.1: Replace Scripts with AppControl Calls
docs.text:
Before (shell script): 

#!/bin/bash
ssh db-01.prod "systemctl start postgresql"
sleep 10
ssh cache-01.prod "systemctl start redis"
sleep 5
ssh app-01.prod "/opt/api/start.sh"
sleep 15
ssh web-01.prod "systemctl start nginx"

After (AppControl CLI): 

#!/bin/bash
appctl start billing-prod --wait --timeout 300

After (AppControl API from another tool): 

curl -X POST https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/orchestration/apps/$APP_ID/start \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY"
curl -s https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/orchestration/apps/$APP_ID/wait-running?timeout=300 \
  -H "Authorization: ApiKey $AC_API_KEY"

docs.title: Step 4.2: Replace XL Release Templates
docs.text: Replace multi-step restart templates with a single API call. See the Integration Cookbook for XL Release-specific recipes.

docs.title: Step 4.3: Replace Scheduler Custom Scripts
docs.text: Scheduler jobs now call appctl or the REST API. Dependencies are managed by AppControl, not by scheduler job chains. See the Integration Cookbook for Control-M/AutoSys/Dollar Universe recipes.

docs.title: Step 5.1: Switch Agents to Active Mode
docs.text:
Update agent configuration:

mode: active    # <-- full control mode

Or: 

export AGENT_MODE=active
systemctl restart appcontrol-agent

docs.title: Step 5.2: Decommission Old Scripts
docs.text:
• Archive (don't delete) old scripts in version control
  • Remove restart templates from XL Release
  • Simplify scheduler job chains to single AppControl calls
  • Update runbooks to reference AppControl instead of manual procedures

docs.title: Step 5.3: Enable Advanced Features
docs.text:
Now that AppControl is the operational authority:

  • DR Switchover: Configure multi-site failover
  • 3-Level Diagnostics: Add integrity and infrastructure check commands
  • Approval Workflows: Enable 4-eyes principle for production operations
  • DORA Reporting: Access compliance metrics and audit trails
  • Webhooks: Route state change alerts to PagerDuty/ServiceNow

docs.title: Identifying Hidden Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependencies aren't always documented. Look for clues in:

  • Sleep commands in scripts: sleep 30 between starts often hides a dependency
  • Retry loops: "Start X, check if Y is ready, retry" means X depends on Y
  • Error messages: "Connection refused to database" in logs means the service depends on the database
  • Startup order in systemd: After=postgresql.service in unit files
  • Network connections: netstat -tlnp shows what each process connects to at startup

docs.title: Handling Components Without Check Commands
docs.text:
If a component has no obvious health check command:

Component Type Suggested check_cmd Systemd service systemctl is-active service-name Process pgrep -f process-name TCP port nc -z localhost PORT or bash -c '</dev/tcp/localhost/PORT' HTTP service curl -sf http://localhost:PORT/health Database pg_isready / mysqladmin ping / mongo --eval 'db.runCommand("ping")'

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Don't try to model everything at once. Start with one critical application, prove the value, then expand.
  2. Don't skip advisory mode. Running in observation before taking control prevents surprises.
  3. Don't delete old scripts immediately. Keep them archived as fallback for the first few weeks.
  4. Don't ignore timeouts. Set realistic start_timeout_seconds and stop_timeout_seconds based on observed behavior.
  5. Don't forget optional components. Mark non-critical components as is_optional: true so they don't block the whole application start.

docs.title: Deploying and testing AppControl on OpenShift
docs.text: The Helm chart in helm/appcontrol is the single source of truth for both Kubernetes and OpenShift. The OpenShift profile adds a TLS Route, disables Ingress, and leaves UID/GID selection to the namespace Security Context Constraint (SCC).

docs.title: What is tested
docs.text:
The OpenShift GitHub Actions workflow has two levels:

  1. Every relevant pull request renders and lints the chart, checks the Route, and rejects fixed UIDs/GIDs, privileged containers, or incomplete restricted-v2 security contexts.
  2. Manual and scheduled runs deploy AppControl to a real OpenShift cluster, verify the SCC selected by admission, deploy an agent, and execute the same start/check/stop/restart scenario as the local full-stack E2E test.

The CI does not install an OpenShift cluster inside a GitHub-hosted runner. OpenShift Local requires a virtual machine and is not suitable for nested virtualization there. Instead, the workflow connects to an existing cluster.

docs.title: Red Hat Developer Sandbox
docs.text:
The no-cost Red Hat Developer Sandbox is suitable for this E2E job. It is a shared, quota-limited trial environment, so use one dedicated project and let the workflow remove its release after every run.

  1. Start a sandbox from Red Hat Developer Sandbox.
  2. In the OpenShift console, open Copy login command, then Display Token.
  3. Record the three values shown by:
oc whoami --show-server
oc whoami -t
oc project -q
  1. In the GitHub repository, create these Actions secrets:
Secret Value OPENSHIFT_SERVER Output of oc whoami --show-server OPENSHIFT_TOKEN Output of oc whoami -t OPENSHIFT_NAMESPACE Output of oc project -q

Tokens and sandbox instances expire. Replace OPENSHIFT_TOKEN when login starts failing, and update all three values when a new sandbox is provisioned.

docs.title: Launch the CI deployment
docs.text:
After the workflow is present on GitHub:

  1. Open Actions → OpenShift.
  2. Select Run workflow.
  3. Select the branch to test.
  4. Follow the Real OpenShift deployment and execution job.

The normal CI / Docker Build matrix builds backend, frontend, gateway, and agent once, in parallel, and publishes immutable SHA-tagged images to GHCR. The OpenShift job verifies and consumes those exact images; it does not rebuild them. It then creates short-lived secrets, installs the chart, runs the E2E scenario, uploads diagnostics on failure, and removes only resources belonging to its appcontrol-e2e release.

Scheduled workflows run only from the default branch. The weekly schedule therefore becomes active after this change is merged into main.

docs.title: Manual Helm deployment
docs.text:
Production deployments should use an external or operator-managed PostgreSQL database. Create secrets without placing credentials in a values file:

oc create secret generic appcontrol-database \
  --from-literal=database-url='postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5432/appcontrol'

oc create secret generic appcontrol-jwt \
  --from-literal=jwt-secret="$(openssl rand -hex 48)"

Deploy:

helm upgrade --install appcontrol helm/appcontrol \
  --namespace "$(oc project -q)" \
  -f helm/appcontrol/values-openshift.yaml \
  --set backend.database.existingSecret=appcontrol-database \
  --set backend.jwt.existingSecret=appcontrol-jwt \
  --set backend.image.repository=REGISTRY/appcontrol-backend \
  --set frontend.image.repository=REGISTRY/appcontrol-frontend \
  --set gateway.image.repository=REGISTRY/appcontrol-gateway \
  --set backend.image.tag=VERSION \
  --set frontend.image.tag=VERSION \
  --set gateway.image.tag=VERSION \
  --wait --timeout 12m

Retrieve the generated Route:

oc get route appcontrol -o jsonpath='https://{.spec.host}{"\n"}'

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
The chart is designed for restricted-v2 and restricted-v3:

  • no fixed runAsUser, runAsGroup, or fsGroup;
  • runAsNonRoot: true;
  • seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault;
  • privilege escalation disabled;
  • all Linux capabilities dropped;
  • application images permit an arbitrary OpenShift UID to access only the files and writable directories it needs.

The frontend proxies /api, /ws, /health, and /ready internally. Only one edge-terminated Route is required for the browser application.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
oc get pods,route,pvc
oc get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
oc logs deployment/appcontrol-backend --tail=200
oc logs deployment/appcontrol-gateway --tail=200
oc describe pod POD_NAME

For CI failures, download the openshift-diagnostics artifact from the failed GitHub Actions run.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
AppControl has two independent permission systems:

System What it controls Assigned to Platform role Admin features (manage users, teams, sites, agents) Each user App permission What a user can do on a specific application Users or teams, per app

docs.title: Platform Roles
docs.text:
Every user has one global platform role. This controls admin features only, not application access.

Role Can do admin Everything. Sees all apps (implicit owner). Manages users, teams, sites, agents. operator Can operate apps they have permission on. Cannot manage users or teams. editor Same as operator but intended for users who edit app configurations. viewer Read-only platform access. Can still operate apps if granted app-level permission.

The platform role does NOT restrict app permissions. A viewer with operate permission on an app can start/stop that app.

Recommendation: Use operator for all regular users. The platform role only matters for admin features.

docs.title: App Permissions
docs.text: App permissions control what a user can do on a specific application. They are assigned to users or teams per app.

docs.title: Permission Levels (lowest to highest)
docs.text: Level Can do view See the application map, component states, and history operate Start, stop, restart components and the full application edit Modify components, dependencies, groups, configuration manage Change permissions, share the app with other users/teams owner Delete the application. Full control.

docs.title: How Permissions Are Resolved
docs.text:
When a user accesses an app, their effective permission is calculated:

effective = MAX(
    direct user permission on this app,
    permission from team A on this app,
    permission from team B on this app,
    ...
)
  • If a user has operate directly AND their team has manage, the effective level is manage.
  • Admin users always have implicit owner on all apps.
  • No permission = app is invisible on the dashboard.

docs.title: Permission Expiry
docs.text: Permissions can have an optional expires_at date. Expired permissions are ignored in the effective calculation.

docs.title: The Model
docs.text:
Admin (sees everything)
                       |
    +-----------+------+------+-----------+
    |           |             |           |
  User A     User B        User C     User D
    |           |             |
    +---Team Prod---+    Team DBA
    |               |         |
    |               |         |
    v               v         v
 App "Banking"   App "CRM"  App "Banking"
   (operate)      (view)      (manage)

docs.title: Visibility Rules
docs.text: User type What they see on the dashboard Admin All applications Non-admin with permissions Only apps where they have at least view (direct or via team) Non-admin without permissions Empty dashboard

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Admin creates users (Users page)
  2. Admin creates teams (Teams page)
  3. Admin adds users to teams (Team detail dialog)
  4. Admin shares apps with teams (Share button on map view, or appcontrol.sh)

docs.title: Provisioning with appcontrol.sh
docs.text:
For automated setup, use the provisioning script:

# Individual commands
./appcontrol.sh create-user --email alice@corp.com --name "Alice" --password changeme
./appcontrol.sh create-team --name "Equipe Prod"
./appcontrol.sh add-member --team "Equipe Prod" --email alice@corp.com
./appcontrol.sh grant-access --app "Core Banking" --team "Equipe Prod" --level operate

# Or bulk provision from a JSON file
./appcontrol.sh provision --file setup.json

docs.title: setup.json Format
docs.text:
{
  "users": [
    { "email": "alice@corp.com", "name": "Alice", "role": "operator", "password": "changeme" },
    { "email": "bob@corp.com",   "name": "Bob",   "role": "operator", "password": "changeme" }
  ],
  "teams": [
    {
      "name": "Equipe Prod",
      "description": "Production operations",
      "members": ["alice@corp.com", "bob@corp.com"]
    }
  ],
  "permissions": [
    { "app": "Core Banking", "team": "Equipe Prod", "level": "operate" },
    { "app": "Data Pipeline", "team": "Equipe Prod", "level": "view" }
  ]
}

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Variable Default Description APPCONTROL_URL http://localhost:3001 Backend API URL APPCONTROL_EMAIL admin@localhost Admin login email APPCONTROL_PASSWORD admin Admin login password

docs.title: UI Quick Reference
docs.text: Action Where Create users Users page (admin only) Create teams Teams page Add users to teams Teams page > click team > Add member Share app with team/user Map view > Share button > User/Team toggle See who has access to an app Map view > Share button > permission list

docs.title: What AppControl Is
docs.text:
AppControl is an operational mastery platform for IT applications. It provides:

  • A single source of truth for application dependency graphs (DAGs)
  • Real-time health monitoring via distributed agents
  • Sequenced operations (start/stop/restart) that respect dependency order
  • DR site switchover orchestration
  • Full audit trails compliant with DORA regulations

docs.title: What AppControl Is NOT
docs.text: AppControl is NOT... Instead, it... A scheduler Integrates with Control-M, AutoSys, Dollar Universe, TWS A deployment tool Integrates with XL Release, Jenkins, GitLab CI, ArgoCD A monitoring tool Complements Datadog, Prometheus, Zabbix with operational context A CMDB Consumes CMDB data; exposes topology for CMDB enrichment A config management tool Complements Ansible, Puppet, Terraform

docs.title: Dependency Duplication
docs.text:
In most enterprises, application dependency knowledge is scattered across:

  • Schedulers (Control-M jobs, AutoSys chains)
  • Release tools (XL Release templates, Jenkins pipelines)
  • Runbooks (Confluence pages, SharePoint docs)
  • Scripts (Shell scripts, PowerShell, Ansible playbooks)
  • People's heads (tribal knowledge of senior operators)

Each tool maintains its own partial, often outdated view of dependencies. When a dependency changes, updates are needed in N places. In practice, some are missed, leading to production incidents when processes start in the wrong order.

docs.title: The Cost of Duplication
docs.text:
• Incidents: Wrong start order causes failures, cascading outages
  • Slow deployments: Teams fear touching dependency chains, delaying releases
  • Knowledge silos: Only specific people know the real dependency order
  • Audit gaps: No single view of what changed, when, and why
  • Operational debt: Each new tool adds another copy of dependency data

docs.title: AppControl's Position in the Ecosystem
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────┐
                    │    AppControl         │
                    │  (Source of Truth)    │
                    │                      │
                    │  • DAG Model         │
                    │  • Real-time State   │
                    │  • Operations Engine │
                    │  • Audit Trail       │
                    └──────┬───────────────┘
                           │
            ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            │              │              │
    ┌───────▼──────┐ ┌────▼──────┐ ┌─────▼──────┐
    │  Schedulers  │ │  Release  │ │ Monitoring │
    │              │ │  Tools    │ │            │
    │ Control-M    │ │ XL Release│ │ Datadog    │
    │ AutoSys      │ │ Jenkins   │ │ Prometheus │
    │ Dollar Univ. │ │ GitLab CI │ │ Zabbix     │
    │ TWS          │ │ ArgoCD    │ │ Dynatrace  │
    └──────────────┘ └───────────┘ └────────────┘

docs.title: How Each Tool Interacts with AppControl
docs.text:
Schedulers call AppControl to: - Start/stop applications via CLI (appctl start myapp --wait) or REST API - Query the current state before launching dependent jobs - Get the correct execution plan without re-defining dependencies

Release/deployment tools call AppControl to: - Restart applications after deployment (respecting dependency order) - Validate that a proposed restart sequence is correct - Export the topology to verify deployment prerequisites

Monitoring tools receive from AppControl: - Webhooks on state changes (component UP/DOWN/FAILED) - DORA compliance metrics - Availability and incident data

docs.title: Coexistence Matrix
docs.text: Tool Relationship Integration Point Control-M AppControl starts apps; Control-M schedules when CLI wrapper: appctl start <app> --wait as a Control-M job AutoSys Same as Control-M CLI wrapper with exit codes (0=OK, 1=FAIL, 2=TIMEOUT) Dollar Universe Same as Control-M REST API call from DU job XL Release XL Release deploys; AppControl restarts HTTP task in XL Release template calling AppControl API Jenkins Jenkins builds/deploys; AppControl manages runtime Post-deploy step: curl -X POST /api/v1/apps/{id}/start Ansible Ansible configures; AppControl operates Ansible module or URI task calling AppControl API ServiceNow ServiceNow tracks changes; AppControl executes Webhook integration for state change notifications PagerDuty AppControl detects; PagerDuty alerts Webhook on FAILED state transitions

docs.title: 1. Native DAG Model
docs.text: AppControl models applications as directed acyclic graphs where components have typed dependencies. This is not an afterthought or a template — it's the core data model.

docs.title: 2. Real-Time State Awareness
docs.text: Before executing any operation, AppControl knows the current state of every component (RUNNING, STOPPED, FAILED, DEGRADED). Smart start skips components already running, handles failed ones specially (pink branch), and starts in parallel where dependencies allow.

docs.title: 3. Topology Export API
docs.text: AppControl's DAG is consumable by other tools via REST API: - GET /api/v1/apps/{id}/topology?format=json — Full topology with start/stop order - GET /api/v1/apps/{id}/topology?format=yaml — YAML for config management tools - GET /api/v1/apps/{id}/topology?format=dot — Graphviz DOT for visualization

docs.title: 4. Sequence Validation
docs.text: External tools can validate their restart sequences against AppControl's DAG: - POST /api/v1/apps/{id}/validate-sequence — Check if a proposed order is correct - Returns specific conflicts: "Service A depends on Service B but starts before it"

docs.title: 5. Execution Plans Without Execution
docs.text: Read-only plan computation for validation and approval workflows: - GET /api/v1/apps/{id}/plan?operation=start — What would happen if we start? - Includes predicted actions per component (start, skip, restart)

docs.title: 6. Advisory Mode
docs.text: Deploy AppControl agents in observation-only mode during migration. Agents monitor health and report state, but don't execute start/stop commands. Lets teams validate the dependency model before going live.

docs.title: From "XL Release for Restarts" to AppControl
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 — Observe: Deploy agents in advisory mode alongside XL Release templates
  2. Phase 2 — Validate: Use validate-sequence API to compare XL Release order with DAG
  3. Phase 3 — Parallel: XL Release calls AppControl API instead of running scripts directly
  4. Phase 4 — Migrate: Remove restart logic from XL Release; AppControl handles operations

docs.title: From "Shell Scripts" to AppControl
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 — Model: Import application topology (YAML import or UI wizard)
  2. Phase 2 — Observe: Advisory mode agents monitor current state
  3. Phase 3 — Test: Dry-run mode to validate execution plans
  4. Phase 4 — Operate: Switch from scripts to AppControl for daily operations

docs.title: From "Scheduler-Managed Restarts" to AppControl
docs.text:
1. Phase 1 — Integrate: Scheduler jobs call appctl CLI instead of custom scripts
  2. Phase 2 — Simplify: Scheduler delegates dependency logic to AppControl
  3. Phase 3 — Optimize: Scheduler only schedules when; AppControl decides how

docs.title: Competitive Positioning Summary
docs.text: "AppControl occupies the gap between deployment and scheduling — operational mastery. Your scheduler knows when to run. Your CI/CD knows what to deploy. AppControl knows how your application works and operates it accordingly. These three work together, each in its domain, with AppControl as the single source of truth for your application's dependency graph."

docs.title: PowerShell command reference
docs.text:
The standalone SQLite deployment and the native Windows/PostgreSQL deployment provide the same administration commands. Only the script name changes:

# Standalone SQLite
.\appcontrol.ps1 COMMAND [ARGUMENTS]

# Windows Server with PostgreSQL
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 COMMAND [ARGUMENTS]

Run commands from an account authorized to administer AppControl. Installation, service and firewall operations additionally require an elevated PowerShell.

docs.title: Installation lifecycle
docs.text: Command Standalone SQLite Windows/PostgreSQL install Downloads and configures the standalone package Installs the PostgreSQL production package start Starts local processes Use Start-Service AppControlBackend stop Stops local processes Use Stop-Service AppControlBackend status Shows local processes Shows AppControl and PostgreSQL services upgrade Replaces binaries/UI and preserves data Planned; follow upgrade procedures meanwhile uninstall Remove the standalone directory after stopping Removes the AppControl service and preserves PostgreSQL/data

docs.title: Standalone installer options
docs.text:
Complete syntax:

.\appcontrol.ps1 install `
  -Email "admin@company.example" `
  -Password "replace-this-password" `
  -BackendPort 3000 `
  -ReleasesBase "https://github.com/xcomponent/appcontrol-release/releases/latest/download"
Option Default Description -Email <address> admin@localhost Initial local administrator email -Password <password> admin Initial administrator password; always set an explicit value -BackendPort <port> 3000 HTTP port exposed by the standalone backend -ReleasesBase <URL> Latest customer release Base URL containing binaries, frontend archive and checksums

-ReleasesBase is useful for an authenticated internal mirror or an air-gapped HTTP repository. It must contain the platform-specific SQLite backend, gateway, agent, appcontrol-frontend.zip and checksums-sha256.txt.

docs.title: Windows/PostgreSQL installer options
docs.text: Open Windows PowerShell as Administrator. Choose exactly one database mode.

docs.title: Install PostgreSQL locally
docs.text:
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 install `
  -PostgresMode Install `
  -AdminEmail "admin@company.example" `
  -AdminPassword "replace-this-password"

docs.title: Use an existing PostgreSQL service
docs.text:
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 install `
  -PostgresMode Existing `
  -DatabaseUrl "postgresql://appcontrol:PASSWORD@db.company.example:5432/appcontrol?sslmode=require" `
  -AdminEmail "admin@company.example" `
  -AdminPassword "replace-this-password"
Option Default Required when Description -PostgresMode Install\|Existing Existing Always choose explicitly Installs PostgreSQL locally or connects to an existing database -DatabaseUrl <URL> None PostgresMode Existing PostgreSQL connection URL used by the backend service -DatabasePassword <password> Generated Optional with Install Password for the locally created appcontrol database role -PostgresSuperuserPassword <password> Generated Optional with Install Password assigned to the local PostgreSQL postgres account -PostgresPort <port> 5432 No Local PostgreSQL listening port -AdminEmail <address> admin@localhost No Initial AppControl administrator email -AdminPassword <password> Generated No Initial AppControl administrator password -BackendPort <port> 3000 No AppControl HTTP listening port -InstallDir <path> C:\Program Files\AppControl No Backend executable installation directory -DataDir <path> C:\ProgramData\AppControl No Frontend, administration files, logs and PostgreSQL data root -AdminScriptPath <path> <DataDir>\admin\appcontrol.ps1 No Installed administration command script -ReleasesBase <URL> Latest customer release No Base URL containing backend, frontend, admin script and checksums -PostgresInstallerUrl <URL> Pinned EDB PostgreSQL 16 installer No Approved installer or internal mirror URL -PostgresInstallerSha256 <hash> Pinned tested hash With an overridden installer URL Expected SHA-256; verification cannot be disabled

When passwords are generated, the installer writes them to C:\ProgramData\AppControl\secrets\installation-secrets.txt (or the selected DataDir) with restricted Windows ACLs. Transfer them to the organization password vault after installation.

The service connection string is readable by local Windows administrators. Use a dedicated least-privileged PostgreSQL role and prefer sslmode=require for a remote database.

docs.title: Standalone-only lifecycle commands
docs.text: Command Purpose enable-autostart Creates the scheduled task that starts the standalone package at boot disable-autostart Removes that scheduled task logs Displays recent standalone component logs help Prints the command summary

docs.title: Sites and hosting
docs.text:
.\SCRIPT.ps1 add-site "Paris" 4443
.\SCRIPT.ps1 add-hosting "France" "French production hosting"
.\SCRIPT.ps1 assign-site-hosting "Paris" "France"
Command Purpose add-site <name> [gateway-port] Creates a site and its gateway/agent enrollment material add-hosting <name> [description] Creates a hosting group assign-site-hosting <site> <hosting> Associates a site with a hosting group

In standalone mode, add-site also starts the locally packaged gateway and agent when AppControl is running. In Windows/PostgreSQL production mode it creates the control-plane objects and enrollment material; install the gateway and remote agents using Agent installation.

docs.title: Users, teams and permissions
docs.text:
