docs.title: Agent will not connect to gateway
docs.text:
Symptom

The Agents page shows the agent as UNREACHABLE. No heartbeat events are received. systemctl status appcontrol-agent reports the binary is running.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Are reconnection attempts visible in the agent journal?
sudo journalctl -u appcontrol-agent --since "5 min ago" | grep -E "connect|gateway|tls"

# 2. Can the agent host reach the gateway TCP port?
nc -vz gateway.example.com 4443

# 3. Does the TLS handshake succeed?
openssl s_client -connect gateway.example.com:4443 \
  -cert /etc/appcontrol/tls/agent.crt \
  -key /etc/appcontrol/tls/agent.key \
  -CAfile /etc/appcontrol/tls/ca.crt -showcerts < /dev/null

Resolution:

Cause Fix Network firewall blocks 4443 Open outbound TCP 4443 from the agent subnet to the gateway Wrong gateway URL Edit /etc/appcontrol/agent.yaml, fix gateway.url or gateway.urls, systemctl reload appcontrol-agent DNS resolution failure getent hosts gateway.example.com — if empty, fix /etc/resolv.conf or /etc/hosts Gateway pod down kubectl get pods -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=gateway; restart if needed tls_insecure: false against self-signed gateway cert Use a CA-signed gateway cert, or set gateway.tls_insecure: true (dev only)

docs.title: Enrollment fails
docs.text:
Symptom

appcontrol-agent --enroll … exits non-zero. Returns HTTP 401, 409, or 500.

Resolution:

HTTP code Cause Fix 401 Token invalid or revoked Generate a new token: appctl pki create-token --name <n> --max-uses 1 --scope agent 409 Token max_uses exhausted Generate a new token with a higher max_uses 410 Token expired Generate a new token; defaults to 24 h validity 500 PKI not initialized appctl pki init --org-name "<your org>" Connection refused Gateway unreachable Verify https://gateway:4443/health is reachable; check the gateway pod Certificate verify failed Agent presented a wrong CA Re-run enrollment which writes the fresh CA to /etc/appcontrol/tls/ca.crt

See Agent Installation §8 for the full enrollment-error table.

docs.title: Heartbeat timeout (components flip to UNREACHABLE)
docs.text:
Symptom

Components managed by an apparently healthy agent transition to UNREACHABLE periodically. The agent process is up but the backend marks it stale.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Confirm the agent is still sending heartbeats
sudo journalctl -u appcontrol-agent | grep -i heartbeat | tail -10

# 2. Compare the configured timeout
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SELECT name, heartbeat_timeout_seconds FROM organizations;"

# 3. Check connection latency between agent and gateway
sudo journalctl -u appcontrol-agent | grep -E "rtt|latency" | tail -5

Resolution:

Cause Fix Network is dropping idle WebSocket connections Reduce keep-alive interval on the load balancer to < 60 s; or raise heartbeat frequency heartbeat_timeout_seconds too low for the network UPDATE organizations SET heartbeat_timeout_seconds = 300; (default is 180 s) Backend heartbeat_monitor is over-aggressive Check backend logs for marking agent stale — verify clock skew with NTP Agent log shows repeated pong timeout A firewall is killing idle WS frames — switch the gateway to port 443 (passes as HTTPS)

docs.title: Certificate expired
docs.text:
Symptom

Agent journal shows certificate has expired or unable to get local issuer certificate. The agent does not reconnect.

Diagnosis:

# Check the agent cert expiry
openssl x509 -in /etc/appcontrol/tls/agent.crt -noout -dates

# Check the CA cert expiry
openssl x509 -in /etc/appcontrol/tls/ca.crt -noout -dates

Resolution:

  1. Generate a new enrollment token: appctl pki create-token --name renewal --max-uses 1 --scope agent.
  2. Stop the agent: sudo systemctl stop appcontrol-agent.
  3. Re-enroll: sudo appcontrol-agent --enroll https://gateway:4443 --token ac_enroll_....
  4. Start the agent: sudo systemctl start appcontrol-agent.

If the CA itself expired, see Disaster Recovery — CA loss.

docs.title: Advisory mode — agent reports but does not execute
docs.text:
Symptom

Operator clicks Start but nothing happens on the host. The map updates check status but no command runs.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Is the application or agent in advisory mode?
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SELECT id, name, settings->>'mode' FROM applications WHERE id = '<app_id>';"

# 2. Check the action log — operations should be recorded even if no-op
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SELECT action_type, details FROM action_log WHERE target_id='<app_id>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;"

Resolution:

Cause Fix Application is in advisory mode Toggle to operate mode in Settings > Application > Mode Component has is_optional=true and was skipped Inspect the sequencer log; flip is_optional=false if required User has only view permission Grant operate permission via the Share dialog

docs.title: Gateway down
docs.text:
Symptom

All agents in a zone go UNREACHABLE at once. The gateway pod is crash-looping or not reachable.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Pod state
kubectl get pods -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=gateway

# 2. Logs
kubectl logs -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=gateway --tail=100

# 3. Health endpoint (from outside the cluster)
curl -k https://gateway.example.com:4443/health
# Returns: ok agents=42 backend=connected buffer_msgs=0 buffer_bytes=0

Resolution:

Cause Fix Backend WebSocket URL wrong Edit BACKEND_URL env var, must end with /ws/gateway TLS cert / key mismatch Verify file paths and openssl rsa -in gateway.key -modulus matches the cert Listening port already taken Check ss -tlnp | grep 4443; change LISTEN_PORT if conflicting OOM kill Increase resources.limits.memory in the Helm values

docs.title: mTLS handshake failure
docs.text:
Symptom

Gateway logs show repeated tls handshake failure or unknown ca. Agents cannot connect.

Diagnosis:

# From the agent host, simulate the full handshake
openssl s_client -connect gateway.example.com:4443 \
  -cert /etc/appcontrol/tls/agent.crt \
  -key /etc/appcontrol/tls/agent.key \
  -CAfile /etc/appcontrol/tls/ca.crt -verify_return_error

# Compare the issuer fingerprint of the gateway's chain and the agent's CA
openssl x509 -in /etc/appcontrol/tls/ca.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256

Resolution:

Cause Fix Gateway and agent use different CAs Re-enroll the agent against the current backend PKI Gateway cert SAN does not include the DNS the agent uses Reissue the gateway cert with the right DNS SANs Clock skew > 5 min Sync NTP on both ends; certs are sensitive to clock drift TLS_ENABLED=false on one side Verify both gateway and agent have tls.enabled: true

docs.title: Rate-limited
docs.text:
Symptom

Gateway returns HTTP 429 on /enroll, or per-agent log spam shows "rate limit exceeded".

Resolution:

# 1. Identify the offending agent
kubectl logs -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=gateway | grep "rate limit" | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c

# 2. The agent is likely sending too many CheckResults — investigate why deltas are flapping
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "
  SELECT component_id, count(*) FROM check_events
  WHERE created_at > now() - interval '5 minutes'
  GROUP BY component_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 10;"

If the rate is legitimate (large cluster of components on one agent), raise the per-agent rate limit in the gateway config; otherwise fix the flapping check_cmd.

docs.title: 5xx errors
docs.text:
Symptom

The frontend shows "Internal Server Error". curl /api/v1/apps returns HTTP 500/502/503.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Backend pod state
kubectl get pods -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=backend
kubectl logs -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=backend --tail=200

# 2. Database reachability
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- \
  curl -s http://localhost:3000/ready

# 3. Recent panics
kubectl logs -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=backend | grep -E "panicked|FATAL|thread"

Resolution:

Cause Fix DB unreachable See DB pool exhausted and /ready Panic on startup (insecure JWT in production) Set a 32+ char JWT_SECRET via openssl rand -base64 48 Missing migration Check kubectl logs for sqlx::migrate errors; investigate the partial migration Unhandled JSON deserialization error Capture the request payload, file a bug report

docs.title: DB pool exhausted
docs.text:
Symptom

Backend logs show acquire timeout or pool timed out while waiting for an open connection. P95 latency spikes.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Current pool size and utilization
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- \
  curl -s localhost:3000/metrics | grep db_pool

# 2. Long-running queries in PostgreSQL
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "
  SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS duration, state, query
  FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' AND query_start < now() - interval '2 seconds'
  ORDER BY duration DESC LIMIT 10;"

Resolution:

Cause Fix Long-running query holds a connection Identify the query, add an index, or rewrite Pool too small Raise DB_POOL_SIZE (default 20; rule of thumb: 10 + apps × 0.5, capped at 50) Idle connection timeout > LB idle timeout Set DB_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECS below the LB idle limit (e.g. AWS ALB = 350) Connection leak in a custom handler Review recent backend changes for missing drop on a tx

docs.title: Slow queries
docs.text:
Symptom

P95 API latency above 2 s. Specific endpoints (/apps, /applications/:id) feel sluggish.

Diagnosis:

-- Identify the slowest queries
SELECT
  substring(query, 1, 80) AS query,
  calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC LIMIT 15;

-- Check check_events partition sizes
SELECT
  inhrelid::regclass AS partition,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(inhrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_inherits WHERE inhparent = 'check_events'::regclass
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(inhrelid) DESC LIMIT 10;

Resolution:

Cause Fix check_events partition not pruned Set RETENTION_CHECK_EVENTS_DAYS=90 and let background task drop old partitions Missing index on a custom query EXPLAIN ANALYZE then CREATE INDEX Sequential scan on state_transitions Verify idx_state_transitions_component_created exists Tablespace fragmentation VACUUM ANALYZE state_transitions; (off-hours)

docs.title: JWT_SECRET insecure panic
docs.text:
Symptom

Backend exits at startup with FATAL: JWT_SECRET must be set to a strong value in production.

Resolution:

# Generate a strong secret
NEW=$(openssl rand -base64 48)

# Update the Kubernetes secret
kubectl create secret generic appcontrol-jwt \
  --namespace appcontrol \
  --from-literal=jwt-secret="$NEW" \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Restart the backend
kubectl rollout restart -n appcontrol deployment/appcontrol-backend

Note: rotating JWT_SECRET invalidates all active sessions — users must log in again.

docs.title: CORS rejects browser request
docs.text:
Symptom

The browser console shows CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header.

Resolution:

CORS_ORIGINS must explicitly list the frontend origin in production. Example:

CORS_ORIGINS=https://appcontrol.example.com,https://admin.example.com

In development (APP_ENV=development), an empty CORS_ORIGINS is permissive. In production, an empty value rejects all cross-origin requests by design.

docs.title: OIDC discovery failed
docs.text:
Symptom

Backend logs failed to fetch OIDC discovery document. Login redirect returns 500.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Verify the discovery URL is reachable from the backend
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- \
  curl -sv https://keycloak.example.com/realms/appcontrol/.well-known/openid-configuration

# 2. Check the variable is set
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- env | grep OIDC

Resolution:

Cause Fix Wrong URL Fix OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL (the realm path matters) Network egress blocked Allow egress from the backend pods to the IdP Self-signed IdP cert Mount the IdP's CA into the backend container's trust store

docs.title: SAML assertion invalid
docs.text:
Symptom

SAML POST to /api/v1/auth/saml/acs returns invalid signature or assertion expired.

Diagnosis:

Inspect the SAMLResponse with https://samltool.com (paste the base64 from the network tab).

Resolution:

Cause Fix Wrong IdP signing cert Re-fetch and base64-encode the IdP cert into SAML_IDP_CERT Clock skew Sync NTP; SAML enforces a 5-min NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter window SAML_WANT_ASSERTIONS_SIGNED=true but IdP sends unsigned assertion Either enable signed assertions in IdP or set the env var to false (not recommended) SAML_SP_ACS_URL mismatch The IdP's "Reply URL" must equal exactly the backend ACS URL

docs.title: API key expired
docs.text:
Symptom

Scheduler integration receives HTTP 401 with key expired.

Resolution:

# 1. Identify the offending key
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "
  SELECT id, name, expires_at FROM api_keys
  WHERE user_id = '<user_id>' AND expires_at < now();"

# 2. Create a new key via the UI or API; copy the plaintext immediately
curl -X POST https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/api-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"name":"scheduler-2026-q2","expires_in_days":365}'

# 3. Update the scheduler configuration with the new key

docs.title: "Forbidden" on a resource you should own
docs.text:
Symptom

User has been granted manage on an application but still gets HTTP 403.

Diagnosis:

-- What permissions does the user have (direct + team)?
SELECT permission_level, source FROM (
  SELECT permission_level, 'direct' AS source FROM app_permissions_users
  WHERE user_id = '<uid>' AND app_id = '<aid>' AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now())
  UNION ALL
  SELECT pt.permission_level, 'team:' || t.name FROM app_permissions_teams pt
  JOIN team_members tm ON tm.team_id = pt.team_id
  JOIN teams t ON t.id = pt.team_id
  WHERE tm.user_id = '<uid>' AND pt.app_id = '<aid>'
    AND (pt.expires_at IS NULL OR pt.expires_at > now())
) x;

Resolution:

Cause Fix Permission has expires_at in the past Update or remove the expires_at Team membership missing Add the user to the team Workspace restriction excludes the site Add the user (or their team) to a workspace that includes the site Stale JWT cached User signs out and back in to refresh claims

docs.title: Component stuck in STARTING
docs.text:
Symptom

The map shows a component blue-pulsing in STARTING for minutes. The sequencer waits forever.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Is the start command still running on the host?
ssh <host> ps -ef | grep -v grep | grep "<expected process>"

# 2. Latest health check
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "
  SELECT exit_code, stdout, duration_ms, created_at
  FROM check_events
  WHERE component_id = '<cid>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;"

Resolution:

Cause Fix start_cmd returned but process actually died Fix the start command; ensure the process daemonizes correctly check_cmd checks a different process Realign check and start commands start_timeout_seconds too short Raise it on the component config (default 120 s) Health check polled too infrequently Sequencer polls every 3 s during transitions — usually fine; if not, file a bug

docs.title: Stuck in UNREACHABLE after agent reconnect
docs.text:
Symptom

Agent reconnects and heartbeats again, but its components remain UNREACHABLE.

Diagnosis:

# 1. Check the last 5 state transitions
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "
  SELECT previous_state, next_state, trigger, created_at
  FROM state_transitions WHERE component_id='<cid>'
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;"

# 2. Force a fresh health check
curl -X POST https://appcontrol.example.com/api/v1/components/<cid>/check \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Resolution:

The FSM expects a fresh CheckResult to leave UNREACHABLE. Trigger a manual check (above). If the issue recurs, see Runbook 1.

docs.title: State oscillates between RUNNING and FAILED
docs.text:
Symptom

A component flips state every 30 s. Operators see "flapping" alerts.

Diagnosis:

-- Inspect recent transitions
SELECT previous_state, next_state, trigger, created_at, details
FROM state_transitions WHERE component_id = '<cid>'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Inspect recent check results
SELECT exit_code, duration_ms, substring(stdout, 1, 80) AS stdout
FROM check_events WHERE component_id = '<cid>'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Resolution:

Cause Fix check_cmd is non-deterministic Make the check idempotent and stable Timeout on check Raise the agent-level command timeout; default is check_interval_seconds Resource exhaustion on host Inspect CPU/RAM; the host may be killing the process under load Race between two agents managing the same process Verify one agent per component; remove duplicates

docs.title: Start times out
docs.text:
Symptom

A start operation runs the configured start_cmd but never completes. The orchestrator marks the operation timed-out.

Resolution:

  1. Inspect the action log: SELECT * FROM action_log WHERE target_id='<app_id>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;.
  2. The details JSON shows which component failed and the timeout that triggered.
  3. Common fix: raise start_timeout_seconds on the offending component (default 120 s).
  4. If many components share the same issue, raise the app-level timeout in Settings > Operations.

docs.title: Stop hangs
docs.text:
Symptom

A stop operation is stuck — components remain in STOPPING.

Diagnosis:

# Is the stop process still running?
ssh <host> ps -ef | grep "<process>"

# Did the agent receive the command?
sudo journalctl -u appcontrol-agent | grep -E "ExecuteCommand|stop" | tail -5

Resolution:

  • The component's stop_cmd may be waiting for graceful shutdown that never completes. Use the Force Stop action in the UI, which sends kill -9 after the timeout.
  • If stop_timeout_seconds is too short, raise it on the component (default 60 s).

docs.title: Sequencer suspends mid-DAG
docs.text:
Symptom

Start operation runs the first DAG levels successfully then halts. UI shows "Operation suspended — operator intervention required".

Resolution:

The sequencer suspends (rather than cancels) on a component failure to give operators a chance to fix the underlying issue without losing in-flight progress. Two next steps:

  1. Inspect the failed component, fix the root cause (often a missing prereq or a bad command).
  2. Resume the operation from the UI ("Resume" button) or via API: POST /api/v1/operations/:id/resume.

If you cannot resume, cancel the operation: POST /api/v1/operations/:id/cancel and start fresh.

docs.title: Error branch not detected
docs.text:
Symptom

A component fails, but the "Restart error branch" button targets only the failed component — not its downstream dependents.

Resolution:

The error-branch algorithm walks downstream (dependent of failed → dependent of dependent…). If your topology has weak coupling that AppControl does not yet treat as dependencies, the dependents are not reached.

  • Verify the dependencies rows for the failed component: SELECT to_component_id FROM dependencies WHERE from_component_id = '<failed_cid>';.
  • If a dependency is missing, add it via the map editor (drag an edge between components).

docs.title: Dry-run says OK but actual run fails
docs.text:
Symptom

appctl start <app> --dry-run reports a clean plan. The same operation without --dry-run fails.

Resolution:

Dry-run validates:

  • DAG (cycles, missing references)
  • Permissions
  • Agent connectivity
  • Command syntax (presence, not semantics)

Dry-run does not execute commands, so it cannot detect:

  • Wrong credentials in start_cmd
  • Missing prerequisites on the host (port already in use, disk full)
  • Race conditions between components

For tighter pre-flight validation, run the diagnostic engine (Level 3) before a critical operation: appctl diagnose <app> --level 3.

docs.title: Discovery / auto-discovery noise
docs.text:
Symptom

Auto-discovery surfaces hundreds of irrelevant processes (cron jobs, OS daemons), making the draft topology unusable.

Resolution:

Discovery is heuristic. Two ways to tame it:

  1. Filter at the agent — set APPCONTROL_DISCOVERY_EXCLUDE in the agent's environment to a comma-separated deny-list. Matching is case-insensitive and uses prefix semantics, so crond also suppresses crond-worker etc. Example: APPCONTROL_DISCOVERY_EXCLUDE=crond,rsyslogd,sshd. The deny-list is read on every discovery scan (no agent restart needed if the variable is exported in the systemd unit and the agent is restarted, or if the variable is sourced from /etc/environment).
  2. Curate in the UI — discovery presents a draft topology; uncheck any process you do not want before promoting it to an application.

If discovery produces no signal at all, check that the agent has permission to read /proc (Linux) or tasklist (Windows). Container agents may need --pid=host to see host processes.

docs.title: Cluster (fan-out) sync issues
docs.text:
Symptom

A fan-out cluster shows divergent member states or a parent state that does not reflect members.

Diagnosis:

-- Are all members reporting check results?
SELECT cm.hostname, cms.current_state, cms.last_check_at
FROM cluster_members cm
LEFT JOIN cluster_member_state cms ON cms.cluster_member_id = cm.id
WHERE cm.component_id = '<cid>' AND cm.is_enabled = true;

-- Does the parent component's state match the policy?
SELECT id, name, cluster_mode, cluster_health_policy, cluster_min_healthy_pct, current_state
FROM components WHERE id = '<cid>';

Resolution:

Cause Fix Member's agent_id is wrong Update cluster_members.agent_id; verify the agent is reachable cluster_health_policy = threshold_pct but cluster_min_healthy_pct too high Lower the threshold or fix the failing members Member's check_cmd_override is wrong Test the override on the host; correct as needed Member's is_enabled = false is skipping live nodes Re-enable: UPDATE cluster_members SET is_enabled = true WHERE id = '<mid>';

docs.title: DR switchover stuck in phase X
docs.text:
Symptom

A switchover starts but stays in phase 1–6 for an unusually long time.

Resolution by phase:

Phase Likely cause Fix 1 (Prepare) Target site agents not connected kubectl logs gateway-dr ...; reconnect agents 2 (Validate) Pre-flight health check failed on target Inspect switchover_log.details; fix the failing component 3 (StopSource) Source component's stop_cmd hangs Raise stop_timeout_seconds, or "force stop" 4 (Sync) Data replication lag exceeds threshold Wait for replication, or trigger an emergency sync 5 (StartTarget) Target component fails to start Fix the host issue, then resume 6 (Commit) Database write contention Should never linger; if it does, file a bug report

Inspect:

SELECT phase, status, started_at, ended_at, details
FROM switchover_log
WHERE application_id = '<aid>'
ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 20;

To force-cancel (only before phase 6): POST /api/v1/apps/:id/switchover/cancel. See Runbook 6.

docs.title: Diagnostic + Rebuild rejected
docs.text:
Symptom

POST /api/v1/apps/:id/rebuild returns HTTP 409 rebuild_protected.

Resolution:

The rebuild engine refuses to touch any component flagged rebuild_protected = true. This is intentional protection for databases of record and other irreplaceable components.

Options:

  1. Rebuild the application excluding the protected components — pass exclude_component_ids in the rebuild request body.
  2. Temporarily unprotect a component (requires manage permission):
UPDATE components SET rebuild_protected = false WHERE id = '<cid>';

Re-protect after the rebuild finishes. The change is recorded in config_versions.

docs.title: How to file a bug report
docs.text: When opening an issue, attach the following so the maintainer can reproduce:

docs.title: 1. Environment
docs.text:
# Version of every component
appctl version
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- /app/appcontrol-backend --version
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-gateway -- /app/appcontrol-gateway --version
appcontrol-agent --version

# Database flavor
psql $DATABASE_URL -c "SELECT version();"

docs.title: 2. Logs (last 200 lines from each)
docs.text:
kubectl logs -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend --tail=200 > backend.log
kubectl logs -n appcontrol -l app.kubernetes.io/component=gateway --tail=200 > gateway.log
sudo journalctl -u appcontrol-agent --since "1 hour ago" > agent.log

docs.title: 3. Configuration (redact secrets)
docs.text:
# Backend env (redact JWT_SECRET, DATABASE_URL password)
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-backend -- env | grep -E '^[A-Z_]+=' | grep -v -E 'SECRET|PASSWORD|KEY|DATABASE_URL'

# Gateway YAML
kubectl exec -n appcontrol deploy/appcontrol-gateway -- cat /etc/appcontrol/gateway.yaml

# Agent YAML
cat /etc/appcontrol/agent.yaml

docs.title: 4. Minimal reproduction
docs.text: A 3-step recipe that triggers the bug on a fresh docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.release.yaml up -d install. If the bug requires a specific application topology, attach the JSON export from Settings > Application > Export.

docs.title: 5. Database state (optional, helpful)
docs.text:
-- Component, last 5 transitions, last 5 check events
SELECT id, name, current_state FROM components WHERE id = '<cid>';
SELECT previous_state, next_state, trigger, created_at FROM state_transitions
  WHERE component_id = '<cid>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;
SELECT exit_code, substring(stdout, 1, 100), created_at FROM check_events
  WHERE component_id = '<cid>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;

docs.title: 6. File log paths reference
docs.text:
Component Log path (Linux) Log path (Kubernetes) Agent journalctl -u appcontrol-agent n/a (runs outside K8s) Gateway journalctl -u appcontrol-gateway (when on a VM) kubectl logs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=gateway Backend n/a (typically Kubernetes) kubectl logs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=backend Frontend (nginx) /var/log/nginx/ inside the container kubectl logs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=frontend PostgreSQL /var/log/postgresql/ depends on managed-service provider

Submit the bundle to the project issue tracker. Reproducible bug reports with attached logs are typically triaged within 48 h.

docs.title: Upgrading AppControl
docs.text:
The supported OpenShift evaluation profile runs one backend replica, with Recreate deployment strategy. Plan an interruption. This release does not claim a zero-downtime upgrade or general N/N−1 protocol compatibility.

For a first installation, use the versioned OpenShift kit and installation guide.

docs.title: Before upgrading
docs.text:
1. Read the target release notes and verify its checksums, image digests and qualification reports. Use components from the same release.
  2. Finish all application operations and suspend new start/stop/rebuild requests. Do not interrupt a destructive reconstruction to upgrade its controller.
  3. Back up PostgreSQL and test restoring the backup in an isolated database. Retain the installation's private state directory (credentials and PKI), current image lock, Helm values and Helm revision. Protect these as secrets.
  4. Rehearse the upgrade on the restored database. An initial-installation test does not prove compatibility with every historical schema and dataset.
  5. Schedule the interruption and plan recovery with the database owner.

docs.title: Apply the version
docs.text:
Import the new kit's OCI archives into the approved registry using scripts/qualification/transfer-images.py. Retain the previous lock; create a new lock for the new version. Do not overwrite immutable image tags.

Update the non-secret installer configuration to point to the new lock. Keep the same private state directory, namespace and Helm release name:

python3 scripts/qualification/install.py --config client.json --preflight-only
python3 scripts/qualification/install.py --config client.json

Check certificate and gateway-token expiry before using this procedure. The installer reuses existing credentials; reuse does not extend their validity. For deployments integrated with a customer PKI, database or SSO, use the reviewed Helm values and the customer's maintenance procedure instead of regenerating evaluation secrets.

The backend applies pending numbered migrations at startup and records them in _migrations. PostgreSQL migrations are supplied with the binary; SQLite also embeds migrations. Ship the matching migration directory with every upgrade. Each migration is transactional; a failure after earlier migrations succeeded can leave the database at an intermediate version. Never edit or remove an already applied migration.

appcontrol-backend --migrate-only applies migrations and exits. --dry-run lists pending migrations without executing their SQL, but can create the migration tracking table. Test both against a restored copy first; they are not a backup or a database rollback mechanism.

docs.title: Verify after the interruption
docs.text:
Check readiness, HTTPS login, gateway and agent reconnection, existing maps and permissions. Test a non-critical application's approved commands. Investigate any interrupted operation explicitly; connectivity recovery alone does not establish whether a command executed before a crash.

The supplied e2e.py --openshift recipe restarts services and creates synthetic commands. Run it only on a dedicated qualification installation, never on a controller operating customer applications.

Upgrade external agents with the matching platform binary and verify its SHA-256 before replacement. Keep the previous binary and configuration for recovery. Stop the service, replace the executable, restart, then verify the reported version, TLS connection and permitted commands. Qualify the actual host OS and procedure dependencies before a fleet rollout.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
helm rollback restores Kubernetes manifests and image references. It does not undo database migrations, commands already executed, or certificate changes. Do not start an older backend against a changed schema unless that combination has been tested. If incompatible, stop new operations, restore the verified pre-upgrade database backup and matching manifests, images and private state. Reconcile any application action that occurred after the backup before resuming.

There is no general supported-version matrix inferred from version numbers. The release evidence describes exactly the paths exercised. Upgrade an existing customer installation only after testing its source version and restored data.

docs.title: AppControl v4 — User Guide
docs.text: Operational mastery and IT system resilience. Map your applications as dependency graphs, monitor health in real time, orchestrate sequenced operations, and maintain full DORA-compliant audit trails.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
AppControl supports multiple authentication methods: OIDC (Keycloak, Okta, Azure AD), SAML 2.0 (ADFS, Azure AD), and local authentication for development environments.

After authenticating, you are redirected to the Dashboard. Your session uses RS256-signed JWT tokens with automatic refresh.

Login page — supports OIDC, SAML 2.0, and local authentication

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The Dashboard is your command center. It provides a real-time overview of all applications you have access to.

What you see at a glance:

  • Application cards — each card shows the application name, overall health status, and a component count breakdown (running, failed, stopped)
  • KPI tiles — aggregate metrics across your portfolio: total applications, components running, components failed, agents connected
  • Live event feed — the most recent operations, state changes, and alerts across all visible applications
  • Quick filters — focus on applications by status (healthy, degraded, failed) or by site
  • Search — locate applications by name or tag instantly

The Dashboard updates in real time via WebSocket — status changes appear immediately without manual refresh.

Dashboard — real-time overview of all applications with KPIs and live event feed

docs.title: Creating an Application
docs.text:
The Onboarding Wizard guides you through creating a new application step by step. No YAML files or CLI commands needed.

The wizard walks you through:

  1. Welcome — introduction and getting started
  2. App Info — name, description, and primary site selection
  3. Sites — configure primary and DR site assignments
  4. Components — define each component with its type, agent, and commands (check, start, stop)
  5. Dependencies — draw the dependency graph between components
  6. Review — verify the complete configuration before creation
  7. Done — application is created and agents start monitoring immediately

Onboarding Wizard — guided application creation

Each component requires at minimum a name, type, and agent assignment. The check command determines how AppControl monitors the component's health. Start and stop commands enable orchestrated operations.

Component configuration — define check, start, and stop commands for each component

docs.title: Importing Applications
docs.text:
For teams that prefer infrastructure-as-code, AppControl supports YAML and JSON import of application definitions.

Import workflow:

  1. Upload a YAML/JSON file defining components, dependencies, and commands
  2. AppControl validates the structure (checks for DAG cycles, missing references, invalid types)
  3. The Import Wizard lets you review the parsed application, map components to agents, and resolve conflicts
  4. The application is created with full version tracking in config_versions

You can also import from existing AppControl v3 configurations — the importer automatically maps legacy component types and command formats.

Import page — upload YAML/JSON application definitions

docs.title: Auto-Discovery
docs.text:
The Discovery feature automatically detects running processes on monitored servers and suggests application topologies.

How it works:

  1. Agents scan their hosts for running processes, listening ports, and service definitions
  2. Discovery correlates processes across agents to identify multi-server applications
  3. A draft topology is generated with suggested component names, types, and dependencies
  4. You review and refine the draft before promoting it to a real application

This is especially useful for onboarding existing applications that don't have formal documentation.

Auto-Discovery — detect and map running applications automatically

docs.title: Interactive DAG Visualization
docs.text:
The Map View is the heart of AppControl. It renders your application's component topology as an interactive directed acyclic graph (DAG) powered by React Flow.

Key capabilities:

Feature Description Pan & Zoom Navigate large topologies with mouse drag and scroll wheel Color-coded nodes Each node reflects its FSM state: green (running), red (failed), gray (stopped), blue pulse (starting/stopping) Dependency edges Directional arrows show which components depend on which Error branch Failed components and their dependents are highlighted in pink for quick identification Toolbar actions Start All, Stop All, Restart Branch, Switchover, Diagnose, Export Layout controls Automatic arrangement: top-down, left-right, or radial Mini-map Overview navigation for large application graphs Keyboard shortcuts Ctrl+F search, Space toggle start/stop, F5 refresh, ? show all shortcuts

Map View — interactive DAG visualization with color-coded component states

docs.title: Component Detail Panel
docs.text:
Click any component node to open the Detail Panel on the right side. It provides deep insight into a single component.

Panel tabs:

Tab Content Status Current FSM state, last check result, uptime counter, state history timeline Checks Results from all three diagnostic levels (health, integrity, infrastructure) with stdout/stderr Metrics Visualizations of metrics extracted from check commands (gauges, sparklines, charts) Commands Execute start, stop, or custom commands with live terminal output Logs Agent log tail for this component with search and filtering Config Component configuration: commands, intervals, timeouts, environment variables

Detail Panel — component status, check results, metrics, and command execution

docs.title: Multi-Site View
docs.text:
When an application is configured with site overrides (primary + DR), the Map View displays split-panel component nodes showing the status on each site simultaneously.

This gives operators instant visibility into both the primary and disaster recovery deployments without switching views.

Multi-Site View — primary and DR status side by side on each component node

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: AppControl supports seven core operations. Every operation is logged in the audit trail before execution begins.

docs.title: Full Application Start
docs.text:
Starts all components following the dependency graph bottom-up:

  • Components with no dependencies start first
  • Each component waits for its dependencies to reach RUNNING
  • Components at the same level start in parallel
  • Progress is tracked per-component with real-time updates on the map

docs.title: Full Application Stop
docs.text:
Stops all components in reverse dependency order (top-down):

  • Components with no dependents stop first
  • Each component waits for all its dependents to reach STOPPED
  • Configurable timeout per component with force-stop option

docs.title: Error Branch Restart
docs.text:
When a component fails, AppControl identifies the error branch: the failed component and all its dependents (highlighted in pink on the map).

The restart sequence: 1. Stop all components in the error branch (top-down) 2. Restart the root cause component 3. Start all dependent components (bottom-up) once the root is running

This avoids restarting the entire application when only a subset is affected.

docs.title: DR Site Switchover
docs.text:
Migrates an application from the primary site to the DR site in six phases:

Phase Name Description 1 Pre-check Validate DR site readiness: agents connected, resources available 2 Quiesce Gracefully stop incoming traffic and drain active sessions 3 Stop Primary Stop all components on the primary site (reverse DAG) 4 Data Sync Verify data replication is complete and consistent 5 Start DR Start all components on the DR site (DAG order) 6 Validate Run health checks to confirm successful switchover

Each phase is logged and can be monitored in real time. Rollback is available during phases 1-3.

Cross-site detection: Before switchover, the system checks if components are already running on the target site (via cross-site probe). If detected, a warning is displayed to the operator.

docs.title: Custom Commands
docs.text: Execute predefined commands on specific components: log rotation, cache clearing, configuration reload, database maintenance, or any custom operation. Commands are subject to permission checks and fully audited.

docs.title: Dry Run Simulation
docs.text:
Simulate any operation without making changes:

  • Validates the DAG and dependency order
  • Checks agent connectivity and user permissions
  • Reports the expected execution sequence
  • Identifies potential issues before they happen

Always recommended before switchovers or large-scale operations in production.

docs.title: Diagnostic & Rebuild
docs.text:
A fresh, site-scoped assessment collects health, configured integrity and independent infrastructure evidence. The result distinguishes runtime restart, application repair and infrastructure reconstruction. Unavailable evidence is reported as unknown; it is not inferred from a component's previous green state.

Review the dry-run, actions, missing-contract blockers and dependency impact. Execution stops consumers in reverse DAG order, verifies a dedicated stop proof, then restores each dependency level with infrastructure, integrity, network, health and post-start gates. A failed command or mandatory proof stops recovery. The meaning of each check is supplied by the application's configured command; AppControl does not provide a built-in bank data-consistency or firewall test.

Users with Manage permission can prepare and execute reconstruction. An explicit confirmation is required, and the returned operation identifier has its own persisted status, steps and errors. A component's live state and an HTTP 202 response are not substitutes for that operation's completed result.

The MCP server exposes the same engine through rebuild_app; review its dry-run before an explicitly confirmed execution. For the demonstration, use the single operator runbook. External jobs and business figures in that package are explicitly labelled simulators.

Configured business projections derive availability from the required components and dependencies. Unknown component references are not silently considered healthy. Personas select a projection and do not confer component permissions.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Agents are lightweight Rust binaries deployed on monitored servers. They execute health checks, start/stop commands, and report status back through the gateway using mTLS.

The Agents page shows:

  • All registered agents with connection status (connected, disconnected)
  • Heartbeat timestamps and latency
  • Agent version and OS information
  • Number of components managed by each agent
  • System metrics (CPU, memory, disk) when available

Communication uses delta-only sync: agents send only state changes, not full status on every check cycle.

Agents — monitor connected agents, heartbeat status, and managed components

docs.title: Gateways
docs.text:
Gateways are the communication hubs between agents and the backend. Each site or zone has its own gateway. Agents connect to their zone's gateway via mTLS WebSocket.

The Gateways page shows:

  • Registered gateways with connection status
  • Associated site and zone
  • Number of agents connected through each gateway
  • Gateway version and uptime

Gateways — manage communication hubs and monitor agent connections

docs.title: Sites
docs.text:
Sites represent physical or logical locations: datacenters, DR sites, staging environments. Every application and gateway belongs to a site.

Site types: primary (production), dr (disaster recovery), staging, development.

Sites are configured at setup time and used during DR switchover operations to orchestrate transitions between locations.

Sites — configure datacenters, DR sites, and environments

docs.title: Hostings
docs.text:
A hosting groups related sites by physical datacenter or cloud region. For example, "Datacenter Paris" might contain sites prod-paris and staging-paris.

Key features: - Create hostings and assign sites to them from the Hostings admin page - During switchover, sites are grouped by hosting so operators can identify intra-hosting vs. cross-hosting failovers - The hosting name appears as a badge on the Sites page and in JSON exports

Hostings — group sites by datacenter or cloud region

docs.title: Cross-Site Probe
docs.text:
When a DR binding profile exists, AppControl automatically monitors the passive site to detect if a component is unexpectedly running there (e.g., started manually outside AppControl).

How it works: 1. Every 5 minutes, the backend sends the component's check_cmd to the passive site's agent 2. If the check succeeds (exit code 0), the component is flagged as running on the wrong site 3. A DUAL warning badge appears on the component in the map view 4. A CrossSiteAlert WebSocket event is broadcast to connected clients

This prevents "split-brain" scenarios where the same application runs on both sites simultaneously after a manual intervention.

docs.title: Enrollment Tokens
docs.text:
New agents and gateways are onboarded using enrollment tokens for secure, authenticated registration.

Enrollment workflow:

  1. An administrator generates an enrollment token (scoped to agent or gateway)
  2. The token is provided during installation via CLI flag or config file
  3. On first connection, the component presents the token and receives mTLS certificates
  4. The token is single-use and expires after a configurable duration

Enrollment Tokens — generate and manage secure registration tokens

docs.title: User Management
docs.text:
Manage all users in your organization. Users can be created manually or auto-provisioned through OIDC/SAML on first login.

User roles:

Role Scope Capabilities Admin Organization-wide Full platform access, manage users/teams/sites/agents Operator Per-application Start, stop, restart where granted operate permission Editor Per-application Modify configuration where granted edit permission Viewer Per-application Read-only access to maps, logs, and reports

Users — manage accounts, roles, and organization membership

docs.title: Team Management
docs.text:
Teams group users for collective permission assignment. When a team is granted access to an application, all current and future members inherit that permission.

Effective permission = MAX(direct user permission, team permissions). Team membership never reduces access.

Teams — organize users into groups for collective permission management

docs.title: Sharing & Permissions
docs.text:
Applications can be shared with users and teams through a Google Docs-style sharing dialog:

  • User search with autocomplete — find users by name or email
  • Permission level selector — view, operate, edit, manage, or owner
  • Share links — generate time-limited, use-limited links for convenient access
  • Bulk operations — share with multiple users or teams at once

All permission changes are recorded in the audit trail.

docs.title: Reports & Compliance
docs.text:
AppControl provides comprehensive reporting aligned with DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) requirements.

Report Description Availability Uptime/downtime metrics per application and component over configurable periods Incidents Failure timeline with root causes, resolution times, and impacted components Switchover History DR switchover history with phase-by-phase timing and outcomes Audit Trail Complete action log: every user action with timestamps and details RTO Analysis Recovery Time Objective analysis comparing actual vs. configured targets

Reports support configurable date ranges, drill-down from summary to component-level detail, and PDF export for regulatory submission.

Reports — DORA compliance metrics, availability charts, and incident timelines

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The Settings page provides access to system configuration, user profile management, and platform preferences.

Configurable options:

  • User profile (name, email, password)
  • Notification preferences (email, webhook, in-app)
  • OIDC/SAML identity provider configuration
  • Organization settings
  • Certificate management and PKI rotation

Settings — system configuration and user preferences

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
API keys enable programmatic access for scheduler integration, automation scripts, and CI/CD pipelines.

Creating an API key:

  1. Navigate to Settings > API Keys
  2. Click Create API Key
  3. Provide a descriptive name (e.g., "Control-M Production")
  4. Copy the generated key immediately — it won't be shown again

Key format: ac_<uuid> — passed via Authorization: Bearer ac_<uuid>

Keys are stored as SHA-256 hashes (plaintext never stored), revocable at any time, and all usage is fully audited.

API Keys — create, manage, and revoke programmatic access keys

docs.title: Supervision Mode
docs.text:
The Supervision Mode provides a full-screen NOC display designed for operations centers and wall monitors.

Features:

  • Auto-rotating views across all monitored applications
  • Large, high-contrast status indicators optimized for wall displays
  • Configurable rotation interval
  • Alert highlighting for failed or degraded applications
  • No sidebar or navigation chrome — maximum screen real estate

Access via the /supervision route or press F11 from any page.

Supervision Mode — full-screen NOC display for operations centers

docs.title: Component Catalog
docs.text:
The Component Catalog allows you to define custom component types specific to your organization. Each catalog entry includes an icon, color, category, and optional default commands that are pre-filled when a user creates a component of that type.

Built-in types: database, middleware, appserver, webfront, service, batch, custom, application

docs.title: Initializing the Catalog
docs.text:
Use the CLI to seed the built-in types and import custom ones:

# Seed the 8 built-in component types (idempotent)
appcontrol.sh init-catalog

# Import custom types from a JSON file
appcontrol.sh import-catalog --file catalog.json

# List all types in the catalog
appcontrol.sh list-catalog

docs.title: Catalog Import Format
docs.text:
The import file is a JSON object with an entries array:

{
  "entries": [
    {
      "type_key": "oracle-rac",
      "label": "Oracle RAC Cluster",
      "description": "Oracle Real Application Clusters",
      "icon": "database",
      "color": "#F80000",
      "category": "database",
      "default_check_cmd": "srvctl status database -d ${DB_NAME}",
      "default_start_cmd": "srvctl start database -d ${DB_NAME}",
      "default_stop_cmd": "srvctl stop database -d ${DB_NAME}"
    },
    {
      "type_key": "controlm-job",
      "label": "Control-M Job",
      "icon": "calendar",
      "color": "#E31837",
      "category": "scheduler",
      "default_check_cmd": "ctmpsm -LISTALL | grep ${JOB_NAME}"
    }
  ]
}
Field Required Description type_key yes Unique slug identifier (e.g., oracle-rac, kafka-connect) label yes Display name shown in the UI description no Tooltip description icon no Lucide icon name: database, layers, server, globe, cog, clock, zap, shield, network, calendar, terminal, box (default) color no Hex color for the icon (default: #455A64) category no Grouping in the palette (e.g., database, middleware, scheduler) default_check_cmd no Pre-filled check command when this type is selected default_start_cmd no Pre-filled start command default_stop_cmd no Pre-filled stop command default_env_vars no Default environment variables as JSON object display_order no Sort order in the palette (default: 0)

Duplicate type_key values are skipped during import (not overwritten).

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
# List catalog entries
GET /api/v1/catalog/component-types

# Create a custom type (admin only)
POST /api/v1/catalog/component-types

# Update a type (admin only)
PUT /api/v1/catalog/component-types/:id

# Delete a custom type (admin only, built-in types cannot be deleted)
DELETE /api/v1/catalog/component-types/:id

# Bulk import (admin only)
POST /api/v1/catalog/component-types/import

# Seed built-in types (admin only, idempotent)
POST /api/v1/catalog/component-types/seed

docs.title: UI Integration
docs.text:
Once catalog entries are loaded, they appear in:

  • Component Palette (drag & drop): dynamically populated with search/filter when more than 8 types, grouped by category
  • Component Editor (type selector): searchable dropdown with icon previews, category labels, and automatic pre-fill of default commands

docs.title: Scheduler Integration
docs.text:
AppControl integrates with enterprise schedulers via REST API and CLI. It is designed to be called by schedulers, not to replace them.

Supported schedulers: Control-M, AutoSys, Dollar Universe, TWS

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
# Start an application (returns operation ID)
curl -X POST https://appcontrol/api/v1/apps/{id}/start \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ac_<api-key>"

# Check application status
curl https://appcontrol/api/v1/apps/{id} \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ac_<api-key>"

docs.title: CLI (appctl)
docs.text:
# Start and wait for completion
appctl app start --name "Trading Platform" --wait --timeout 300

# Check status
appctl app status --name "Trading Platform" --format json

# Stop a specific component
appctl component stop --app "Trading Platform" --component "Order Service"

docs.title: TLS Architecture
docs.text:
EXTERNAL NETWORK
  Browsers/CLI  ────► :443  (HTTPS via nginx)
  Agents        ────► :4443 (WSS mTLS direct to gateway)
                         │
           ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
           ▼                           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │  NGINX (web UI) │       │  GATEWAY (zone)  │
  │  /api/* → :3000 │       │  :4443 direct    │
  │  /     → :8080  │       │  mTLS for agents │
  └─────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘

docs.title: Certificate Security (5 Layers)
docs.text:
1. Token-based enrollment — SHA-256 hashed, scoped, expirable, revocable
  2. mTLS — per-organization CA, mutual authentication on every connection
  3. Certificate pinning — fingerprint verified on every reconnect
  4. Certificate revocation — real-time revocation deactivates agents/gateways immediately
  5. Audit trail — all enrollment and certificate events logged in append-only tables

docs.title: Certificate Rotation
docs.text:
Seamless CA migration without downtime:

  1. Import new CA certificate
  2. Dual-trust period — both CAs trusted
  3. Agents automatically request new certificates
  4. Monitor progress in the UI
  5. Finalize — remove old CA

docs.title: Authentication Methods
docs.text: Method Use Case OIDC Browser SSO (Keycloak, Okta, Azure AD) SAML 2.0 Enterprise SSO (ADFS, Azure AD) API Keys Machine-to-machine (schedulers, CI/CD) Local Development and standalone deployments

docs.title: Approval Workflows (4-Eyes)
docs.text:
For critical operations in regulated environments:

  1. Operator initiates an operation requiring approval
  2. Approvers receive notifications and review details
  3. Once required approvals are reached, the operation executes automatically
  4. All decisions are recorded in the audit trail

docs.title: Break-Glass Emergency Access
docs.text:
Bypass normal permissions in emergencies:

  • Immediate access with justification required
  • High-priority alert sent to all administrators
  • Time-limited window (default: 30 minutes)
  • Every action logged with break-glass flag
  • Mandatory post-incident review

Screenshots are auto-generated by CI from the running application. To regenerate, run npm run screenshots from the frontend/ directory with the full stack running, or trigger the docs-screenshots workflow manually.

docs.title: Recovery evidence and configured projections
docs.text:
The Recovery lens includes a preparation inventory of each component's base commands and assigned agents. Expand a component to find missing declarations and open its existing configuration. This inventory is not an execution verdict: site overrides, fresh observations and blockers are resolved by the backend when you assess a concrete recovery plan.

Under Operations & diagnosis, expand Backend, gateway and agents to inspect the control path and the configured runtime and infrastructure assignments. The backend authorizes, plans and records; the gateway relays; agents execute configured commands or invoke external tools and return evidence. An independent infrastructure agent only helps while that agent and its own dependencies remain available.

Selecting dependencies, impact or an infrastructure asset preserves each card's state background and border. Context is shown with an outer outline, labels and edges; the mini-map also keeps state colors. STARTING and STOPPING are blue, STOPPED is gray, FAILED is red and RUNNING is green.

A reconstruction plan is scoped to an explicit site. Review fresh health, integrity and infrastructure evidence, missing-command blockers and dependency order before confirming. Network checks then gate each service start during execution. Track the returned operation identifier and its final result; an accepted HTTP request or a component's previous green state is not completion. The recovery workflow stops on failed mandatory checks or commands. Runtime restart, application rebuild and infrastructure rebuild are distinct choices. Selecting a reconstruction site does not silently perform a site failover.

Business personas and architecture lenses are configured projections, not component access controls. Effective permissions remain determined by roles, teams and application sharing. Infrastructure inventory can declare shared assets; a declared status is displayed separately from an observed component or agent state.

Metric metadata supports units, precision and threshold direction; synthetic data retains its visible provenance. Each metric shows the timestamp and exit code of the check that produced it. The map and metric panels refresh every five seconds and after recovery reaches a terminal result. Values from before a reconstruction remain visible with an explicit waiting-for-fresh-check notice until a newer check arrives. Preparing another site does not establish fresh evidence for the nominal site. The operation panel first confirms acceptance, then displays the recorded completion or failure; acceptance alone is never presented as recovery success.

The banking demo's HTTP simulator jobs are correlated with the AppControl operation, and its second Retail application uses the same contracts. Neither demo is evidence of a connection to Digital.ai or a bank cloud. See the single operator runbook.

docs.title: Application knowledge and reviewed map proposals
docs.text:
The Application knowledge page adds a native repository-to-map workflow. Select an existing application, submit selected UTF-8 text sources and PNG/JPEG diagrams with their full source commit, then inspect the extracted assertions, verbatim evidence and audit. The same app-scoped API is available to CI and through the MCP tools get_application_knowledge, ingest_application_sources and propose_application_map.

Configure KNOWLEDGE_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and KNOWLEDGE_ANTHROPIC_MODEL on the backend to enable model extraction. This path sends selected source content to Anthropic. The explicit-claims API supports offline structured ingestion without calling a model. Do not submit secrets; the CI collector's credential checks are conservative checks, not a full DLP system.

Bundles are limited to 100 sources, 100 KB per text source, 750 KB per image before base64 encoding, and 1.5 MB total encoded source content. PDF, Word and arbitrary external repositories are not fetched by this first version. PNG/JPEG diagrams are interpreted by the vision model; their labels and arrows require human review. The CI collector reads explicitly allowlisted blobs from the checked-out Git commit, ignores generated knowledge as evidence, and refuses symlinks. Removed sources are retained and marked withdrawn; automatic publication is blocked pending reconciliation. Updates do not silently delete components or startup dependencies.

Knowledge revisions are immutable. Every text claim identifies its source and verbatim excerpt; command values must occur in that excerpt. Image claims preserve a model transcription, not a deterministically verified quotation. Images cannot supply executable commands. Approval requires acknowledgment of the exact image source hashes included in the proposal. This verifies provenance, not semantic correctness or operational safety. Missing procedures, conflicting command/type values, unknown startup targets and cycles block map proposals. No model confidence score authorizes publication.

Assign execution agents explicitly before requesting a proposal. Agents must belong to the application's organization and site. A proposal contains an immutable before/after diff, stable component IDs, source commit and digest. The initial projection handles basic shell-command components; native-command, referenced-application and cluster component changes require manual reconciliation and cannot be published through this projection.

An account with Edit permission can ingest and propose. A different human account with Manage permission approves the exact digest in AppControl; API keys cannot approve. A publishing account with Manage permission may then apply the approved proposal. API key profiles Map design (read, design) and Map publication (read, publish) restrict the two automation identities independently, intersecting account and site permissions. GitHub PR review does not itself replace the native approval record.

Publication uses a transaction and an application operation lock. It rejects a newer knowledge revision or concurrent changes to the projected map fields (identity, name, type, shell lifecycle commands, agent and dependencies). Other component settings remain unchanged. It preserves component IDs, records a configuration snapshot and publication receipt, and does not reapply an already published unchanged map. It may cause assigned agents to begin their regular health checks; it does not request application start/stop/rebuild.

Runnable CI conductor and workflow templates are in integrations/knowledge-agent/. Install them in the application repository, protect the workflows and target branch, configure separate design/publication secrets and the publishing environment. Source changes trigger consolidation and a map PR; generated-artifact changes do not recursively trigger ingestion. The templates have not, by their presence alone, configured repository protection or verified procedures in a sandbox. Test the proposed commands in an isolated environment before approving them for operational use.

docs.title: Windows Server: standalone evaluation
docs.text:
This is the recommended way to evaluate AppControl on an internal Windows Server. It installs the web interface, backend, gateway and agent without Docker and without a separate database server. Data is stored in an embedded SQLite database.

When to use this mode

Use it for a customer evaluation, a proof of concept, a demo, or a small single-server installation. For a durable shared production service, use Docker Compose on Linux or OpenShift with PostgreSQL.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Windows Server 2019 or later, x64
  • Windows PowerShell 5.1 or later
  • an account allowed to download release assets from GitHub
  • administrator rights only if you enable startup at boot or open firewall ports

Docker, Rust, Node.js and PostgreSQL are not required.

docs.title: Install in a few minutes
docs.text:
Open PowerShell in the directory where AppControl should keep its data:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\AppControl | Out-Null
Set-Location C:\AppControl

Invoke-WebRequest `
  -Uri "https://github.com/xcomponent/appcontrol-release/releases/latest/download/appcontrol.ps1" `
  -OutFile appcontrol.ps1

.\appcontrol.ps1 install -Email "admin@my-company.example" -Password "replace-this-password"
.\appcontrol.ps1 start
.\appcontrol.ps1 add-site "Evaluation"

Open http://localhost:3000, then sign in with the email and password passed to install.

From another workstation, use http://SERVER_NAME:3000 and open the port once in Windows Firewall:

New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "AppControl Web" `
  -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 3000 -Action Allow

The gateway listens on port 4443 by default. Open that port only when agents on other servers must connect to this gateway:

New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "AppControl Gateway" `
  -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 4443 -Action Allow

docs.title: Start automatically after reboot
docs.text:
Run PowerShell as Administrator:

Set-Location C:\AppControl
.\appcontrol.ps1 enable-autostart

This creates a Windows scheduled task running under SYSTEM. To remove it:

.\appcontrol.ps1 disable-autostart

docs.title: Daily operations
docs.text:
Action Command Check all processes .\appcontrol.ps1 status Start .\appcontrol.ps1 start Stop .\appcontrol.ps1 stop Read recent logs .\appcontrol.ps1 logs Add a site .\appcontrol.ps1 add-site "Site name" [gateway-port] Upgrade .\appcontrol.ps1 upgrade

An upgrade replaces only binaries and the web interface. The database, configuration and site definitions are preserved.

User, team, site, hosting, map and catalog commands are documented once in the PowerShell command reference.

docs.title: Backup and uninstall
docs.text:
Stop AppControl before copying its data:

.\appcontrol.ps1 stop
Copy-Item C:\AppControl\data C:\Backup\AppControl\data -Recurse -Force
Copy-Item C:\AppControl\config C:\Backup\AppControl\config -Recurse -Force

To uninstall, stop AppControl, disable automatic startup, then archive or remove C:\AppControl. No system-wide database or container runtime remains.

docs.title: Directory layout
docs.text:
C:\AppControl\
  appcontrol.ps1
  bin\          downloaded executables
  config\       configuration and sites (preserved by upgrade)
  data\         SQLite database and agent state (preserved by upgrade)
  frontend\     web interface
  logs\         component logs

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text: The quick install serves HTTP directly. It is suitable on a protected internal network for evaluation. Do not expose port 3000 to the Internet. For a production deployment, put it behind the company HTTPS reverse proxy, change the initial password, restrict firewall access, and follow the hardening checklist.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
.\appcontrol.ps1 status
.\appcontrol.ps1 logs
Get-Content .\logs\backend.err.log -Tail 100

If PowerShell blocks the script for the current process:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass

docs.title: Windows Server production with PostgreSQL
docs.text:
This deployment runs AppControl and PostgreSQL as native Windows services. It does not use Docker Desktop and it uses the PostgreSQL backend rather than the standalone SQLite backend.

Use the standalone installer for a quick customer evaluation. Use this page when the Windows installation must retain production data in PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Choose the database location
docs.text:
Mode Command option Use when Install PostgreSQL locally -PostgresMode Install A self-contained single-server installation is acceptable Existing PostgreSQL -PostgresMode Existing The organization operates a shared, managed or highly available database

For a critical production service, an externally managed PostgreSQL instance is preferable: AppControl and its database then do not share the same failure domain.

docs.title: Local PostgreSQL: automated installation
docs.text:
Open Windows PowerShell as Administrator:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force C:\AppControl-Install | Out-Null
Set-Location C:\AppControl-Install

Invoke-WebRequest `
  -Uri "https://github.com/xcomponent/appcontrol-release/releases/latest/download/appcontrol-windows-server.ps1" `
  -OutFile appcontrol-windows-server.ps1

.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 install `
  -PostgresMode Install `
  -AdminEmail "admin@my-company.example"

The script:

  1. downloads the pinned PostgreSQL 16 installer from EDB;
  2. verifies its SHA-256 checksum;
  3. installs PostgreSQL server and command-line tools as a Windows service;
  4. creates a dedicated appcontrol role and database;
  5. downloads the PostgreSQL AppControl backend and web interface;
  6. installs the backend as an automatic Windows service;
  7. verifies the application health endpoint.

Generated credentials are stored in C:\ProgramData\AppControl\secrets\installation-secrets.txt. Its ACL grants access only to SYSTEM and local administrators. Move those credentials into the organization password vault, then protect or remove the bootstrap file according to company policy.

Open http://localhost:3000.

The administrator, database role and PostgreSQL superuser passwords can be provided explicitly:

.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 install `
  -PostgresMode Install `
  -AdminEmail "admin@my-company.example" `
  -AdminPassword "APP_PASSWORD" `
  -DatabasePassword "DATABASE_ROLE_PASSWORD" `
  -PostgresSuperuserPassword "POSTGRES_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD" `
  -BackendPort 3000 `
  -PostgresPort 5432

If a password is omitted, the script generates a strong random value. See all Windows/PostgreSQL installer options, including custom directories, internal release mirrors and PostgreSQL installer pinning.

docs.title: Create sites, users and teams
docs.text:
The production script exposes the same administration commands as the standalone script:

.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 add-site "Paris" 4443
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 create-user "alice@company.example" "Alice Martin"
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 create-team "Production"
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 add-member "Production" "alice@company.example"
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 list-users

See the canonical PowerShell command reference for sites, hosting groups, permissions, maps and the component catalog.

docs.title: Existing PostgreSQL
docs.text:
The database and role must already exist. Include sslmode=require when the database endpoint supports TLS:

.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 install `
  -PostgresMode Existing `
  -DatabaseUrl "postgresql://appcontrol:PASSWORD@postgres.internal:5432/appcontrol?sslmode=require" `
  -AdminEmail "admin@my-company.example"

The connection string is stored in the private environment block of the AppControlBackend Windows service, not as a machine-wide environment variable. Local administrators can still read it; use a dedicated, least-privileged PostgreSQL role.

The existing PostgreSQL service must permit the role to connect to the selected database and create/alter the application schema through migrations. The installer does not create or modify the remote PostgreSQL server itself.

docs.title: Status and removal
docs.text:
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 status
.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 uninstall

Uninstall removes the AppControl Windows service but deliberately preserves PostgreSQL and all data.

docs.title: Installer pinning and internal mirrors
docs.text:
The script pins a tested PostgreSQL maintenance release and checksum. An organization can mirror the installer internally:

.\appcontrol-windows-server.ps1 install `
  -PostgresMode Install `
  -PostgresInstallerUrl "https://packages.internal/postgresql-16-windows-x64.exe" `
  -PostgresInstallerSha256 "EXPECTED_SHA256"

Never disable checksum verification.

docs.title: Before production
docs.text:
• put port 3000 behind the company IIS or reverse proxy with HTTPS;
  • do not expose PostgreSQL port 5432 outside the required network scope;
  • store generated secrets in the password vault;
  • configure PostgreSQL backups and test a restore;
  • review hardening, backup and restore and upgrade.

docs.title: Network Topology
docs.text:
+------------------+
                        |    Browser /     |
                        |    appctl CLI    |
                        +--------+---------+

                                 | or HTTP :3000 (direct API)

                   |        :80/:443            |

                   |  /api/*  --> backend:3000  |
                   |  /ws     --> backend:3000  |

                   +-------------+--------------+

                    HTTP/WS (internal network)
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
         v                                               v
+------------------+                          +-------------------+
|    Backend API   |                          |    PostgreSQL 16  |
|    :3000         |                          |    :5432          |
|                  +------- sqlx pool ------->+                   |
|  REST API        |                          +-------------------+
|  WebSocket /ws   |
|  (JWT auth)      |
+--------+---------+
         |
         | WebSocket /ws/gateway
         | (internal, gateway connects here)
         |
+--------+---------+       +------------------+
|    Gateway PRD   |       |    Gateway DR    |
|    :4443         |       |    :4443         |
|                  |       |                  |

| to agents (mTLS) |       | to agents (mTLS) |
+---+-----------+--+       +---+-----------+--+
    |           |              |           |
    | WSS :4443 | WSS :4443    | WSS :4443 | WSS :4443

    v           v              v           v
+--------+ +--------+      +--------+ +--------+
| Agent  | | Agent  |      | Agent  | | Agent  |
| srv-01 | | srv-02 |      | dr-01  | | dr-02  |
+--------+ +--------+      +--------+ +--------+

Note: Agents connect DIRECTLY to gateways, NOT through nginx.
      Each gateway is exposed on its own IP/DNS.

docs.title: Component Roles
docs.text:
Component Role Inbound Port Config Source nginx TLS termination for web UI :80/:443 nginx.conf Frontend React SPA :8080 (internal) Build-time env Backend REST API + WebSocket hub + FSM engine :3000 (internal) Env vars only Gateway Agent connection multiplexer (one per zone) :4443 (exposed directly) YAML + env var overrides Agent Local process manager + health checker None (client only) YAML + env var overrides CLI CLI client for automation/schedulers None (client only) Env vars + CLI args PostgreSQL Persistent storage :5432 Standard

Important: Gateways are exposed directly on their own IP/port (e.g., gateway-prd.company.com:4443). They do NOT go through nginx. Each zone (PRD, DR, DMZ) has its own gateway.

docs.title: Communication Protocols
docs.text:
Browser ---HTTPS---> nginx:443 ---HTTP---> backend:3000
                                     (proxy_pass /api/* and /ws)
                               ---HTTP---> frontend:8080
                                     (proxy_pass /* for SPA)

appctl  ---HTTP(S)---> backend:3000
                       (direct API calls, no nginx needed)

Gateway ---WebSocket---> backend:3000/ws/gateway
          (internal, persistent connection, reconnect on failure)

Agent ---WSS (mTLS)---> gateway:4443/ws
         (DIRECT connection, not through nginx)
         (outbound only, reconnect with exponential backoff 1s..60s)

docs.title: Agent → Gateway (WSS, mTLS)
docs.text:
• Agent initiates outbound WebSocket connection to gateway
  • No inbound port needed on the agent (firewall-friendly)
  • mTLS: agent presents its certificate, gateway verifies it
  • WSS on port 443/4443 passes through most corporate firewalls (indistinguishable from HTTPS traffic)
  • Automatic reconnect with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s... max 60s)
  • Offline buffer: agent stores messages locally if gateway is unreachable

docs.title: Gateway → Backend (WebSocket)
docs.text:
• Gateway connects to backend WebSocket endpoint
  • Routes messages bidirectionally: agents ↔ backend
  • Reconnect on disconnect with configurable interval
  • In-memory message buffer during backend unavailability

docs.title: Frontend → Backend (via nginx)
docs.text:
• nginx proxies /api/* to backend:3000/api/
  • nginx proxies /ws to backend:3000/ws (WebSocket upgrade)
  • All other routes serve the React SPA (client-side routing)

docs.title: CLI → Backend (HTTP)
docs.text:
• Direct HTTP calls to backend REST API
  • No nginx/frontend needed
  • Configured via APPCONTROL_URL env var or --url CLI arg
  • Exit codes designed for scheduler integration (0=OK, 1=Fail, 2=Timeout)
